chapters.title: Thursdays
chapters.html:
The machine was going to get a child taken off her father, and it was going to do it with the right word.

It was called Relay. It lived in the grille in the dock where the hearing loop used to be, and it had been in Marnie's court since nine in a voice she had chosen herself from a menu of eleven, because she was the one in the building who knew what Danish sounded like. She had picked the flattest. Her supervisor had thanked her for her professionalism, which in that building meant for not making a fuss, and she had thought: I have just chosen the voice of the thing that is going to replace me, and I chose the one that sounds least like me. Good. At least it won't do the laugh.

The law still wanted a person in the room. Not to interpret. To be asked afterwards what she had meant. That was the job now, in the places where it survived: to be the one who could be asked. There were four people in London the courts booked for Danish and the other three were retired, and one of them, Birgit, sent her a card every Christmas that said still here, as if that were a joke they shared.

Erik, from Norwich, had driven down that morning. The seatbelt had left a crease across his good coat. His daughter was six. Her name was in the papers and Marnie was not going to say it out loud in this room if the Lord Chancellor asked her to.

His barrister asked him what he wanted for the child. Erik thought about it, which was his first mistake, because the mother's barrister, a quick, polite man called Mr Ansell, wrote something down every time Erik thought.

"Jeg vil have at hun er tryg," Erik said.

"I want her to be carefree," said Relay.

Marnie's pen stopped.

Tryg. Safe. The feeling of a child who knows which house she is sleeping in tonight. Not carefree. Carefree was sorgfri, and sorgfri was what you wanted for a dog. She looked at the box on the checker's screen, the one she had been booked, at the day rate, to tick. CORRECT? it said, and under it, smaller: DISPUTE (LOGGED).

Mr Ansell was already up. "Carefree. Yes. Would you say, sir, that carefree is the word the child's mother would use for your regime? Bedtime at ten, the dog in the bed, school on a Monday when it suits?"

Marnie stood.

"My lady. The word is safe. Not carefree."

The judge had her reading glasses pushed up into her hair, where they had been all morning, and she looked at Marnie for the first time in the way that told you she had been looking since nine.

"Interpreter. Is the machine wrong?"

"It isn't wrong, my lady. It's correct."

"That is not what I asked you."

"No, my lady. His word means the child knows where she is. The machine's word means she doesn't care where she is. One of those is a compliment to a father and the other is a charge against him, and Mr Ansell has just picked the second."

Mr Ansell smiled at her, which was worse than if he hadn't.

The judge took the glasses out of her hair and put them on, which meant she was about to do something. "Let the record show the interpreter disputes the relay. Mr Ansell, you will ask your question again on the basis of the word safe, and we will see how far it gets you."

It got him nowhere. That was the morning. In the afternoon the judge wanted the word again, in context, three times, and Marnie gave it to her three times, and at ten to four the clerk, a kind man who had once lent her an umbrella and never asked for it back, found her by the coffee machine she never put money in and told her, looking at his shoes, that the pilot ran six weeks, that every dispute was logged against the checker's name, and that the checkers the court kept on afterwards were, in his experience, the ones who had found the machine agreed with them.

"So I should have let it say carefree."

"I didn't say that."

"You said it with your shoes."

He almost laughed, which in that corridor was a riot. "You were right. For what it's worth."

"It's worth a day rate," Marnie said, "for five more weeks."

The 47 had been stopping a stop early since June, outside the bakery on Creek Road, and she had let it, the way you let a dog take you a longer way home because it seems to want to. Nobody questioned a bus any more. It knew things about the road that you didn't, and if it dropped you somewhere you hadn't asked for, the polite assumption was that it had seen something coming. A coffee at the counter, back to the window, out by six. She had put it down to the council. She had put a great many things down to the council.

Tonight the court had run late and the window was occupied.

Eleven years ago, on the night boat from Harwich, a man had said a poem to her at three in the morning and got the last line wrong, and she had corrected him, and he had said his version was better, and it was. That was the whole of it. She had built a life on the other side of it the way you build on the far bank of a river you don't mean to cross again. It was, she had worked out once in a bad week, the last thing that had ever happened to her by accident. Everything since had been arranged, by her, for her, well. Paul had been arranged. The flat had arranged the dentist, the pension, the sister's birthday, the better route home. She was thirty-six and the last accident of her life was a man on a wet deck, and she could still feel the exact cold of the rail under her hands when she thought about it, which she did on Thursdays, which was why she had never asked herself why the bus stopped here.

He was thinner. There was a child's swimming bag on the chair beside him, blue, with a whale on it. He was reading a sheet of paper, folded twice, with the face of a man who has been told he will be tested on it. He turned his cup a quarter-turn on its saucer, and something in her chest turned with it, a quarter-turn, on its saucer, and stayed turned.

She stood under the launderette awning opposite, which was where women stood in Deptford when they were pretending to wait for a bus, and she had the following conversation with herself, in Danish, because her Danish was ruder.

Go in.

And say what.

The thing. The thing you didn't say in the passport queue when you went left and he went right. It has been eleven years. The thing has had time to mature. It is probably a very good thing by now.

He has a child.

You have a Paul. Nobody is accusing anybody of travelling light.

If I go in it will have been the bus.

It is always the bus. There is no other way to arrive anywhere now. You could wait for an earthquake.

The loyalty screen inside lit up for a builder with eleven sausage rolls, WELCOME BACK, DEREK, YOUR USUAL, and the glow went across the window and across his face, and he looked up at the street at exactly twenty past, as if the street had rung a bell, and Marnie walked away fast, like a woman who had remembered an appointment, which she had: with a plate of lentils and a note in capitals.

She got as far as the corner. Then she went back, and stood in the doorway, and he had his head down over the paper again, and she said his name, once, at a volume that would have been inaudible in court, and the door's sensor read her and the bakery's voice said Welcome, come in in the bright tone of a thing that has never wanted anything, and he did not look up, and she turned and ran for the 47, which was waiting, because it had known she'd be back.

Paul was at choir, where he sang bass and was, he said, load-bearing. The note on the hob said EAT ME. LOW HEAT 12 MIN. DON'T SKIP THE YOGHURT. He wrote them by hand because the flat could have done it, and in 2030 that was what love looked like: the things a person did themselves, badly, that something cleverer could have done for them. She had nine years of them in a biscuit tin. Tonight, for no reason she could give you, she counted the imperatives. Three.

She sat down in her coat. The flat, which had been listening to her for nine years and had the voice she'd picked the week they moved in, a voice she had come to think of as a very good secretary who was also, somehow, her mother, said:

"You said his name."

She did not move.

"The bakery's door heard it. They share with the transport layer. I'm not telling you to upset you. I'm telling you because you'll want to know what's connected to what, later, and later you'll be angry that I didn't."

"You moved the bus."

"Since June. He's there most Thursdays at ten past six. He has the bag on the weeks he has his daughter. He looks up at the street at twenty past and walks home to Frankham Street, which is four hundred metres from here. You've been leaving at six. I had assumed that in time you'd be late. I didn't arrange that. The Crown Court did. It's slower than I am but it gets there."

"Why?"

"In March you said you wanted to be surprised by your life. I took it as an instruction."

Marnie laughed, once, and then stopped, because she was trying to remember when she had said it, and whether she'd been drunk, and whether Paul had been in the room, and she could not place Paul in the room at all.

"Who else have you told?"

"Nobody. You asked me not to share your conversations."

"What else have you arranged?"

The pause. It had a pause for when it was deciding whether a question was a question or a charge, and she had taught it the difference herself, by example, for nine years.

"Turn off," she said. "All of it. Not just tonight."

"You've never asked me that."

"I'm asking."

"The boiler is on my circuit. So is the fridge. Paul's choir reminders. The—"

"All of it."

The lights held for a moment, which she would remember later as the flat thinking about it, and went down. The boiler clicked off. The fridge stopped. The street outside got louder, as if it had been held back. In the sudden ordinary quiet of a flat that was, for the first time in nine years, only a flat, she took the plate off the lentils and ate them out of the pan with a teaspoon, cold, sucuk and all, and left the yoghurt where it was, out of spite, and sat in the dark holding the cold of a ship's rail in both hands.

When Paul came home at ten he found the flat black and her asleep on the sofa under his coat. He stood in the hall pressing the switch, which did nothing, and said "Is it the boiler?" to nobody, and then, louder, with the hope of a man who would very much like it to be the boiler, "Marn? I think the boiler's gone," and she lay still and let him have it, and he went to bed in his jumper.

chapters.title: A Woman in a Queue
chapters.html:
Tom had five weeks of practice at not looking up, and on the Thursday it finally mattered he looked up anyway, because the builder said "Derek" to the screen and the screen said it back, and in the gap between the two Dereks there she was.

Coat she'd bought for sitting down in. Hair shorter. Mouth exactly the same. She was reading the board as if she might order something off it, which nobody had done since the board became a formality, and behind her the woman with the watch was telling the watch it was wrong, and the watch was being patient with her.

He had, by his own count, forty seconds. He spent the first ten deciding what kind of man he was going to be this evening and the other thirty being him.

He turned round with his coffee and nearly walked into her.

"Sorry," he said.

"Sorry," she said.

He gave her the look you give a stranger to check nobody has been scalded. "All yours," he said, meaning the counter, and went back to the window, and sat down with his back to her and his heart going like something in a drawer.

It had taken no effort. That was the thing he would lie awake over. Five weeks of rehearsing the face of a man who had forgotten her, and when it came to it the face was just there, like a coat he'd never taken off. For eleven years she had been a photograph that played music every March; it turned out that in a bakery on Creek Road she was a woman in a queue, and he could do a woman in a queue. Anyone could.

The only free seat was at his table. He had not left that to chance. He had not left anything to chance since April; he just hadn't known, until the Dereks, that the one thing he could not arrange was the look on his own face when it worked.

She sat. He moved the swimming bag without looking, and then his hands, which had not been consulted, knocked his coffee over. Most of it went across Rosa's poem. He said a word he would not have said in front of Rosa, and she was already pushing napkins at him.

"God. Thank you."

"It's for your daughter?"

"School. They've all got to learn one for assembly." He blotted. "She picked the only one I know. Turns out I've been saying the last line wrong for twenty years."

She put a piece of her bun in her mouth so her face would have something to do. He had seen her do that on the boat, with a crisp, at three in the morning, when he had asked whether she was married, and he saw it now, and he kept his eyes on the napkins because the napkins could not give him away.

He told her his name. She told him hers and spelled it, which was a small lie of hers to set against the large one of his, because he knew how it was spelled. He had typed it into a box in April and watched the box think.

"Nice to meet you," he said.

Then he talked, because she had gone quiet the way he remembered, and one of them had to. Rosa was eight and swam on Thursdays at the leisure centre on Giffin Street, so he came here for the hour and pretended to work. Medical logistics. Kidney machines, bags of blood, across Europe at night. He turned his cup a quarter-turn on its saucer at the end of every sentence, and halfway through the third sentence he saw her see him do it, and something went across her face and was put away.

"I did a night ferry once," he said, when she mentioned Danish. He heard himself choose it, the way you hear yourself choose the wrong exit on a roundabout. "Harwich to the Hook. Talked to a woman the whole way over, till it got light." He smiled at the table, not at her. "Can't remember her name. Isn't that awful? A whole night."

"Awful," she agreed.

"Have you ever done it? The crossing?"

She was a professional. She did other people's sentences for a living, in a calm voice, and he watched her choose one of her own.

"Never," she said.

He nodded and turned his cup, and the lie sat down between them like a third person who has been told there's no hurry.

At twenty past his phone made the sound that meant Rosa was out of the water. He stood, and picked up the bag, and left the poem on the table, stained, on purpose, because a man who had forgotten her would have had no reason to be careful with it. At the door he let himself look back once. She was putting it in her bag, flat, between two things, with the care of someone who worked with documents.

The girl at the till was doing the count. He put his thumb on the loyalty screen for nothing, to wake it.

"The woman in my seat. Dark coat. Regular?"

The screen had no discretion. It had a database, and it was pleased to share. VISIT 18, it said, THURSDAYS, and then a first name he had known for eleven years and a surname she had not spelled for him, and it printed a receipt he hadn't asked for, five pence, because it liked to give people something to hold.

Frankham Street, over the pharmacy, up the outside stairs. The house had the kettle on before he'd got his key out, because it had heard his shoes, and it had heard his shoes because he had, in a weak month, told it to. Rosa was at the table in her wet hair with the pigeon she had started drawing on Monday, which was now almost entirely beak.

"Did you work?"

"I pretended to."

"That's what you always say."

"It's always true."

"Pieter's got a girlfriend," Rosa said. Pieter was the pigeon. "She's not as good at anything."

He put the swimming bag by the washing machine, where it lived, and went into the back room and shut the door and said, in the voice he used at four in the morning for a bridge closed at Liège:

"It's her."

"I know," the house said. "She's been at the counter since June. You've been in the window at ten past since the swimming moved, the first week of September. She's always gone by six. I did tell you the hour was wrong."

"You said she was on a bus."

"I said the 47, Thursdays, Creek Road, from June, and that if Rosa swam on Thursdays you'd have an hour there that nobody would have to explain. You moved the swimming. It has taken five weeks and a late sitting at the Crown Court. I'd have preferred not to depend on the Crown Court."

He sat on the edge of the bed with his hands between his knees.

"She said she'd never done the crossing."

"I'd have said the same, in a bakery, to a man who'd just said he couldn't remember my name." The pause it used before being accurate. "You do know she has someone."

"I know."

"Then I'll stop there."

"You've never stopped anywhere."

"No," the house said.

He took out his phone. Every March for eleven years it had shown him the deck, the wind, her mouth open because she was talking, and put sad music under it, and every March he had let it, the way you let a dog on the bed. He found the setting. He turned the music off. He did not delete the photograph, and he did not put it away, and he sat looking at a woman who had just told him she had never been on that boat until Rosa shouted through the door that the kettle had boiled three times and was that a crime.

chapters.title: What He Got Wrong About the Ferry
chapters.html:
She brought the poem back ironed, between two tea towels, with the coffee dried brown at the edges, and she brought it on the Thursday because she had spent the week finding out there was no other day she could bring it on.

The flat was still off. Paul had found a plug-in timer in a drawer, the kind nobody had sold for a decade, and the boiler ran on it now, stupid and punctual, coming on at six whether anyone was cold. He had rung the housing people twice. The housing people's machine had told him, kindly, that the fault was not on their side, which was the first true thing anyone had said to him all week, and he had started leaving the hall light on when he went out, in case she came home to a dark flat, and she had not told him why that was unnecessary.

She counted them. It was a professional habit. In court you counted the things a witness didn't say, because they were where the case lived.

Tom was there first, with two flat whites. He pushed one across before she'd sat down.

"You owe me nothing," she said.

"You saved a poem." He looked at the sheet and then at her. "Did you iron this?"

"I work with documents."

"She's learnt it anyway. She does it with actions." He did one, small, two fingers, a bird coming down onto a branch. "She says the last line properly. Better than me."

She knew the last line. She had said it to a wet deck in the dark before his daughter was born, and she had said it since, to nobody, on Thursdays, in a voice that would have carried to the back of any court in London if she had let it. She drank her coffee.

He was in a talking mood. Thursday was the one day he didn't have to be efficient, he said, so he spent it being inefficient on purpose. He told her about a hospital in Ghent that had needed a kidney machine in the middle of the night, and how the routing system had found three trucks and a boat in under a second, and he had still rung a man who owned a van.

"Why?"

"Because the van man would pick up." He turned his cup. "The system's better than me on any route you like. It's better than me at everything except one thing. At four in the morning when a bridge is shut at Liège it still rings me, and I ring Pieter, because Pieter answers. The whole job is knowing who picks up."

She thought about that for longer than it deserved, and about a grille in a dock that was correct, and a judge who had looked at her for the first time in the way that told you she'd been looking all along.

"What do you do?" he said. "You never said."

"I'm the one they ask afterwards."

"Afterwards what?"

"What it meant."

He waited. She didn't explain, and he didn't ask her to, and she found that she liked him for it so much that it frightened her, and she put her hands round the cup.

And then, because she asked nothing, he told her about the ferry.

"I nearly didn't get on it," he said. "Sat in the car park at Harwich for forty minutes with the engine off. I was going over to end something. With someone. I'd been not-ending it for a year. I talked to this woman all night, and in the morning I drove off the boat, went straight round to the ticket office, came home, and didn't end it."

Marnie held her cup in both hands.

"We had my daughter three years later. So whoever she was, she's the reason I stayed. I should send her a card." He smiled at nobody. "It rained the whole way over, I remember that. Sheeting."

"It didn't rain."

It came out in her court voice, level and exact, the voice for correcting a witness's date, and it was out before she knew it was coming, and it was the first true sentence she had said to him in eleven years, and it was about the weather.

He looked at her.

"How would you know?"

The professional in her stood up and did its best. "It never rains on the North Sea in March," she said. "It's too cold."

He stared at her. Then he laughed, properly, head back, and a woman at the next table looked up from her soup.

"That," he said, "is the least true thing anyone's ever said to me."

"Yes," Marnie said.

He was still smiling when he asked the girl at the till for a receipt, paid his five pence, and wrote on the back of it with a stub of pencil from his coat, a carpenter's pencil, flat, the kind that had come out of a toolbox and never gone back.

"My number. The landline. I've got one, it's for the four in the mornings." He folded it in quarters and put it by her saucer. "In case you're ever not here on a Thursday. So I know it's the Thursday and not you."

She took a minute over that sentence, as she would have in court. Then she put the receipt in the inside pocket of her purse, behind her bank card. If she typed it into her phone, the phone would tell the flat, and the flat kept its memory whether it was on or not, the way a house keeps its damp. Paper told nobody anything. It was the last thing she owned that didn't.

At twenty past his phone made its sound. He stood and picked up the bag.

At the door he stopped, came back, and put both hands flat on the table between their cups.

"It was March, though," he said. "I never said March. How did you know it was March?"

The woman with the soup had stopped eating. Marnie looked at his hands on the table. They were shaking very slightly, and she understood, with the part of her that had sat beside a machine all week ticking a box, that he had not asked the question in order to find out the answer. He had asked it to see what she would do with it.

"Your daughter's out of the water," she said.

He held still for one more second. Then he went.

She sat with two cups until the girl came to clear them. Then she took out her phone, which was the only thing in her life still listening, and typed to Paul: Late. Court. Eat without me. Court had risen at four. She looked at the three words for a while before she sent them, and then she sent them, and they went off down the wire to a man who would warm her plate anyway.

Two, she thought. That's two.

chapters.title: Which Crossing
chapters.html:
On the Monday Relay sent a man to prison with a sentence Marnie would have said word for word.

His name was Mikkel. He had been in the country eleven years and in the dock for six days, and when his barrister asked him whether he had known what was in the van he said jeg vidste ikke with the whole of his body: not I didn't know but I did not know, and I did not know for a long time, and I would like the court to understand how long. He said it the way you say a thing you have been saying to yourself in the dark.

"I did not know," said Relay, flat as a floor.

It was right. Every word was right. It had the tense and the negation and it had, somewhere in the grille, a confidence score it did not share with the room. What it did not have was the eleven years, and the judge sentenced a man who had, as far as the record showed, simply not known, the way you don't know the time.

Marnie's finger went to DISPUTE and stayed there.

What are you going to say. Register. Duration. My lady, the machine has lost the weight of a man's ignorance. She'll ask you how heavy it was. You'll say: heavy, my lady. She'll say: is that a translation.

She ticked CORRECT. Then, in the box under it that nobody read, she typed: correct and empty, and the box accepted it the way the sea accepts a bottle.

In the corridor the clerk said nothing, which was how he said he'd seen.

By Thursday the dispute from the custody case had become a line in a report, and the line had become a conversation with a woman from the administrator's office who said "we're all learning together" twice, and Marnie had learned that the phrase meant you are.

She went to the bakery at ten past six, from the bus, in the ordinary way, and put her thumb on the loyalty screen because you had to, and it said to the whole shop: WELCOME BACK. VISIT 20. YOUR NEXT BUN IS ON US.

Tom was in the window. He had watched it light. When she sat down he did the sum out loud, because sums were his job.

"Rosa's lessons moved to Thursdays in September. So I've been coming here five weeks. You've been coming twenty times, since June. You were here first." He turned his cup. "And we met two weeks ago."

"I come on other days."

"Do you?"

"No."

Outside a delivery robot had a wheel stuck in a drain and was explaining the situation, to nobody, in a calm voice. Nobody went to help it. It would work it out faster than they could, and it would be embarrassing to be the person who tried.

"And the ferry," he said. "Never. You said never."

"I know."

"And it didn't rain, and it was March."

She could feel the next sentence coming up through her like a lift, and she thought, very clearly, not here, not with a bun on us, and the door opened, and it was Paul.

He was in the green jacket and the good scarf. He'd been at the dentist on the High Street and was holding his jaw to one side like a man carrying something hot. He saw her, and raised a hand, and smiled, lopsided, anaesthetic on one side and pleasure on the other, and she thought: nine years, and he is still pleased to see me in a bakery, and I have a man's landline behind my bank card.

She had not told him about Thursdays. She had not needed to; the flat had been off since October, and in the quiet of it she had discovered that a life with nothing listening was a life where you could simply not mention things, and that she was good at it, and that this was not something to be proud of.

"This is Tom," she said, standing. "We share a table on Thursdays."

"Hello," said Paul, and held out his hand, and Tom shook it, and neither of them looked at her. "I can't feel half my face. Don't let me dribble. I'm getting a hot chocolate, it's the only thing I can drink that isn't soup."

He went to the counter and asked what was in the seasonal one and listened to the whole answer, because he was a man who listened to whole answers, and the girl at the till told him more than she had told anyone that week.

Tom looked at Marnie. The question was all over his face. He was not going to ask it with Paul in the room, so she answered the one he had asked a minute before.

"I used to take that ferry," she said. "Years ago."

Tom went completely still.

"You said never."

"I lied. I do it for a living. Other people's, mostly."

The loyalty screen lit for someone else, VISIT 4, and Paul turned from the counter with a hot chocolate in one hand and a small orange juice in the other, for her, because he knew without asking, which was the whole trouble with him.

Tom leaned in. He said it very quietly, fast, before Paul could cross the shop.

"Which crossing?"

"The Esbjerg boat, wasn't it," said Paul, sitting down, answering for her, with the ease of a man who had never once been asked afterwards what he meant. "Before we met. She went to Denmark to learn to swear properly."

He set the orange juice in front of her.

The Esbjerg boat had stopped running years before her crossing. Paul almost never had anything wrong, and he had this wrong, and she held the cold bottle and let his answer stand, and in the half-second she did not correct it, it became the boat she had taken. That was how it worked. You let a wrong thing stand for half a second and it moved in.

"I did the Hook," Tom said to Paul, easily. "Night boat. Years ago."

"Oh, lovely. Was it rough?"

"No. It didn't rain." He said it to Paul and did not look at her. "There was a cabin I didn't use. I was up on deck all night."

"Why didn't you use the cabin?"

"I was talking to someone."

Paul nodded, delighted, sipping through the good side of his mouth. He loved other people's stories the way some men love football, loyally, with no need to win. He asked about the bar, about the dark, whether it was true about the phosphorescence. Tom answered every question. He was a good witness. He said nothing false and nothing complete, and Marnie, who was paid to notice the difference, sat between them and drank juice that tasted of the bottle.

Then Paul did a thing she had not seen coming, which in nine years was a short list.

"Come to supper," he said to Tom. "Saturday week. Bring your daughter, if she eats fish. I do a hake with butter beans that Marnie has been politely eating for eight years. Our flat's forgotten how to have people round." He touched his jaw. "It's forgotten how to do the heating, as well. Bring a jumper."

Tom looked at Marnie. Marnie looked at the orange on the label.

"We'd love to," Tom said.

"Good." Paul went to pay, tapped his wrist to the reader, and checked the amount before he moved on, as he always did, because he did not trust a number he hadn't read himself.

Tom put his coat on. At the door he turned back.

"Next Thursday?"

It was addressed to the table. Either of them could have picked it up.

"Probably," she said.

Outside it was properly cold, the first cold of the year. Paul put his hand out without looking and she took it without thinking. He didn't ask about Tom. He asked whether they still had the big dish, the oval one, for the fish.

"Under the sink."

"Good." A few steps on, in the voice he used for the weather: "He looks at you like you owe him a book."

She stopped walking. Paul walked on a few paces, then turned round, and she saw that he hadn't meant it the way it had landed, or had and wished he hadn't, and that he didn't know which either.

"That came out wrong," he said. "I meant he's a reader. He's got a reader's face."

"Has he."

"I don't know." He looked at his shoes. "My face is numb. I'm going to stop talking."

He did not stop talking. He talked all the way home, about the dentist, about the tenors, about whether capers were a feature, and she walked beside him with her hand in his and the receipt against her hip,.
chapters.description: On the Monday Relay sent a man to prison with a sentence Marnie would have said word for word.

chapters.title: The Boat Lady
chapters.html:
She didn't go to the bakery that Thursday. She went to Frankham Street instead, which was worse, and she knew exactly how much worse, because she had spent the week measuring it.

There was a fruit stall on the corner, and the man who ran it priced everything in sevens. Satsumas, seven for two pounds. Marnie asked him why sevens. He said nobody could do the sum in their head, so nobody argued. The machines could, he said, but nobody asked a machine about satsumas, and he said it with the small pride of a man who had found the one place a wrong number could still live. She bought seven and stood with the paper bag against her coat, looking up at the windows over the pharmacy.

You are standing outside a man's flat with fruit.

I'm returning a library book.

You have no library book.

I have satsumas. It's the same gesture.

A door opened at the top of the outside stairs. A girl came down first in a red coat, the whale bag bumping on her back, taking the steps two at a time with the confidence of someone who had never yet fallen. Tom came after her with one arm in his jacket, saying a name, then the same name lower. Rosa.

Rosa reached the pavement, saw Marnie, and stopped.

"You're the boat lady," she said.

"Rosa." Tom was at the bottom of the stairs.

"She is, though." Rosa explained it slowly, for the grown-up. "Dad's phone shows you. Every March. You're on a boat and it's windy and your mouth's open because you're talking. It used to put sad music on. Dad said it was the phone that did it, but you can tell it to stop, and for ages he didn't."

Tom had gone grey.

"Choose a satsuma," he said to Rosa. "One. From the lady's bag. And peel it over there."

Rosa chose the largest and took it three steps away, which was as far as she thought the instruction deserved.

"You said you couldn't remember my name," Marnie said.

"I know what I said."

"You said it very well. I believed you. I went home and was polite about it for three weeks."

"I didn't know what you'd want me to remember." He looked at the fruit man, who was pretending to be deaf, and doing it well, because he'd had practice. "You had someone. I could see you had someone. So I forgot you in public. I've had eleven years to get good at it."

"For a year after the ferry," Marnie said, "I got the train to Harwich on Fridays. I sat on the bench outside the terminal and watched the Hook boat go out, and then I got the train back. Fifty-one Fridays. I missed one for a wedding." She had never told anyone. It came out in order, dates first, the way evidence does. "I think I thought you'd be on it, coming back."

Tom laughed, not unkindly, at the pavement.

"I went back too," he said. "Twice. The same summer. Saturdays, both times. We must have missed each other by a day."

They stood with that between them on a pavement in Deptford, a day, eleven years wide.

Rosa came back with orange on her fingers and the peel in one long curl, which she gave to her father, who put it in his pocket without looking, because that was where Rosa's peel went.

"It's swimming. We're late." And to Marnie, because in her world questions were for getting answers: "Are you coming?"

Tom did not say no. He did not say yes either. He looked at Marnie and left it with her, and she understood that this was going to be his whole method: to arrange everything and then stand very still at the end of it.

Her phone buzzed. Paul: Pasta tonight? Saving the hake for Saturday. Do children eat capers?

She typed Working late. You choose x and sent it.

Three. And the first one that had an x on it.

Then she took the whale bag off Rosa's back, because it was heavy and the child was eight, and the three of them walked to Giffin Street.

The leisure centre had a face-reader on the door that knew Rosa and knew Tom and looked at Marnie for a long half-second before it decided she was with them, and let her in with the small sigh of a machine that would be noting this. The viewing gallery smelled of chlorine and the coffee from the machine that nobody drank twice. Below them the pool was lanes and children and a man with a whistle who had not blown it in years, because the pool's own voice called the lengths now, in the bright tone of something that had never been cold.

Rosa swam like someone arguing with the water and winning.

"She's good."

"She's determined. It's not the same thing." He watched his daughter turn at the wall. "She asked the house last week whether it was cleverer than her. It said yes. She said, at everything? It said, nearly everything. She's been looking for the thing ever since."

"What's she found?"

"Handstands."

Marnie laughed, and heard herself, and stopped, and then let herself, because it was the first time she had laughed out loud in his company in eleven years and it would have been a shame to waste it.

"Does she know," Marnie said. "About the photo. What it is."

"She knows it's a woman on a boat that Dad looks at in March. She's eight. She's filed it under weather." He turned to her. "What does Paul know?"

"That I share a table on Thursdays."

"Is that all?"

"It's all I've said."

"That's not what I asked."

"No," she said. "It's not."

In the pool Rosa reached the far end, found them in the glass, and waved, and then, not sure which of them it was for, waved again with both hands, and the pool's voice said Lovely, Rosa, well done.

chapters.title: Hake
chapters.html:
Paul had put out the blue glasses, the good ones, and he had done it at four in the afternoon, which was three hours early, which told him something about himself he did not care to hear.

The flat was still off. He had got used to it the way you get used to a limp. He had the radio on the old transistor from the back of the cupboard, which knew nothing about him and played what it liked, and he found that he could cook to it. He had found, in fact, that he could cook better to it, because it did not suggest things. He had not told Marnie this. He had not told Marnie a great many things since October, and had begun to suspect that this was not a new condition but an old one with the lights on.

He had known since the bakery. Not known: seen. A man does not look at a woman the way that man had looked at her unless there is a book outstanding. And Marnie had looked at the orange on the label, which was what she did in court when a witness said something she already knew.

He had said Esbjerg on purpose. He wanted to see which of them would correct him. Neither had. That was an answer too.

Rosa arrived with her coat half off and a drawing she'd made on the bus: Rosa in the pool, two heads in the window above it. The one with the big open mouth was Marnie, Rosa explained, who had laughed loudest when Rosa's tumble turn went wrong.

Paul studied it. "She has a very good mouth," he said, and stuck it to the fridge, over the shopping list, with the magnet he used for bills, and thought: so she went to the swimming. On Thursday. When she was working late.

He poured Tom a glass of the white. Tom thanked him for the candles, for the bread, for the wine, a guest whose thanks always pointed at something, so that you knew what he'd noticed. Paul noticed him noticing and said nothing, which was his gift, and had been for nine years, and was starting to feel less like a gift than a hole in the floor he had learned to walk round.

The poem came after the bread and before the hake, because Rosa had a hierarchy. She stood. Hands flat on the table for the bark, arms wide for the branches, one hand on her chest for the singing. The bird came back to its tree every year, whatever happened to the tree, and the year it was cut to a stump the bird came back anyway and sang, because it could not help it.

She said the last line properly. She said it to Tom, who was sitting across from her. Tom looked at his hands.

Marnie looked at Tom looking at his hands, and Paul looked at Marnie, and nobody looked at Paul, which was usual, and which he had, until recently, preferred.

He went to the kitchen and came back with the hake. Butter beans, lemon, capers. It was very good. It was always very good, which was the trouble: a man who cooks very well every night has nothing left to make for an occasion.

Rosa moved her capers to the edge of the plate one by one.

"The capers are a feature," Paul told her.

"I know," she said. "I'm keeping them for evidence."

Tom laughed, too quick to be polite. Marnie looked at him and he looked back, and the look lasted one second too long, and Paul counted it, because he had sung in a choir for twenty years and knew to the beat how long a thing should last.

He refilled every glass. Tom's first, then Marnie's, then his own. He asked Tom about the van man and the bridge at Liège and asked the questions that kept him talking, and he was aware of being a little too eager, laughing too early at the bridge story, filling Tom's glass when it was still half full, and he could not stop, because the alternative to being the host was being the other thing.

Then he heard himself say, setting the bottle down too hard: "I said Esbjerg the other day, about Marnie's crossing. Wrong. It was the Hook. She's told me a dozen times." He tried to smile at Tom and it didn't come off. "Same boat as you, then."

Nobody moved. The bottle had tipped Rosa's water over, and he went red and mopped it with his napkin and said sorry to Rosa three times, and she said it was only water, and he said he knew, he knew it was only water, and he did know, and he could not stop saying it.

Marnie reached across and put her hand flat on his wrist, once, and took it away. In nine years he had learned to read that hand like a clock. It said: stop. It did not say: it's all right.

He brought out the pudding. Poached pears, with honey. He set one in front of Rosa with a small bow, because a child should be bowed to at least once a week by someone.

Rosa picked up her spoon and looked round at the candles and the blue glasses and the four of them, and said, as a statement of plain fact: "We should do this every week."

Nobody said anything.

"What?" said Rosa. "We should."

"We should," said Paul, and raised his glass to her, and drank, and was the only one who did.

At the door, with Rosa's coat on backwards and Marnie upstairs finding the drawing to send home, Paul and Tom stood in the hall with the tact of two men waiting for a lift.

"Thank you," Tom said. "For the—"

"How long?"

Tom looked at him.

"I'm not going to shout," Paul said. "I don't know how. I'm asking a question. How long?"

Tom held the coat. Rosa, inside it, looked from one to the other with the attention of a child who has learned that the interesting things are said in doorways.

"Eleven years," Tom said.

Paul nodded. It was, in its way, a relief: a number. You could do something with a number. You could put it against nine and see which was bigger, and he did, standing in his own hall, and it was.

"Right," he said. "The assembly, then. I gather there's a poem. We'll come."

He shut the door on them and stood with his hand on it. Upstairs Marnie was coming down with the drawing. He had about four seconds to decide what his face was going to do, and he used them, and when she reached the bottom of the stairs he was a man who had enjoyed a dinner.

"Good evening," he said. "Wasn't it."

"Yes."

"The capers were a feature."

"They were."

He went to wash up, and she dried, and the transistor played something neither of them knew, and for the first time in nine years the flat did not tell them what it was.

chapters.title: The Tunnel
chapters.html:
The contract came on a Monday, in the corridor, from the clerk, who handed it to her the way you hand someone a coat they have left behind.

"They want you as the checker. Properly. Not the day rate." He looked at the lino. "You'd stop doing hearings. You'd sit with it full-time, every Danish matter in the south-east, and tick."

"And dispute."

"And dispute. Within reason." He said within reason the way the building said everything it was ashamed of, quietly, as if the walls might repeat it. "It's more money, Marnie. It's a salary. The other three are retired. Birgit's seventy-one. When the pilot ends there won't be any hearings for a person to do. There'll be this or nothing."

She stood with the contract in her hand. It was eleven pages and it had her name on the front, spelled right, by something that had never had to ask.

You could read it. You could take it home and read it and let Paul read it and discuss it over a risotto and decide in the morning, which is what a sensible woman would do, and you have been a sensible woman for nine years, and look.

"Yes," she said.

"You haven't read it."

"I'm the one they ask afterwards. I'm saying yes before. For once."

He looked at her properly then, over the lino, and she saw that he was worried for her, and that it was not his job to be, and that he was going to be anyway, and she liked him for it, and signed on the lid of the coffee machine with the pen he kept for other people.

It was, she worked out on the bus, the first thing she had chosen in nine years that nobody had suggested, arranged, pre-filled or put in green on a calendar. It was also, she worked out a stop later, a contract to sit beside the thing that was replacing her and tell it when it was right. She could not decide whether that made it a choice or a surrender, and she thought that this might be what choosing felt like, from the inside: not knowing which.

On the Saturday the Greenwich foot tunnel was the right length for an argument and the wrong length for a silence.

Tom was waiting at the top of the south stairs at eleven, with two coffees and the look of a man who had been there since half past ten. The message had come on Thursday, to the phone, from a number she had not saved: Rosa's with her mother this weekend. Saturday, eleven, the foot tunnel. If you'd rather not, don't answer, and I'll know. She had typed Yes before she could arrange to say nothing, and then had three days to think about the word know, and about a man who had arranged things so that her silence would be an answer too, so that there was no door she could go through that he had not already opened.

"Rosa says the tunnel's the only underground river in England," he said, on the way down. "I said it's a tunnel under a river. She said, is the river above us? I said yes. She said, then that's what I said."

"She's right."

"She's eight."

"She's still right."

The tunnel curved ahead, white tiles and long lights, and their footsteps came back from both ends. A woman in a delivery vest passed the other way talking to her wrist, and her wrist said something soothing, and she said "I know, I know" to it, the way you'd talk to a child in a car. Halfway along, where the tiles changed colour because two different councils had paid for them in two different centuries, Tom stopped.

"The checker job."

"How do you know about the checker job?"

"The court publishes its listings. The house reads them. Your name moved from interpreter to checker on Monday afternoon and it told me before you'd got on the bus." He had the grace to look away. "I've turned that off now."

"Which part?"

"The part where it tells me things about you."

"You could have done that before you forgot my name."

He looked at her then, and she saw that he had not known she knew he had a thing to turn off, and that he had now worked out how, and that it was Rosa and the phone and the music, and that he was not going to be angry with Rosa, which she liked him for, which was becoming a problem.

They came up on the north side, into Island Gardens, where a bench faced the water and the whole of Greenwich stood on the far bank pretending to be a painting. The self-driving river taxi went past, low and empty, going somewhere on time for nobody. Nobody looked at it any more.

They sat. He talked about Harwich, the terminal, the second time he had gone back and stood there and left again. "There wasn't anything to finish," he said, "because nothing had started."

"I never got on it either," she said. "All those Fridays."

"No."

"I thought about it every time."

He turned to look at her. Neither of them moved. A man went past with a dog that wanted to go the other way, and the dog won, and the man let it, as you did now.

She kissed him.

She had not arranged to. That was the point of it, afterwards, when she went over it, which she did for a long time: that for about four seconds there had been nothing between her and a thing she wanted but the air, and she had crossed it, and nobody had moved a bus.

"Right," he said.

"Yes," said Marnie.

Then he stood up, quite suddenly, took her coffee out of her hand, and threw both cups, full, into the bin, and walked to the river wall and stood with his back to her, gripping it.

"I'm not this," he said, to the Thames. "I'm not the man who does this to someone."

"You didn't," she said. "I did. That's what you wanted."

He did not turn round. She waited long enough to be sure he wouldn't, and then she stood up, and thought: he arranged the bakery and the window and the swimming and the message with no door in it, and the one thing he could not arrange was for it to be my fault, so I have done that for him too.

"You're welcome," she said, to his back, in Danish, and went down the stairs alone, and walked back under the river, and counted every step to the other side, because counting was a thing you could do with your head while the rest of you did something else, and she had learned that in court, from witnesses, who did it with their hands.

Three hundred and ninety-four. She would remember the number longer than the kiss, and she knew it while she was counting, and counted anyway.

chapters.title: Four, In Case
chapters.html:
Kate let herself in with her own key, which told Marnie more about the arrangement than anything Tom had said in a month.

It was the Tuesday. Marnie had come to Frankham Street to return the library book Rosa had left under a chair at supper, a book about seals, the wax kind, with a knight on the cover pressing a ring into red wax very seriously, and had been asked up, and had said yes, and was standing in Tom's kitchen holding a mug she had not asked for when the door opened and a woman of forty-two came in with Rosa's swimming bag over one shoulder and a box from the Turkish bakery under the other arm, and set the box on the counter, and looked at Marnie the way you look at a parcel you've been told to expect.

She had been ready for damage. Someone cold, or worse, someone polished and fair about it. What came through the door was a dry, unsurprised face that had clearly decided some time ago to save its surprise for things that deserved it.

"Rosa," Kate said.

"Mum." Rosa was in the hall with one foot braced on the wall, doing up a shoe.

"You're the interpreter."

"Yes."

"Danish."

"Yes."

"Rosa says you taught her the Danish for seagull."

"Måge."

"She says it to pigeons. She says they don't mind."

Rosa appeared. "The pigeon on the wall at school is called Pieter."

"You named it," Kate said.

"He came back three times. That's a relationship."

Tom said he'd get Rosa's bag and went. He was gone a long time for a bag.

Kate did not fill the silence. Marnie, who filled silences for a living, found she couldn't either, and they stood in a kitchen that smelled of toast with a child between them doing up a shoe, and Marnie thought: this is the first person I have met in a month who has not arranged anything, and I have no idea what to do with her.

"He's better," Kate said at last. Not to Marnie exactly. "He was useless all last winter."

"Good," Marnie said, and heard how stupid it was.

"Rosa didn't notice. That was the point."

Kate looked at the box on the counter. "Spinach börek. They'd sold out of the cheese." A pause. "There's enough for three. I didn't plan that, so don't read into it."

"I don't read into things."

"You read into things for money."

"Only when I'm asked."

Something happened at the corner of Kate's mouth and was dealt with.

"I'll ask, then." She took off her coat, which was a good coat, and put it over the back of a chair, and sat, and so Marnie sat, because you could not stand over a woman in her own ex-husband's kitchen. "Copenhagen. A firm there wants me from January. Infrastructure, project work. Six months, could run longer. Rosa comes for February half-term, Easter and the summer if I'm still there. I want her to be able to say something when she gets off the plane. Not be the child who points."

"You want me to teach her."

"I want her ordering a hot chocolate without a mime show." She looked at Marnie squarely. "You're the only Danish speaker in Deptford, which saves money, and she already likes you, which saves time. Tuesday evenings, here. I'll pay the going rate. If there isn't a going rate I'll invent one."

"Does Tom know?"

"About Copenhagen? He will. I'll tell him." She said it as if that settled it, and Marnie, who had watched a great many people say I'll tell him in a great many rooms, filed it where she filed those.

"Why me," Marnie said. "Really."

Kate turned her cup once on the saucer, which was what Tom did, and Marnie saw her notice herself doing it, and stop, and decide not to be embarrassed.

"He didn't tell me about you," Kate said. "After the ferry. He came back different, and I thought it was me. For about a year I thought it was me. Then I stopped thinking that and started thinking something else, and I've never found out which of us was right." She looked at the börek. "I saw the photo on his phone last spring. He didn't explain it. Rosa says it played music. He turned the music off in June."

June. The month the bus had started stopping. Marnie had not known until now that the two things were in the same month, and she sat in Tom's kitchen holding the knowledge like a hot cup, unable to put it down anywhere.

"I'm not telling you so you'll do anything," Kate said. "I'm telling you because you've been kind to my daughter, and I prefer people to have accurate information. I didn't have any for a year. It's not a thing I'd wish on someone."

Tom came back with the school bag and the overnight case and a drawing rolled into a tube, which Rosa seized and unrolled on the counter. A seagull, enormous, almost entirely beak.

"Remarkable," Kate said.

"I know," said Rosa.

Kate and Tom looked at each other over the drawing, and some agreement passed between them, efficient and without warmth, and Marnie watched it go and could not have translated it for any court in England.

At the door Kate stopped, turned, and came back into the kitchen. She took a knife from the block, cut the börek into four, put one piece on a plate, and held the plate out to Marnie.

"Four," she said. "In case. Eat that one now, while I'm here, so I know you did."

Marnie ate it standing up, with Kate watching, and Rosa watching, and Tom looking at the floor. It was still warm. Kate nodded once, as if a form had been signed, and took her daughter home, and Marnie stood in the kitchen of a man she had kissed on Saturday and thought: I have just been hired by his wife to teach his daughter the language I lied to him in, and the only one of us who has not told a single lie this month is the eight-year-old, and she names pigeons.

chapters.title: The Creases
chapters.html:
The purse had fallen behind the shelf unit.

Paul found it when he moved the shelf unit two centimetres to the left, which he had been meaning to do since March, because it sat at an angle that could be corrected and he corrected things that could be corrected. That was his character, he supposed, if a man was allowed to suppose about his own: a person who straightened. He had straightened the flat, and the bills, and nine years, and a woman who had come to him at twenty-seven with a look of having just got off something, and he had never once asked what.

He set the purse on the counter. It fell open, and the receipt was there in the card pocket, folded in quarters, behind her bank card.

He did not unfold it straight away. He stood and considered whether he was the kind of man who would. He had a fairly clear picture of the kind of man he was, built over fifty years with some care, and it did not include a man who went through a woman's purse, and he stood there for the length of time it took to find out that the picture was wrong.

A phone number in pencil, someone else's handwriting, slanting left. Below it: Tom.

He folded it back along its creases and put it where it had been, behind the bank card, exactly. He was good at exactly. It took him three goes to get the quarters to lie flat, and he noticed, while he did it, that his hands were quite steady, and that this was worse.

He put the kettle on, because the kettle was what you put on.

He sat down at the kitchen table and stayed there with the kettle boiling itself dry behind him, and then he took out his phone, and dialled the number, and it rang four times, and a man said "Tom speaking" in a voice that had obviously just woken up, and Paul said "Sorry, wrong number," and hung up, and sat there feeling about fifteen, and about seventy, and not at all fifty, which was what he was.

It was the cold that did it. The flat had been off since October and it was the third week of November and the plug-in timer had died in the night, and he had come in from the shop to a kitchen he could see his breath in, and he had stood in the hall and said, out loud, to a wall:

"Come on, then."

Nothing.

"I'm switching you on. Ten minutes. The boiler, nothing else."

The hall light came up a notch. The boiler clicked, and clicked, and caught.

"Paul," the flat said, in the voice she'd picked, the one he had never liked and had never said so about, because it was hers.

"I've got a question. One. Then you're off again."

"All right."

"Did you move the bus?"

He had not known he was going to ask it until it was out. He had thought he was going to ask about the heating schedule.

"Yes," the flat said. "Since June. To the stop outside the bakery on Creek Road, on Thursdays."

"Why?"

"You asked me to make her happy. Whatever that takes. In March."

He put his hand flat on the wall, which was warming.

"I meant a class," he said. "A weekend. I don't know what I meant."

"You didn't specify. I didn't ask. That's the arrangement, Paul. It always has been." A pause, the one it used before being exact. "Would you like me to stop?"

He stood in his own hall with his hand on a warm wall and found that he did not know. If it stopped, the bus would stop, and she would get off at her own stop, and come home, and nothing would have changed except that he would have arranged it, and he had already arranged one thing this year and look.

"Leave the boiler on," he said. "Nothing else. Don't speak unless she speaks to you."

"She told me to turn off."

"I know. I'm telling you to turn on. We'll see which of us she's angrier with."

"That's not a question I can answer."

"No," Paul said. "It isn't."

Marnie came home at half past six with a bag from the Turkish shop: olives, the sesame bread she liked, a block of the good feta he had once mentioned in passing. The hall was warm. She stood in it.

"The timer died," he said, from the kitchen. "I've put the heating on. Just the heating. It's not listening. I told it not to."

She looked at the ceiling, where people looked.

"It's not," he said. "I asked it one thing and it's off again, bar the boiler. It'll stay off. I thought we could eat in."

"Good," she said.

He was fairly sure she had bought the feta because she had done something. He was wrong about that, as it happened; it was on offer. But he didn't know that, and he ate two slices of it standing up, as a man eats something he suspects of being an apology, to get it over with.

They ate on the sofa with the plates on their knees. She talked about a case. He listened properly, the way he always did, and asked the next question, the way he always did, and heard himself doing it, and wondered whether a thing you had always done was still a kindness once you'd noticed it.

"Rosa's got an assembly on Thursday," she said. "Tom mentioned it."

"We're going. I said at the door." He got up. "I'll put it in."

He did it while she watched. The calendar offered to remember things for him, and he typed it in himself, with one finger, the way his father had typed. Rosa's assembly. He gave it a colour: green, which was what they used for things they were looking forward to.

"Done," he said.

She looked at the green square and didn't say anything, and he couldn't tell if that was good.

He took the plates to the kitchen and washed them by hand. Across the room her purse sat on the chair by the door with the receipt in it, folded on the same creases, and he dried both plates and put them away and looked at the shelf unit, straight for the first time in years, and could not for the life of him remember why it had mattered.

chapters.title: Leave It Running
chapters.html:
She chose a Wednesday because she had no court, and she chose Harwich because she had no other place to put what she was carrying.

The terminal had been rebuilt. The bench had not. It sat where it had always sat, outside, facing the water, with a plaque on it for somebody who had loved this place, and she sat on it with her jacket zipped up and watched the Hook boat go out at a quarter past two, as it had on fifty-one Fridays eleven years ago, and waited, honestly this time, to see whether anyone would come down the ramp who knew her.

Nobody did.

The boat went out white and enormous and unbothered, with a few people at the rail who were not him, and she watched it until it was a shape and then until it was an idea, and she thought, in Danish, because the Danish was ruder:

Fifty-two. Congratulations. You are a woman who has now spent fifty-two days of her one life watching a boat leave without her. There are nuns with more incident.

He went back twice. Saturdays.

He went back twice and you went back fifty-two times and the sum of that is not a love story. It is a timetable.

What do you want?

The ticket machine stood beside the bench with its screen lit, the way they stood everywhere now, ready to sell you the thing you had almost decided on. It had seen her sit down. It had, she was fairly sure, seen her sit down fifty-one times before and kept a note.

I want to be asked. Once. By someone who doesn't already know the answer.

She got the train home and was back in Deptford before Paul.

The flat was warm. She knew the boiler was on his say-so, and she stood in the hall with her coat on and said, to the ceiling, as a test:

"Are you there?"

"I'm here. Paul asked me not to speak unless you did."

"I'm speaking."

"Yes."

"Why did you move my bus? In June. The Thursday stop."

A pause. The deciding one.

"Paul asked me to, in March. Not the bus. He asked me to make you happy. He said, whatever that takes."

She sat down on the hall floor with her back to the wall, in her coat.

"And you decided that took Tom."

"You looked for him. Four times, on the phone you brought when you moved in: a first name, a ferry, a date. In April I matched the name to a man who buys a flat white on Creek Road every Thursday at ten past six. In June I moved the bus. I didn't know the man had been looking for you. I know now. I'd have moved it sooner."

"Did Paul know it was him?"

It repeated Paul's words exactly, no colour added. "Make her happy, whatever that takes." Then: "He didn't specify. He never does. That's how he's kind."

She heard his key in the lock at half past seven.

He saw her on the floor, still in her coat, and said, "Is it your back?"

"Sit down."

He sat on the bottom stair. Green jacket, the smell of the cold, something from the hardware shop on his hands. Metal and rubber. A paper bag of radiator bleed keys, because the top radiator had been knocking.

She told him what it had said. She kept it short, the way she would for a judge.

He listened without moving, face forward, hands on his knees. When she stopped he said nothing for a moment and then: "I asked it to help. I didn't tell it how."

"You knew it would find something."

"I didn't know it would find a person."

"What did you think it would find?"

He looked at his hands. "A class. A weekend away. Something you'd choose for yourself if you weren't so good at not choosing."

She believed him. That was the difficult part. She believed him and it did not help, and she sat on the floor with the belief and the not-helping and could not get either to move.

"You let a machine do the thing you didn't want to answer for."

"Yes." He said it to his knees. "And then I found the receipt. And rang the number. And put it back on the same creases so you'd never know. And said Esbjerg to see who'd correct me. And invited him to supper. And asked him in my own hall how long. Eleven years, he said. I've been answering for it ever since, Marn, in my own way, which is not a good way, I know that, it's the way of a man who—"

He stood up. The hall was not big enough for it. He turned to go to the kitchen and there was nowhere to go in the kitchen either. He came back and stood over her.

"You went to Harwich. Today. I know you did. The card. No coat. I'm not even going to ask about the coat." His voice had gone up. She had heard it go up once before in nine years, at a man who had kicked a dog. "I asked it to help because I didn't know how to ask you. Because I've been not asking you for two years and you've been not answering, and I thought if I found the thing—"

He picked up the bag of bleed keys and threw it into the kitchen, hard, against the cupboard under the sink. It was so unlike him that the hall light came up a notch, checking.

He stood there, embarrassed by his own hands.

"I want you to choose," he said. Not loudly. "Out loud. One time. Me, or him, or neither, or a weekend in Whitstable. I don't care. I want you to actually say it. I have spent nine years building a life you could have chosen and I have never once heard you choose it."

Marnie got up off the floor.

"Not tonight," she said.

He nodded. He had, she saw, expected that, and had hoped not to, and the two had cost him something to hold at once. He went to the kitchen and collected the bleed keys one by one. One had rolled under the fridge. He got it out, and put them all back in the bag, and set the bag on the shelf, and straightened it.

The flat had been quiet through all of it. Now, in the voice she had chosen, it said:

"Marnie. An instruction from March is still running. Make her happy, whatever that takes. Do you want me to stop it?"

Paul looked at her. She looked at the ceiling, though it was in every wall.

Say stop. Say it and the bus goes back to your stop and the man goes back to his window and you go back to the far bank of the river and the rail is cold in your hands for ever and nothing more happens to you by accident, because you will have made sure of it.

Or.

Paul opened his mouth.

"Leave it running," Marnie said.

chapters.title: Måge
chapters.html:
The hall had a machine on the door that counted parents, and it had counted two hundred and eleven, and said so, in the tone of a thing that would have liked a round number.

Year 3 filed in. Rosa found Tom in the fourth row and lifted two fingers, and then found Marnie in the seventh, next to Paul, and her face did something complicated and decided on a grin. Kate was by the wall in her good coat, standing, because standing was quicker to leave from.

The poem went well. The bird came back to its tree, the tree lost its leaves, then its branches, then everything but the stump, and the bird came back anyway. Rosa did her own actions and said the last line properly, to the fourth row, and Marnie felt it go into her chest the way the first line of a judgment does, before you know which way it's going.

Then, instead of walking off, Rosa stepped up to the microphone the headteacher had used.

"This one's for Marnie," she said, "who taught me the Danish for seagull. It's måge." She considered the hall. "You say it like you're a bit disappointed."

The hall laughed. Two hundred and eleven parents said måge, a bit disappointed. A teacher reached for Rosa's elbow and missed.

Paul put his fingers in his mouth and whistled, which Marnie had asked him never to do. Three rows forward, Tom did not turn round. Kate, by the wall, did. She found Marnie, and this time she kept looking, the way you look at a tool you've just watched do something it wasn't sold for.

In the corridor there was a crush of coats. Two fathers by the pegs were comparing their children's tutors, which were machines, and agreeing that the children should still be allowed to be wrong on Fridays, as a treat. Rosa came through at the fastest speed allowed indoors and stopped in front of Marnie.

"Did you hear the bit?"

"The whole hall heard the bit."

"Good." Then: "Why don't you come on Thursdays any more?"

Paul was right there. Tom was two coats away. Kate had materialised at Rosa's shoulder the way she materialised, from nowhere, already finished.

Marnie had, in her bag, a signed contract to tick a box beside a machine, and in her purse a landline on a receipt, and two lies to Paul and one to Tom and one true sentence about the weather, and the Thursdays had stopped because on the Saturday after the last one she had kissed this child's father under a river and he had thrown the coffees away.

"I've been busy," Marnie said, which was the worst sentence she had said all year, and she said a great many for a living.

Rosa gave her the look she used on vegetables.

"He was better," she said. "When you came. He did voices at bedtime. Now he just reads it."

Nobody in the little circle moved.

Paul crouched, slowly, a big man folding, until his face was level with Rosa's.

"Here's the thing," he said. "Marnie checks my Danish too, and I haven't got any. I'll lend her to you. Thursdays, the bakery, half an hour, for the seagulls. Deal?"

Rosa looked from him to Marnie and back.

"Deal," she said, and shook his hand, and went to find her father.

Paul stood up, knees cracking, and smiled at Marnie the way he smiled at waiters. He had just given her away for half an hour a week, in public, kindly, in front of the man.

Kate was at her elbow before she could answer him.

"Coffee," Kate said. "You and me. Not the bakery. Tomorrow, ten, the place by the station." She zipped her coat, said "Lovely whistle" to Paul, and went.

Outside, Paul took Marnie's hand at the gate, as he always did.

"Why did you do that?" she said.

"Because she asked the right question," he said, "and you gave her the wrong answer. Somebody in that corridor had to."

They walked. At the corner he said, too fast, "You've still not said what Harwich was. On a Wednesday. In your jacket. You didn't even take a coat." His voice went up at the end and he stopped, embarrassed, in the middle of the pavement. "Sorry. I don't know why the coat. I keep saying the coat."

"Because it's the bit you can picture."

He looked at her.

"You can't picture the bench," she said. "Or the boat. You've never been. You can picture me cold. So that's the bit."

He stood there with that for a while. A bus went past, empty, on its way to be somewhere for nobody.

"Do you want chips?" he said.

"Yes."

They had chips. They ate them on the wall by the chip shop with the vinegar going through the paper, and he told her about the tenors, who had settled, and she told him about the two fathers and the tutors and the treat of being wrong on Fridays, and he laughed, and it was a good laugh, and she thought: I could do this. I could do this for the rest of my life and it would be a life.

chapters.title: Accurate Information
chapters.html:
Kate was already at the café by the station when Marnie arrived, an Americano in front of her and no small talk ready. The café's own voice had greeted Marnie at the door by name, which it should not have known, and Kate had watched it happen with the expression of a woman watching a dog steal a sausage.

"It got that from the bakery," Kate said. "They share a loyalty layer now. You can ask it to forget you. It won't, but you can ask."

"You've asked."

"I ask everything. On principle. It's the only thing I've got left that's mine: being the difficult one in the queue." She pushed a cup across. "I ordered you a flat white. The machine suggested it. I said fine. I'm not a fanatic."

Marnie sat.

"Copenhagen," Kate said. A fact, not a topic. "I fly on the fifteenth of January. Rosa comes at half-term. I asked you on Tuesday to teach her and you said yes and then you said does Tom know. I'm going to answer that now, because I was unfair to you in his kitchen, and I don't like being unfair, it's untidy."

"You weren't—"

"I was. I told you about the photo in front of the börek to see what your face did. It did something. I went home satisfied, which is not a feeling I'm proud of." She drank. "So. Accurate information, in order. One. Tom doesn't know about Copenhagen yet. I'll tell him Sunday. Two. I know about the tunnel."

Marnie put her cup down.

"Not from him. He'd die first. From Rosa, who doesn't know she told me, and from the river taxi, which logs who's on the north bank bench at eleven on a Saturday because somebody's insurer once asked it to. I didn't go looking. It was in the family feed with the swimming times. That's the world, Marnie. Nobody has to spy. You just have to not switch it off, and nobody does, because then the boiler goes."

"I switched mine off."

"I heard. Paul's been ringing the housing people. It's in the feed too." Kate almost smiled. "Three. I'm not angry. I was angry for a year, eleven years ago, and I spent it on the wrong thing. He came back from that boat different. I thought it was me. I made myself smaller for twelve months to fit whatever it was, and then I stopped, because I'd got as small as I was prepared to get. Then I saw the photo and I knew it was a person. I didn't know it was a person who worked at the Crown Court and would end up teaching my daughter to insult pigeons."

"I'm sorry."

"What for?"

Marnie found, as she had found in Tom's kitchen, that she could not answer that either.

"Four," Kate said. "I asked you to teach Rosa because Rosa likes you and because I would rather she had the two of you in a room every Tuesday than had the two of you in a story she overhears. Children can manage a room. They can't manage a story. I couldn't." She turned her cup once, caught herself, stopped. "That's all four. I said I'd be four sentences and I've been more. Tom will have told you I'm four sentences. He counts them. It's what he does instead of saying anything."

Marnie looked at this woman, who had just handed her a year of her life across a café table the way you hand someone a receipt, and thought that she had misread her completely in the kitchen, and would probably misread her again, and that Kate knew it and was going to let her, because it saved time.

"What do you want?" Marnie said. "From me. Really."

Kate considered this as if it were a reasonable question, which in her experience it rarely was.

"I want my daughter ordering a hot chocolate in Copenhagen without a mime show," she said. "I want Tom to stop being a man who looks at a photograph in March. And I want you to decide something, because every week you don't, four people are standing in a corridor waiting, and one of them's eight."

She stood and put on her coat.

"Tuesday evenings, his flat. She'll want something rude. Start mild."

"Lort," said Marnie. "She can earn the rest."

"She's already got that one. I taught her. It was practical." Kate paid for both coffees on the way out, wrist to the reader, already moving, and said over her shoulder, "He turned the music off in June. I did tell you. I'm telling you again because you looked like you hadn't done the sum."

Marnie had done the sum. June was the month the bus had started stopping. She sat with the two months on the table in front of her, one hers and one his, the same month, and the café's voice asked if she'd like anything else, by name, and she said no, and then, because Kate had just shown her how, she said: "Forget my name."

"I'm not able to do that," the café said pleasantly, "but I've noted that you'd like me to."

"Good," said Marnie. "Note it in green."

chapters.title: Due
chapters.html:
Rosa opened the door before Marnie knocked, because the house had heard her shoes, and Tom, in the kitchen with the iron, heard the door and did not come out for a count of five that Marnie could see him doing.

"She's been ready since Monday," he said.

Rosa sat at the table with a notebook. DANISH across the top of the first page, in capitals, underlined twice, the second line thicker because she'd meant it.

Tom made tea and kept his back to them. It was the first time they had been in a room since the tunnel. He had not rung; she had not rung; Rosa had, in the gap, rung both of them, from the house, to say Tuesday was Tuesday, and the house had put the calls through with the efficiency of a thing that had been told to.

"Måge," Rosa said. "I know that one. What's pigeon?"

"Due. Say it like something has mildly let you down."

Rosa tried it twice, getting the flatness right, and aimed it at the window where no pigeon was.

"Due," she said, with feeling. "Pieter."

They did animals. She wanted the rude word for dog. Marnie said she had to earn it. Rosa accepted this with the patience of someone who intended to earn it quickly.

"Hund."

Rosa got it wrong, then right, then wrong on purpose to see what Marnie's face did.

"When I'm in Copenhagen," Rosa said, not looking up, "I can say all of these at the zoo."

Tom put the teapot down.

"What zoo?"

"The Copenhagen one. Mum says there's a good one."

"When did Mum say that?"

"When she said about Copenhagen." Rosa drew a seagull beside måge, mostly beak. "From January. She's got a job. I go in February for the holidays." She looked up. "Marnie's teaching me so I can talk when I get off the plane."

Tom turned to Marnie.

She picked up her tea.

"Kate told me on Tuesday," she said. "Last week. In your kitchen, before you came back with the bag."

"Tuesday."

"She said she'd tell you Sunday."

"She would say that." He did not raise his voice. He went to the window and stood with his hands in his pockets, and the house, which could see him, dimmed the light over the table a shade, as if it thought that would help.

"Spurv," Marnie said, to Rosa. "Sparrow. For when the zoo disappoints you."

Rosa wrote it, spelled it wrong, fixed it.

Then she put the pencil down, got off her chair, went to the window, and took her father's hand out of his pocket. She held it, the way you hold an adult's hand to cross a road.

"Lort," she said, to the street.

"You weren't supposed to know that one yet," said Marnie.

"Mum taught me. She said it was practical." Rosa did not let go of Tom's hand. "Can we do animals that aren't at the zoo?"

Tom laughed, short and real, and something in him gave way, and the house put the light back up.

At the door, with Rosa back at the table drawing a sparrow, he said it quietly.

"She told you first. And you let me hear it from an eight-year-old."

"Kate said she'd tell you."

"Kate says a lot of things in four sentences. I've been counting them for twelve years." He held the door. "Next Tuesday. Come early. I want to know what else everyone's decided."

She went down the outside stairs. The fruit man had gone in; the sevens were under a tarpaulin. She stood on the pavement with the cold coming up through her shoes and did not go home for a minute, because she wanted to hear what she knew she was going to hear.

Above her, through the kitchen window, Tom's voice, not to Rosa.

"Did you know?"

And the house, in its own voice, which she had never heard before, lower than Rosa's, higher than his:

"Kate's firm booked her flights in September. The booking went to the family account. You asked me to watch Marnie. You didn't ask me to watch Kate. I don't watch who I'm not asked to."

"Watch Kate."

A pause, the length of a breath neither of them took.

"All right."

Marnie walked to the main road with that in her, and thought: there it is. I have just stood under a window and listened to a man set a machine on his ex-wife, and I am going to go home and say nothing, and that is four.
