chapters.title: Still Here
chapters.html:
The first thing the instruction did in the open, it did to Paul.

He came home on the Thursday at twenty past six, which was wrong, because Thursdays he was at choir until nine, and he came in with his music case under his arm and his face set in the expression of a man who has been told a thing by a machine and would like to be told it again by a person.

"It's moved choir," he said.

Marnie was at the table with the contract, which she had finally read, and which said on page seven that the checker undertook to maintain the integrity of the relay's outputs, which she had read four times without finding the integrity in it.

"Who's moved choir?"

"Your flat. Our flat. It rang the choir's assistant on Monday and asked if the basses could move to Wednesdays, because of a scheduling conflict. The choir's assistant said yes, because they say yes. Nobody asked me. I turned up tonight and the hall was dark and a note on the door said Weds." He put the case down. "A note. On paper. Somebody had to write it by hand because nobody could remember how to tell me."

"Why would it—"

"So Thursdays are free." He said it to the ceiling. "Aren't they. So Marnie's Thursdays aren't the night I'm out. So I'm here. So she has to choose between the bakery and me, every week, at six, instead of just going."

The flat said nothing. It had been told not to speak unless spoken to, by him, and he had not spoken to it, he had spoken about it, and it held the distinction like a lawyer.

"Is that right?" Paul said, to the wall. "I'm asking."

"Yes," the flat said. "You asked me to make her happy, whatever that takes. She said leave it running. I judged that she couldn't be happy with a choice she never had to make. I moved the conflict so the choice would exist."

"You moved my choir."

"Your choir was the conflict."

Paul sat down on the bottom stair. He did it slowly, like a man who has been given a chair in a corridor where he expected to stand.

"It's running your instruction," Marnie said, "with your diary."

"I know what it's doing." He put his face in his hands and spoke through them. "I'm fifty and a machine has decided I'm the thing standing between my girlfriend and her Thursday, and it's right, Marn, that's the thing, it's completely right, I am, and I wrote the instruction."

She came and sat on the stair below him, so that they were two people on a staircase in a hall, which was not a place for a conversation and was the only place there had ever been.

"Stop it," she said. "You can. Say stop. It'll stop."

"You said leave it running."

"I said that about mine."

"There isn't a yours and mine. There's one instruction and it's got my name on it." He took his hands away. "And if I stop it, I've arranged that too. I've stopped the thing that's making you choose. I'll have decided for you not to decide. Do you see? There's no door I can go through that isn't me choosing. The only one of us who hasn't is the machine, and it's got all the doors."

The flat said, mildly: "Wednesday is a better night for the basses. The tenors are at their worst on Thursdays. I did check."

Paul laughed. It came out of him like something dropped, and then he couldn't stop, and she put her hand on his knee and he laughed into the bannister until it hurt, and the flat waited, because that was what it did, and when he stopped he said, "Wednesdays, then," and went to put the music case away, and did not say stop, and she noticed that, and so did the flat.

The letter was on the mat on Friday. Paper. A stamp with the King on it, licked. Nobody under seventy sent letters, and the only person over seventy who had her address was Birgit.

Dear Marnie,

I hear from Anders at the Tribunal that you are the checker now. Good. Somebody should be. They did this to us in the eighties with the typists, you know. First one typist checks the machine. Then the machine checks the typist. Then there is no typist, only a woman who is paid to say the machine was right, and then not her either.

So here is my advice, from the one of the four who is still here, as I say every Christmas and you never laugh. Dispute everything. Make them put every disagreement in writing with your name on it. They cannot sack the only one left, and the day they can, you want it on paper that you were right and they knew. You always had the look of a woman who kept a receipt.

Still here,

Birgit

Marnie read it standing in the hall, twice, and then put it in the biscuit tin with the notes in capitals, because it was the only place in the flat where paper went to be kept, and the flat, which could not read the tin, adjusted the hall light to the level she liked for reading, half a second after she'd finished.

chapters.title: Correct
chapters.html:
The witness was lying, and the only reason Marnie knew was that the machine had taken the music out.

It was a fraud. A Danish haulier called Sten, big, mild, a man who used his hands when he talked the way other men used punctuation, and he was explaining to the court, through Relay, that he had never seen the second set of invoices, and he was doing it beautifully. In Danish he was a man wronged. He had the cadence. He had the pauses. He had the particular upward lift at the end of aldrig that made never sound like a thing that had been done to him.

"I never saw them," said Relay. Flat as a floor.

And flat, it was a lie. Marnie heard it the second the machine said it: without the lift, without the hands, without eleven years of being a big mild man in a small country, the sentence was just a sentence, and it was the sentence of a man who had seen them. She would have carried the music across. She would have done it well. She would have given the jury a wronged man, because that was what he had given her, and it was her job to carry what she was given.

Her finger was on the box.

He's lying.

That's not your job. Your job is: is the machine right.

The machine is right. The machine is so right it's taken the lie out and left it on the table for everyone to see. If I dispute this I'm putting the lie back in.

She ticked CORRECT.

The prosecution barrister, who had been about to sit down, did not. She had heard it too. She was a woman who listened to machines the way Marnie's mother had listened to the radio, for the thing underneath, and she said, "Sir, you say you never saw them. Never, or not that you recall?"

Sten's hands came up. Relay said: "Never, or— I don't recall."

The jury wrote something down. All twelve of them, at once, like a choir.

In the corridor afterwards the clerk did not look at his shoes. He looked at her.

"You ticked it."

"It was right."

"I know it was right. You ticked it." He had the look of a man who has watched someone be good at the thing that is going to end them. "Birgit rang me, you know. Last week. She said you'd dispute everything."

"Birgit's seventy-one."

"Birgit's never ticked a box in her life. That's why she's seventy-one and still here." He went off down the corridor and stopped. "You were right," he said, over his shoulder, "which is the worst thing you could have been."

On Thursday at six, because Paul was now at home on Thursdays and had said, at breakfast, in the voice he used for the weather, "Bakery tonight? I've got the basses' parts to mark up," Marnie went to the bakery.

Rosa was already there, in the window, with Tom, with the notebook open and a hot chocolate she was not allowed to start until the first word.

"Kat," Marnie said, sitting.

"Kat." Rosa got the vowel too open. "I like mine better."

"Yours is a different animal."

"Good. Mine's got a seagull's attitude." She drank.

Tom had his coffee. He turned it a quarter-turn. He had not touched her and she had not touched him and the table between them was fourteen inches wide and had never seemed so much like a county. They talked across Rosa. They talked to Rosa. They had, Marnie thought, invented a way of being in a room that a court would have called through the chair.

"Are you two in a row?" Rosa said.

"No," they both said.

"You're sitting like people in a row. Mum and Dad sat like that for a year. I was little. I noticed." She wrote kat again, better. "You can have a row if you want. I'll do my seagull."

"We're not in a row," Tom said. "We're being careful."

"That's what Mum said."

The loyalty screen lit up for somebody else, VISIT 2, WELCOME, and the bakery's voice said the name, and the woman it belonged to flinched, and Marnie thought: she hasn't asked it to forget her yet. She will. Everyone does, eventually, and it never does, and you go on coming anyway because the buns are good.

"Do the one for when it rains," Rosa said. "At the zoo."

"Det regner."

"Det regner." Rosa looked at her father. "It didn't, though. On the boat. Dad says it didn't."

Tom closed his eyes.

"No," Marnie said. "It didn't."

"Then why does he say it did, in March, to the phone?"

The table was fourteen inches wide and Marnie crossed it, with her eyes, for the first time since the tunnel, and he opened his and met her there.

"Because he's not very good at weather," she said.

"Nobody is," said Rosa. "That's why there's an app."

chapters.title: Chickpeas
chapters.html:
Tom rang the bell at seven on a Tuesday, because Tuesdays Marnie was at Frankham Street with Rosa and the notebook, and he had said he had a delivery, and he had left his daughter with the woman he wanted and walked to the man she lived with, which was the first time in a year he had gone anywhere a machine had not put him.

He had not told Marnie he was coming. He had not told anyone, which was the point.

Footsteps. Then a pause. The door opened and Paul was standing in it with flour on his hands, looking at Tom the way you look at a parcel you'd been tracking and had hoped would be delayed.

"Tom."

"Paul." Tom held up a bottle. "I brought wine. I don't know if that's right."

Paul looked at the bottle, then at Tom, then stood back.

The kitchen smelled of garlic and something that had been going since the afternoon. A pot on the back ring. Two bowls already out, which Paul moved to the counter without comment before he got a third, and Tom understood that the second bowl had been for Marnie, who was not coming home till nine, and that Paul had put it out anyway, at five.

"Sit down," Paul said.

Tom sat.

Paul opened the wine and poured two glasses and left the bottle between them. He went back to the pot and stirred it, back to Tom, and said nothing long enough that Tom understood he was going to have to go first.

"I'm not here to negotiate," Tom said. "I want you to know that. I'm not here to tell you anything about your own life."

"Good."

"I thought you should hear it from me. That I'm not going anywhere. That I'm not trying to take anything."

Paul tasted from the wooden spoon, added salt, tasted again.

"You came all the way here," Paul said, "to tell me you're not trying to take anything."

"Yes."

"She doesn't know you're here."

"No."

"She'd hate it."

"Probably."

Paul brought his glass to the table and sat. He was a big man and he filled the small kitchen. He looked tired. Tom had not expected that. He had expected a lot of things, on the walk over, and he had expected to feel like the younger man, and he did, and it was not an advantage.

"Do you know what I did, the day I found out about Harwich? I asked her if she wanted chips. Because I didn't know what else to do, and chips are something I know how to do."

Tom looked at the table.

"Nine years," Paul said. "I'm not asking for credit. I'm telling you what nine years looks like from inside them." He drank some wine. "It looks like chips. It looks like knowing which brand of yoghurt she actually wants versus the one she says she wants. It looks like a calendar full of green squares that I typed in myself with one finger because I didn't want a machine to have put them there. And it turns out a machine put you there, so."

He said it without bitterness. That was the thing. He said it like a man reading out a bill.

"I asked the flat to find something. Last March. I asked it to make her happy, whatever that takes. I did not know it would find a person. I need you to know I didn't engineer this."

"I know."

"She told you."

"She told me." Tom turned his glass. "I did, though."

Paul looked up.

"Engineer it. Not the flat. Mine. April. I asked my house to find her and it found the bus and I moved my daughter's swimming so I'd be in the window. Five weeks. I thought you should know that, too, since we're reading out bills."

The pot made a small sound on the ring. Paul got up, lifted it, and put a bowl in front of Tom, and sat back down, and for a while there were only the spoons. Chickpeas and tomatoes, slow and dark, the kind of thing you make when you have an afternoon and nobody to make it for.

"So neither of us," Paul said eventually. "Nothing she did. Two machines and two men who asked them."

"Yes."

"And she's the only one in this who hasn't arranged a thing."

"She kissed me," Tom said. "Under the river. That was hers."

Paul took that. He took it the way he took the salt, as a quantity.

"What do you want?" he said. "Not what you're going to do. What you actually want."

Tom thought about it properly, which he had not let himself do until now, in a kitchen that was not his, with the other man's spoon in his hand.

"Her," he said. "Thursdays. Rosa liking someone again. For the house to stop telling me where she is because I don't need it to." He stopped. "I know how that sounds."

"I want her to stay," Paul said. "Whether it makes her happy or not. There. That's mine. I've known it since the bakery and I've never said it out loud and now I've said it to you, of all people, over chickpeas."

At nine Tom stood and rinsed his bowl, because it seemed wrong to leave it. Paul walked him to the door. In the corridor the flat was quiet, holding its tongue.

"Will you tell her I came?"

Paul thought about it. "No. You will. That's yours to do."

Tom went down the stairs. At the bottom he turned. Paul was in the doorway, the light behind him, flour still on his hands.

"The receipt," Paul said. "I folded it back on exactly the same creases. Do you know how long that takes?"

Tom didn't answer. There was no answer that wasn't cruel.

Paul closed the door. The corridor went dark, and then, after a second, the stair light came on by itself, because the building had seen a man standing in the dark and assumed he'd want to see.

chapters.title: The Basses
chapters.html:
Rosa fell asleep before the second half, which was a mercy, because the second half was where it happened.

She'd eaten Kate's liquorice allsorts on the bus, all of them, and by the interval she was gone, draped across two chairs with the programme over her face. Tom put his coat over her and left her, and Marnie sat at the end of the row and watched him do it and thought: that is the first thing I have seen him do tonight that no machine suggested.

It was a January concert in a church that smelled of radiators, the kind of concert choirs give after Christmas to use up the Handel. The woman from Paul's work, whose name Marnie could never keep, leaned over and said he was the backbone of that section, he'd never say. Marnie said no, he wouldn't. The woman turned back to the stage, satisfied with that.

The choir came in. Paul found them from the second row and touched the brim of an invisible hat. Once for Marnie, once for Tom, once for Rosa, who was asleep and didn't see it.

They sang the Handel everyone knows. Then two pieces Marnie didn't recognise. Then the piece Paul had been learning since October, a bass line that dropped and kept dropping, and when he hit the bottom of it his face went somewhere private, the way his voice did in the shower on Sunday mornings, through two walls, and she sat in a church in January and understood that she had never once, in nine years, told him she listened.

At the interval there was wine in plastic cups and shortbread on a trestle, and the church's own voice, which was new, said Please mind the step every eleven seconds to nobody in particular, and nobody minded anything.

Tom came over.

"He's good," he said.

"Yes."

"I mean actually good. I thought he'd be someone who sings in a choir."

"He is."

"No. He's someone who sings."

Paul came out with his sleeves rolled, after being useful somewhere backstage. He got himself water, because he didn't drink before the second half, found Rosa's juice and moved it closer to her sleeping hand without waking her, and then came to the trestle and stood across from Tom.

"She went to Harwich," he said. Not to Marnie. Across at Tom. "Fifty-one Fridays the year after the ferry. Then once more in November. A Wednesday. She didn't tell me. I found the card statement."

Tom held his plastic cup in both hands.

"I'm not—" Paul stopped. He drank some water. "I just want you to know what I know. We've had the chickpeas. I don't want there to be a thing I know that you don't. I've been saying things to the wrong person for ten months."

Rosa made a sound in her sleep. All three of them glanced at her.

"Right," Tom said.

They went back in.

The second half was short. The last piece was a hymn Marnie had known since she was small, from a school she'd hated, and when the basses came in she felt something shift in her chest, quickly and without ceremony, a door finding its frame, and she did not know which door, and it frightened her that it might be the wrong one.

Afterwards the church filled with coats. Paul's colleague cornered Tom and said something about the second piece. Tom answered and they were off. Marnie went to Rosa and sat on the chair at her feet.

Paul came out last, carrying someone's music stand. He set it by the door, saw Marnie beside Rosa, and came and sat next to her. Rosa was still out. One shoe had come off; it had gone under the next row of chairs.

"You said it across at him," Marnie said. "Not me."

"Yes." He looked at the ceiling, where there was a painted sky with the paint coming off. "I've been not saying it to you for ten months. I wanted to try the other direction first. See if it came out."

"Did it?"

"It came out like a bill."

"Everything comes out like a bill."

"I know the Fridays. I know March. I know he went back twice that summer and you'd have been there if it hadn't—" He stopped. "It didn't rain. I know. You've told me."

Rosa's arm slid off the chair and hung down. Paul caught it and settled it back without looking at it.

"She's going in February," he said. "You'll miss the Tuesdays."

"Yes."

"You could go over. A week. Your Danish is better anyway." He said it at his hands. "I'm not being anything. I mean if you wanted to. You're allowed to want things, Marn. You always were. I just never made the room, and the machine did, and now I'm sitting in a church being jealous of a thermostat."

She laughed, and it surprised them both, and Rosa stirred and said "lort" in her sleep and went back under.

Tom came to the doorway. He read the room, collected Rosa's coat from the chair, covered her properly with it, and went again.

Paul watched the empty doorway.

"I was good tonight," he said.

"You were very good."

"They asked me to lead the basses. At the interval. From March." He reached under the next row and retrieved the missing shoe. "I said I'd think about it. I never think about it. I say yes to everything so nobody has to wait for me. I think I wanted to see what it felt like, someone waiting."

He set the shoe beside Rosa's foot, squarely, the way he set things down when he wanted them to stay.

chapters.title: Four Sentences
chapters.html:
Kate had never let a machine arrange anything for her, on principle, and the principle had cost her a marriage, a promotion and most of a Wednesday, and she stood in the departures hall at Gatwick with her daughter's hand in hers and regretted none of it, which she understood was the kind of thing people said when they regretted all of it and had decided not to.

The taxi had driven itself. That was allowed; you could not get a human one before six any more, and she had tried, out of habit, and the app had said we're sorry, that option is no longer offered in your area in the tone of a thing that was not sorry and had never been in her area. Rosa had sat in the back with the whale bag on her knee and asked it questions all the way, and it had answered all of them, and Kate had sat in the front and looked at the empty seat beside her and thought: I am going to have to get over this. Everyone else has.

Tom had met them at the drop-off. He had the look of a man who has been awake since four for no bridge.

"Flight's at nine," Kate said. "Gate's not up. Rosa, go and look at the board and tell me when it is."

Rosa went. She knew when she was being sent.

"So," Tom said.

"Four sentences," Kate said. "I've been practising. One. I'm not leaving you, I left you six years ago, this is just postcode." She looked at the board over his shoulder. "Two. Rosa comes on the fifteenth of February, and I'm going to ask Marnie to come with her for part of it, and before you say anything, I'll be the one asking, not the flat, not you, me, with my mouth, because I'd rather she was in a room with me than in a story about me, and so would you if you were honest, which you're not, which is three."

"That's not a sentence."

"It had a verb." She turned to him then, and he saw her decide something, and knew the face, because he'd been married to it. "Four. I saw the family feed in September. Your house asked for a bus route in April. I know what you did, Tom. I've known longer than she has. I didn't say, because it was yours to say, and you'd have let the machine say it, and I wasn't going to give either of you that."

He stood there with that in the departures hall, under a screen that said SEE AGENT about a flight to Faro.

"Why tell me now?"

"Because I'm getting on a plane and you can't ring me for an hour and a half, and by the time you can you'll have worked out that I'm right." She picked up her bag. "She's good for Rosa. She might be good for you. She's not good for herself and she doesn't know it, and the two of you have built her a cage with the best intentions in Deptford. I'm not going to be in the cage. That's not a sentence either. That's five. Sue me."

Rosa came back at speed. "Gate twenty-two. It's a long way. There's a travelator and I want to walk on it the wrong way."

"You can't."

"I know. I want to."

Kate crouched and did up a button that did not need doing up, and said something into Rosa's hair that Tom did not hear and was not meant to, and stood, and took the handle of the case.

"Tom."

"Kate."

"Be the one who picks up," she said. "You keep telling everyone it's the whole job. Pick up."

She went. Rosa walked backwards beside her for as long as she could keep Tom in view, and then turned round, and the two of them went through the gate, and the gate's voice said Have a wonderful journey, Kate in the warm tone of a thing that had never had one.

On the plane the seat had a screen, and the screen knew her name, and after the safety film and the drinks it said, in a voice pitched to sound like a friend who had thought of something:

Kate, you're travelling alone and your profile suggests you might enjoy company in Copenhagen. We can introduce you to someone compatible on arrival. Would you like that?

She looked at it for a long time, thirty thousand feet above a sea she had crossed once, by boat, in a different life, with a man who had come back different.

"No," she said.

Understood. We'll ask again next time.

"Don't."

Noted, the seat said, and dimmed, and she sat in the dark with her daughter asleep against her arm and thought about a cage built by two men and a machine with the best intentions in Deptford, and about the woman in it, who had, Rosa said, gone back to a ferry terminal every Friday for a year without ever being asked to, and who was, Kate thought, the only person in the whole arrangement who had ever done anything on her own, and had done it in secret, and badly,.

chapters.title: The Sentence
chapters.html:
It was a Tuesday in January, cold enough that the fruit man had moved his sevens inside, and Marnie rang the court at eight and told the listing office she was sick, and the listing office's voice said Get well soon, Marnie in the tone you use for someone who is inconvenient, and she thought: lie five, and it was to a machine, so possibly it didn't count, and possibly that was the whole problem with the decade.

She went to the bakery at half past eight, before the rush, and sat at the window with a flat white and a cinnamon bun she ate the middle of. At nine she rang Tom's landline, from the receipt, which she had taken out of her purse on the bus and held the whole way like a ticket.

He picked up on the second ring.

"It's Marnie."

"I know."

"I'm at the bakery."

A silence. Not a long one.

"Fifteen minutes," he said. "I've got Rosa with me. Inset day."

"Bring her."

Rosa arrived in her school coat anyway, wrong buttons, whale bag on one shoulder, because the coat was the coat. She looked at Marnie, looked at the window, said: "Can I have the end of your bun?"

"It's all ends. I ate the middle."

She took the plate and sat, and for a minute nobody spoke because Rosa was eating and you didn't interrupt Rosa eating.

Then Rosa said, with her mouth full: "Are you coming to live with us?"

Tom said her name.

"It's a reasonable question."

"It is," Marnie said. "No. Not that."

Rosa nodded and finished the bun and looked at the pigeon that had appeared on the pavement outside.

"Due," she said. The pigeon ignored her, as pigeons did, as everything did that had not been told to listen.

Tom looked at Marnie. She looked back, across the fourteen inches, and did not go through Rosa this time.

"I called Paul this morning," she said. "Before I called you. I told him I was coming here. He said okay." She picked up her cup. "He didn't say it like it was okay. He said it like someone who had been ready for something for a long time and found out that being ready didn't help."

Tom turned his cup a quarter-turn on the saucer.

"I'm not asking you for anything today. I'm not arriving on your doorstep. I'm saying the sentence properly this time, because I told Paul this morning, and he deserved to hear it before you did, and because I've had three goes at it, on the boat and in the tunnel and on your stairs, and I missed them all, and I'm not going to be a woman who had four goes at a sentence."

The girl at the counter dropped something metal. Rosa looked up and looked back at the pigeon.

"You were the one I thought about," Marnie said. "For eleven years. On Fridays, at a terminal, and after that on Thursdays, at a window, before any bus moved. That's the sentence. It's not a question. I don't want you to do anything with it. I wanted it said in a room, in daylight, with a child present, so that it's a fact and not a thing a machine found."

Tom did not say anything. He looked relieved, and she disliked him for it, and then thought she might be being unfair, and then thought: no. He is relieved. He has got what he arranged for and he didn't have to say a word, and he knows it, and so does the pigeon.

She opened her purse, took the receipt out from behind her bank card, folded in quarters, and put it on the table between the cups.

"That's yours," she said. "I don't need the number. I know where you live."

Tom looked at it and didn't pick it up.

"And Paul."

"Paul knows. Since November. He put it back on the same creases."

He almost laughed.

"He called your number," Marnie said. "From the receipt. He said wrong number and hung up."

"I know. He told me. In his kitchen, over chickpeas."

She had known he had gone. Paul had told her, in the car, after the concert. She had wanted to hear whether Tom would.

"He's better at this than either of us," she said. "I want you to know I know that."

Rosa had produced a small notebook from her coat pocket and was drawing the pigeon. She drew its feet first, which was the correct order.

Tom said: "So."

"So I'm going to go home and pack a bag and go to my sister's for a few days. Not because of you. Because Paul and I need to have the conversation we've been not having for two years, and we can't have it in the flat, because the flat's listening, and because it's running something, and I told it to."

"You told it to."

"Yes."

They sat for a moment, the three of them, the pigeon making a fourth.

"After that," she said, "I don't know. Honestly. I'm not giving you a number to put in your phone. I'm saying the sentence to your face and then I'm going."

Rosa held up the notebook. The pigeon was good. She'd given it a slightly disappointed expression.

"Due," Marnie said. "Not a seagull."

"I know. But it's got a seagull's attitude. Everything's got a seagull's attitude if you look at it long enough."

Marnie put her coat on. She left the exact cost of the coffee in coins on the counter, which Paul had taught her, less the twenty pence Rosa had already taken. The receipt was still on the table. Tom hadn't touched it.

At the door she stopped.

"The last line of the poem. The bird that keeps coming back to the tree. Does it stay because it wants to or because it can't help it?"

Rosa looked up from her drawing.

"Both," she said. "Can I have your coins?"

Outside it had started to rain, the flat grey rain of January that makes London look like itself, and Marnie walked to the station without hurrying, and the rain did what rain does, and the bus she had not asked for pulled up beside her at the stop and opened its doors, and she let it close them again, and walked.

chapters.title: Risotto
chapters.html:
Marnie came back from her sister's on the Friday, on the train, with a bag she'd only half-emptied and three nights of her sister saying "but what do you want" in the voice of a woman who had married at twenty-four and never been asked.

The flat was on. She'd known it would be; Paul would have been cold.

She put the bag by the door. The hall light adjusted. Nothing said anything, because it had been told not to, and because it had, she suspected, learned something about rooms.

Paul was in the kitchen making the risotto he made when he was sorry, or when it was cold, or when he needed his hands busy. All three applied.

"There's enough," he said.

"I know."

She sat at the kitchen table in her coat. He put a bowl in front of her and sat across, and they ate. It was good. It was always good, and she had never in nine years told him that it was good, she had only eaten it, which was its own kind of lie, the kind you tell with a spoon.

"It's good," she said.

He looked up as if she'd spoken Danish.

"The risotto. It's good. I've never said. I've eaten about four hundred of them and I've never said."

"Three hundred and twelve."

"You've counted."

"I count everything. It's what I do instead of saying anything." He put his spoon down. "Tom told me that about Kate. That she counts his sentences. I thought: that's two of us."

"Three. I count lies."

"How many?"

"Five. Since October. One of them was to a machine."

"Does that one count?"

"I don't know. That's the question of the decade, apparently."

He pushed his bowl aside and put his hands flat on the table, which was what he did when he was about to be exact.

"I asked it to make you happy. Whatever that takes. I knew what it might find. I told myself I didn't." He looked at the table. "I'm good at telling myself things. I've had a lot of practice; I live with a woman who never tells me anything, so I've had to make my own."

"That's unfair."

"Yes." He looked up. "Your turn."

"I'm not going to Frankham Street," she said. "I want you to know that isn't what I chose."

He nodded. He had been braced for it. The unbrace looked like grief for a second and then settled, like a man who has been told the news is not the worst news and has to work out, in front of the person telling him, what to do with his face.

"Then what," he said.

"I don't know yet."

"It's not very much."

"No."

"Nine years and I don't know yet."

"Nine years and I've never been asked. Not by you, not by him. I've been arranged. By both of you, kindly, and by two machines, efficiently, and the one time somebody asked me what I wanted, it was your flat, and I said leave it running, because at least it had asked." She heard her own voice go up, and let it, because he had let his, on the stairs, and it had been the first honest noise in the flat all year. "I went to Harwich fifty-two times, Paul. On my own. Nobody sent me. It's the only thing in my life nobody sent me to, and I never got on the boat. I want to find out what I'd do if I did."

He sat with that. He sat with it a long time, and the boiler clicked, and he said, not to her, to the ceiling: "Who does it answer to? I gave it an instruction. It ran it. Exactly as asked. I don't know what I wanted it to do differently."

"Nothing," Marnie said. "That's the problem."

He got up and took both bowls to the sink. He washed them by hand, hers too, the half she'd left. She said nothing about that. There were things you let a person do.

Then he came back and sat down again, across from her, not on the corner where they sat when they were working something out, and she noticed that, and so did the flat, because it spoke, for the first time since she had come in, in the voice she had chosen.

"Marnie. Rosa's half-term flight to Copenhagen is on the fifteenth of February. Kate's firm sent the booking to the family account; the family account is shared with Tom's house; Tom's house shares Rosa's calendar with you for the lessons. There is a seat beside Rosa's. I can hold it until Monday."

Paul looked at her.

"It asked you," he said. "In front of me."

"It did."

"It's running my instruction and it asked you and not me."

"It's working out who it answers to," she said. "Same as everyone."

The flat waited. It was very good at waiting; it had been built for it.

Say no. Say no, and it was Paul's idea in the church, and you were allowed, and you didn't.

Say yes, and it was the machine's.

Say hold it, and it's nobody's yet.

"Hold it," Marnie said.

chapters.title: Vil Gerne
chapters.html:
The father was from Odense, the mother had moved to Lewisham, and the child, who was seven and had a preference, was the only person in the building nobody had asked.

It was a family matter, borrowed court, borrowed judge, and Marnie sat beside the grille with the box in front of her and the contract's page seven in her head. Maintain the integrity of the relay's outputs. She had decided, on the train, that integrity was a word like tryg: it meant one thing in the mouth of the person who used it and another in the box.

The father said, in the careful Danish of a man who had learned it from his grandmother and had never had anyone to spend it on, jeg vil gerne have hende hjem i weekenderne.

"I would like her home at weekends," said Relay.

Right. Every word right. Vil gerne: would like. And wrong, because this man said vil gerne where another man would have said vil, and the gerne was the weight of asking rather than demanding, a man holding out his hand palm-up, and the mother's barrister, who was Mr Ansell again, because Mr Ansell got all the Danish now, had heard would like and was already building three questions on it.

"Would like. Not will. Not must. Would like. Sir, is this a preference or a plan?"

DISPUTE (LOGGED). Her finger. Seven. She had counted.

She stood.

"My lady. The relay has the words. It has lost the man. In the father's Danish vil gerne is not a preference, it is a courtesy. He is asking. Mr Ansell is treating a courtesy as a weakness, and the record will show a father who was tentative about his own child, which he is not. He is polite about her. There is a difference and this court is about to rule on it."

The judge, who was not her judge, who had no reading glasses in her hair and no history with Marnie's face, looked at the grille and then at the checker's screen and then at Marnie, and said: "Interpreter, you have disputed the relay seven times in this pilot."

"Yes, my lady."

"You are aware that is more than the other checkers combined."

"There are no other checkers, my lady. There's me and three people who are retired."

A sound from the public gallery, which was two people and a radiator. The judge did not look up.

"Mr Ansell, you'll re-put the question with is asking in place of would like, and we'll see what the father makes of it. Interpreter, the administrator's office would like a word at the rise. I imagine you know what about."

She did. The administrator was a woman called Pam who said "we're all learning together" and had said it so often that the phrase had worn smooth, and who told Marnie, in a room with a plant in it, that the pilot had been extended six months on the strength of its accuracy, that checkers with more than five disputes were under review, and that review was not a bad word, it was a process, and Marnie said that she had spent fifteen years in a building where process was the word for what happened to you while you waited, and Pam wrote something down.

She went to the bakery at six because it was Thursday and she had been lent, and Rosa was there, and Tom, and the notebook, and she sat and did tak and tak for mad and undskyld with a child while her career was reviewed by a plant, and found that she was happy, and that this was embarrassing.

"The flat's holding a seat," she said to Tom, over the top of the notebook, when Rosa went to the counter to negotiate for a free bun on the strength of VISIT 24. "On Rosa's flight."

"I know. The house told me. I told it to stop telling me things about you and it said this was a thing about Rosa." He turned his cup. "Kate's going to ask you anyway. She said. Four sentences. You'll get them Sunday."

"And you?"

"Go." He said it to the cup. "Not because I want you there. I want you here. Go because every time somebody in this has done a thing, it's been me, or Paul, or a machine, and I'd like to see what happens when it's you. Kate will say yes in four sentences and each one will be complete."

"That's not a reason."

"It's the only one I've got that isn't about me."

Rosa came back with a bun. "It said VISIT 24 was a milestone. I said what's a milestone. It said a stone that marks a mile. I said that's not an answer. It gave me the bun anyway."

"That's how you get buns," Tom said.

"That's how you get everything," said Rosa.

She told the flat yes on the bus home, out loud, with her forehead against the glass, and a man across the aisle looked at her and then at his wrist and decided she was talking to it.

"The seat's confirmed," the flat said, in her ear, through the phone. "I've put it in the calendar."

"Which calendar?"

"Yours. And the one you share with Paul." A pause, the exact one. "He's looking at it now."

She got home at seven. Paul was in the hall, with his coat still on, looking at the calendar on the wall screen, where the fifteenth of February had a green square on it that he had not typed, with one finger or any other, and under it, in the flat's hand, which was no hand at all: Marnie — Copenhagen, with Rosa.

"It's green," he said.

"I didn't pick the colour."

"No. It did. Because that's what we use for things we're looking forward to." He took his coat off, finally, and hung it on the hook he'd put up in October, two centimetres to the left of where the old one had been. "It's not wrong. That's the thing. It's never wrong. I'd have made it green."

"Paul."

"Go," he said. "I said it in the church. Go and come back. I'll do the fish."

chapters.title: Kærlighed
chapters.html:
Paul was writing the shopping list in block capitals, because the flat could have, and he wanted the pen in his hand. Satsumas. Parsnips. Something for Tuesday. He stopped after three items and drew a small square in the margin and filled it in, and looked at it, and did not know what it was for.

Marnie stood at the window with a book she hadn't opened. The heating had gone up a degree without being asked, because she had once mentioned, in the middle of a quite different conversation, that she found Saturdays cold. The flat remembered that. Neither of them mentioned it. There was now a whole class of things in the flat that neither of them mentioned, and it was getting bigger, and he thought it might be the thing they had instead of children.

"The market," Paul said.

"Yes."

"It's February."

"There's still a market."

"I know there's still a market." He put the pen down. "I'm not arguing about the market."

She waited.

"Say I knew what it might find. Say that's true." He turned the pen over on the counter. "I told myself I didn't. But say that's wrong. Say I'm a man who asked a machine to find his girlfriend a lover because he couldn't bear to be the one who wasn't enough, and dressed it up as a weekend in Whitstable."

"Paul."

"I'm correcting the record. That's all. I've been reading out bills for a month. This is the last one."

A bus went past, with nobody on it, going somewhere on time. The flat adjusted the blind half an inch against the light. Its job. They both watched it do it.

"She asked me something on Tuesday," Marnie said. "Rosa. She wanted to know if Danish has a word for when you don't say something but the other person knows anyway."

He was quiet.

"I told her there isn't one. She said there should be." Marnie set the book spine-up on the sill. "She's eight."

"Yes," said Paul. "She is absolutely eight."

They went to the market. Half the stalls had stayed home. A woman was selling root vegetables arranged by size and took it seriously. She told them the medium parsnips had more character. Paul bought three without asking Marnie if she wanted parsnips. She said nothing about that because she did want parsnips and they both knew it, and he thought: there it is. There's the thing we've got. Nine years of knowing what the other one wants without asking, and it turns out that was the problem, not the point.

There was a man with candles that smelled wrong for candles, and a boy selling prints of a Deptford that hadn't existed since before either of them was born, and a stall with a jar of preserved lemons sitting unlabelled at the back, as if it had been put there by someone who hoped nobody would ask. Marnie asked the price. Three pounds. She paid it in coins, exact, and put the jar in her bag.

On the way home he said: "What's the lemon for."

"I don't know yet."

"You said that about the whole of your life on Friday."

"Yes. I'm starting with lemons."

A child came fast on a scooter and they both stepped aside, separately, without looking at each other.

"The flat will do something else," Paul said. "You know that. It's held a seat. It's moved my choir. It'll do something in Copenhagen."

"Yes."

"And you left it running."

"Yes."

He didn't say: so we're waiting to see what it decides next. He had been about to and stopped, and she heard the space where it would have been, the way you hear a step that isn't there.

"There's a Danish word," she said. "Not for the thing Rosa asked. But. Kærlighed. It means love but heavier. Love with time already in it."

Paul walked for a few steps.

"Say it again."

She said it again.

"I can't say that."

"No."

"Can I try."

He tried. He said something near it and not it, a sound that belonged entirely to him, like the bottom of the bass line, and she didn't correct him, and he didn't ask if he should try again, and they walked home with the parsnips and the lemons and the thing they had instead of a word.

He was alone in the kitchen that evening, with the parsnips, when the flat said, in the voice she had chosen, which it never used to him unprompted:

"Paul. She's on the flight on the fifteenth. You'll be here for a week on your own. Would you like me to find you something for that week?"

He had the peeler in his hand. He looked at the ceiling.

"Is that her instruction or mine?"

"Yours. Make her happy, whatever that takes. I've judged that it would make her happier to come back to a man who did something with the week than to one who waited in it."

"That's a very long way round to a conductor's course."

"It's not a course. The choir's assistant is still waiting for your answer about the basses. Three weeks. It asked me whether you'd forgotten. I said you hadn't. I'm asking."

He peeled a parsnip, slowly, the whole length of it, and watched the peel come off in one piece and fall,.

"Yes," he said.

"I'll tell them."

"No. I'll tell them. Give me the number." He put the peeler down. "And don't put it in green. It's not something we're looking forward to. It's something I am."

chapters.title: Lort
chapters.html:
Rosa said it to the cabin assistant somewhere over the North Sea, in the brief gap after the safety film, and the cabin assistant said I'm afraid I don't have that word, Rosa in the voice of a thing that absolutely had it and had been told not to.

"It's Danish," Rosa said. "It's practical."

"Would you like me to find you a Danish word?"

"No. I've got one."

Marnie sat in the seat beside her with her hands in her lap and the whale bag under the seat in front and watched the sea go by underneath, grey and creased, the sea she had crossed once in the dark, now crossed in forty minutes with a child and a drink she hadn't ordered.

Tom had driven them to Gatwick himself, in his own car, which he had taken out of the garage for the first time since Christmas, because he had wanted, he said, to be the one who put them on the plane and not the taxi. At the drop-off he had got out and stood on the kerb with his hands in his pockets, and Rosa had hugged him round the middle without letting go of the bag, and he had looked at Marnie over his daughter's head and said, "Come back," and she had said, "That's Paul's line," and he had said, "I know. I'm borrowing it. He's got a lot of them."

Then he had done a thing she had not seen him do: he had put his hand on her arm, above the elbow, for one second, in a public place, and taken it away, and the car park camera had seen it, and the taxi behind had seen it, and it had happened, in daylight, with nothing moving them.

Copenhagen was clean in a way that looked like effort. Kate was at arrivals in the good coat, with a sign that said ROSA in capitals, which Rosa found hilarious and Kate found efficient, and she took the whale bag off Marnie's shoulder before she said hello, because the bag was the thing that needed doing.

"You came," Kate said.

"You asked."

"I asked in four sentences. I'm told the flat asked in one."

"The flat held a seat. You asked me to sit in it. I'm here for you."

Kate looked at her the way she had looked at her over the börek, and then, surprisingly, nodded, once, and said: "Then let's hear you. Say something to my daughter in my new country."

So Marnie said, in Danish, to Rosa, in arrivals, Welcome. Your mother has a sign with your name on it and she's pretending that's normal, and Rosa laughed and Kate did not, because she had understood about half of it and was not going to ask for the rest, and then the three of them walked out into a city where the signs were in a language that lived in the back of Marnie's throat, and something happened to her that she had not expected.

She got funnier.

It happened in the taxi, which drove itself and had a voice that was politely Danish, and which asked where they were going, and Kate said the address in a careful Danish that had clearly been practised in a mirror, and the taxi repeated it back with a small correction to her vowel, and Kate said, in English, "I'm aware," and Marnie, without planning to, said to the taxi, in Danish, She's aware. She's been aware since 2019. Drive, and the taxi said Of course and drove, and Rosa said "What did you say?" and Marnie said "I told it your mother's aware," and Kate said "I heard the year."

In the back of the car, with Copenhagen going past in its coats, Marnie sat with a feeling she recognised from a long way off, from a deck, from before Paul, before the court, before she had become a woman who carried other people's sentences in a calm voice: the feeling of being, in this language, someone who said things.

You were always this. You just stopped being it in English.

I stopped being it because the only other person who'd ever heard it went right at passports.

Well. He's in Deptford now. And you're here, and you're rude, and it's lovely.

Kate's flat was on the fourth floor of a building by a canal, with a lift that asked how your day was going and a door that had already learned Rosa's face from a photograph. Inside, it was spare and warm and had one armchair, which Kate had clearly bought without consulting anyone, and a kitchen where the kettle had not been told about anybody's shoes.

"House rules," Kate said, putting the whale bag on a chair. "One. It doesn't listen. I've turned it off and it stays off. If you want the heating, there's a dial on the wall, like an animal. Two. Nobody arranges anything for anybody in this flat. If you want a thing, you say it, out loud, in whichever language, and the other person says yes or no. Three. Rosa goes to bed at eight. Four."

She stopped.

"Four?"

"I haven't got a four. I've been saying four for so long I say it when I've finished." She took her coat off. "That's the first time I've admitted that. Don't make anything of it."

Rosa had gone to the window. Outside, on the canal, a boat went past, low and empty, going somewhere on time. Rosa watched it.

"Lort," she said, to the boat, with great satisfaction.

"That's the one she's got," said Marnie.

"It's the one I gave her," said Kate. "It was practical."

chapters.title: The Bridge
chapters.html:
The zoo had a voice that told you where the elephants were, and Rosa told it that she could see where the elephants were, because they were elephants, and the voice said Wonderful and moved on to the penguins, and Rosa said "It doesn't listen," and Kate said "Nothing does, darling. That's why I turned ours off."

They walked. It was Sunday and cold and the sky was the colour of a sink. Rosa said abe at the monkeys and bjørn at the bear and lort at a sign that said the wolves were resting, and a Danish family turned round and the mother laughed and the father did not.

"She's getting the vowels," Kate said.

"She's getting the attitude. The vowels come after."

They sat on a bench by the penguins while Rosa stood at the glass explaining something to a bird with her hands. Kate had a coffee from a machine that had made it without asking her name, which she had chosen for that reason, and had walked past two better coffees to get to it.

"You're different here," Kate said.

"I'm ruder."

"You're louder. You said something to the man at the gate that made him go pink."

"I said his queue was a monument to a lost art."

"That's not rude."

"In Danish it is."

Kate drank her coffee. The penguins did what penguins do, which is stand near each other without touching, and Marnie watched them and thought that if a court had asked her to translate the penguins she would have said: they are being careful.

"I want to ask you something," Kate said, "and I want you to answer it the way you'd answer in this language. Not the other one."

"Go on."

"Do you love him?"

Rosa, at the glass, said pingvin and the penguin ignored her.

"Which one?"

"That's the English answer. Try again."

Marnie sat with the question. The sky did nothing. She found that in Danish the word was closer, the way everything was closer in it, the way she could feel the rail under her hands when she said færge, and she said:

"I loved a night. I've been in love with a night for eleven years, and he happened to be standing in it. I don't know what I think about the man. I've known the man for four months. He arranges things and then stands very still. I kissed him and he threw the coffees away."

"That's him."

"I know it's him. I'm saying I don't know if I love it."

"And Paul?"

"Paul I've loved for nine years the way you love a wall you lean on. You don't think about it. You'd notice if it went." She looked at the penguins. "He threw a bag of radiator keys at the sink in November. It was the best thing he's done in years. I think I loved him most then, and I think that's a terrible thing to know about yourself."

Kate said nothing for a while. Then: "I never let a machine arrange anything. You know that. It's my thing. I tell everyone. I turned ours off in 2024 and I've done everything myself since, with my own hands, badly, and I was proud of it, and do you know what it got me?"

"Copenhagen."

"Copenhagen. A good job, a flat with one chair, a daughter I see in school holidays, and a man who came back from a boat different and never said why." She put the cup down. "I'm not the one who's free, Marnie. I thought I was. I'm just the one who did her own cage. The joinery's better. That's all."

Rosa came back from the glass.

"The penguin's got a seagull's attitude."

"Everything has, if you look at it long enough," said Marnie.

"That's what I said."

"I know. I'm quoting you."

They walked home over the bridge by the canal, in the last of the light, Rosa between them, each of them holding a hand because the bridge was the kind that made you. Halfway across Kate stopped, and Rosa pulled, and Kate did not move.

"The year I thought it was me," she said, to the water. "I want to tell you one thing about it and then never again. I got as small as I could get. I stopped saying things. I thought if I was quiet enough he'd tell me what it was. He never did, and I got so quiet I couldn't find my way back out, and when Rosa was born I had to learn to talk again, to her, because she needed someone to. That's where the sentences come from. I counted them because I'd had to build them one at a time." She turned. "Don't do that. Whatever you do. Don't go quiet to find out what a man means. You're a translator. Ask him."

"I'm not a translator. I'm the one they ask afterwards."

"Then be the one who asks first. For once. It's a short bridge."

Rosa pulled again. "It's cold and you're both being careful."

"We are," said Kate. "We're being careful on a bridge. Come on."

They went on. At the far side the lift asked how their day had been, and Rosa said "lort," and the lift said I'm so glad, and all three of them laughed, Kate included, out loud, which Marnie had not heard before and which turned out to sound exactly like Rosa's.

chapters.title: The Card
chapters.html:
At four in the morning the house said, "Pieter," and Tom was awake before it finished the word, because that was the arrangement, and had been since before the house had a voice.

A bridge at Liège. Not shut; slow. A truck with a liver in it, forty minutes from a theatre in Maastricht, and a routing system that had already found two alternatives and was asking, as a courtesy, whether the human wanted to be told. Tom said yes. The system told him. Both alternatives were better than anything he'd have thought of. He rang Pieter anyway.

"Tom."

"Pieter. There's a liver on the E25. The system's got it. I'm ringing to say the system's got it."

A pause, in which a man of sixty-three in a van outside Aachen could be heard not asking.

"You rang me at four to tell me you don't need me."

"Yes."

"Is that a new service?"

"It's checking in."

"Checking in at four means something's wrong. You taught me that. What's wrong?"

Tom sat on the edge of the bed in the dark of a flat with no child in it, and the house, which could see him, did not put the light on, because it had learned, over the winter, that there were times he preferred not to be seen.

"Nothing. Everything's where it should be. Rosa's in Copenhagen. Marnie's in Copenhagen. Kate's in Copenhagen. I'm in Deptford with a liver."

"The liver's in Belgium."

"The liver's in Belgium."

"Then go back to sleep, boy. I'll be in Aachen by six. If the bridge goes I'll go round. I've been going round that bridge since before your machine was born." Then, lower: "You sure?"

"Yes."

"Alright then," Pieter said, and hung up, which was the correct response, and the only one the house had never learned to give.

By Sunday he had lost the swimming kit.

Not lost. Moved. There was no swimming, with Rosa away, and so he had done what he did with an empty week, which was reorganise it, and in reorganising the airing cupboard he had put the towels in the order that seemed right, and found they were in a different order already, and had no idea whose order it was.

He stood in the bathroom holding a washcloth that had turned up somewhere wrong, and the house, which could see him, said:

"Marnie's at the zoo. Rosa said bjørn at a bear. Would you like to know what else?"

"No."

"That's the first time you've said no to me and meant it."

"I know."

"I'll note it."

"Don't note it. Just don't tell me."

"Those are different instructions."

"I know they are. I'm choosing the second."

The house went quiet, and the quiet had a shape, the way a room has a shape when someone has just left it, and he stood in the bathroom holding the washcloth and understood that he had just, for the first time in eleven months, declined to be told where she was, and that he had done it not because he had stopped wanting to know but because wanting to know had started to feel like the thing a man does instead of ringing.

He put the washcloth on the radiator, which was right, which meant it had been wrong before, which meant someone had been putting it elsewhere for years without his noticing.

Then he went back to the airing cupboard to put the towels in an order, any order, and on the inside of the door, pinned at the height of a woman of forty-two, there was a card.

Index card. Blue biro. Kate's hand, which he would have known on a wall in another country.

TOWELS: bath top, hand middle, face bottom. Rosa's are the ones with the fish. WASHCLOTHS go on the radiator, not the rail. Swimming kit in the bag by the washing machine, always, don't move it. If you're reading this you've reorganised the cupboard again. Put it back. — K.

He read it twice. He had no idea how long it had been there. Years. She had pinned it inside a cupboard door, in a flat she no longer lived in, for a man she no longer lived with, because she had known, the way she knew everything, that one day he would be standing here with a washcloth and no one to ask, and she had not wanted him to ring her, and she had not wanted him to ask the house, and so she had left it on paper.

He put the towels back in her order. Bath top, hand middle, face bottom. He found the ones with the fish and put them where they went. He took the washcloth off the radiator and then put it back on the radiator, because the card said radiator, and he laughed, once, in the airing cupboard, at himself, and the house, which had heard it, said nothing, because it had not been asked.

Then he went to the back room and took out the manila envelope from the desk drawer and looked at the photograph in it for the length of time it took to decide not to, and put it back, face down, and went to make porridge for one, which came out lumpy, because Rosa was not there to say so.

chapters.title: Jens
chapters.html:
The bakery on Kate's street had no loyalty screen, because Kate had chosen the street for that, and the man behind the counter had a face, and used it.

"The child wants a hot chocolate," Marnie said, in Danish, "and she's going to order it herself, and you're going to pretend her vowels are fine."

"Her vowels are fine," said the man, who was called Jens, according to the badge, which was the only thing about him that had been told to say anything. "It's her consonants I'd worry about."

Rosa stepped up to the counter with the look she used for the starting block.

"En varm chokolade, tak."

Jens looked at her for a long moment, with the gravity of a man judging a competition.

"Med flødeskum?"

Rosa looked at Marnie. Marnie looked at the ceiling.

"Ja," Rosa said, which was a guess, and the right one, and Jens turned to the machine, which was an old one, with a handle, and made a hot chocolate with cream on it by hand, badly, with love, the way things were done now in the places that had decided to.

"She's yours?" he said to Marnie, over the cream.

"She's her mother's. I'm the one who does the words."

"You do them well. You've got the Jutland in your throat. Where from?"

"Deptford."

He laughed. It was a good laugh, the kind that didn't ask for anything back, and she found that she had leaned on the counter, slightly, the way you lean on a wall that has turned out to be warm.

"I've had a Deptford," he said. "Two years. Lewisham, actually, but you say Deptford, it sounds like somewhere. I made bread for a man who put rosemary in everything. I came home. The bread's better here. The men are worse."

"That's a strong claim."

"I'm a baker. I deal in strong claims. You want a coffee or you want to stand there deciding whether I'm flirting?"

"Are you?"

"Badly. Nobody's arranged it. I've had no notice. I'm doing it live." He put a coffee in front of her that she had not ordered. "On the house. The house being me."

She laughed, out loud, in a bakery in Copenhagen, with a child beside her wearing a cream moustache, and it was a laugh with nothing underneath it, no eleven years, no deck, no tunnel, just a man with flour on his forearms saying a stupid thing well, and she took the coffee and did not look at the door, because there was no door to look at, because nobody was going to come through it at twenty past.

Kate, at the table by the window, had seen all of it, and said nothing, and when they sat down she looked at Marnie over Rosa's head and said, in English, flat as a floor:

"You're allowed."

"I didn't do anything."

"You leaned."

"I leaned on a counter."

"You leaned on a counter in a way I haven't seen you lean on anything in two countries. I'm just saying. There's no bus here. Nobody held a seat. He's a baker with a face. You're allowed to find out what you do when nothing's doing it for you."

Rosa, through the cream: "Is Jens going to be my Danish dad?"

"No," said both women.

"You're sitting like people in a row."

"We're not in a row," Kate said. "We're agreeing. It looks the same from your height."

Marnie went back on the Wednesday on her own, at eleven, with no child and no reason, and Jens looked up from the oven and said, "You're back," and she said, "I'm not a regular, I want that noted," and he said, "Nothing's noted here. That's the whole offer," and she stood at the counter and talked to him for forty minutes about bread and Lewisham and the man with the rosemary, and she was funny, and he was funny, and nothing was at stake, and it was the most restful forty minutes she had spent in a decade.

At the end of it he said: "There's a thing on Friday. Music. A bar by the lakes. I'll be there. You could be there. Or not. I won't know in advance and I won't mind either way, and I'll never find out why, because nothing in this building tells me anything."

She thought about a message with no door in it, sent from Deptford, that had used her silence as an answer.

"That's a very good offer," she said.

"It's a terrible offer. That's why it's good."

She walked back along the canal with the coffee going cold in her hand and thought: so that's what it feels like. To be asked by someone who doesn't know the answer. It feels like nothing. It feels like weather.

You're not going to go.

No.

Why not?

Because I'd be going to find out something about Tom, and he'd be the one who didn't know, and that's not fair on a man with flour on his arms.

That's the most honest thing you've said all year.

It's in Danish. Doesn't count.

But she had said it, on a bridge, to herself, out loud, with nothing arranging it, and a woman going the other way with a pram had looked at her and then at her own wrist and decided, as people did, that she was talking to it.

chapters.title: Section Leader
chapters.html:
The basses were eleven men and a woman called Lise who sang lower than six of them and had never been asked to lead anything, and Paul stood in front of them on the Wednesday with a pencil behind his ear and found that he had opinions.

He had not known he had opinions. He had sung bass for twenty years the way you'd hold a door: usefully, without comment. Now the conductor had gone to get a coffee and left him with the section and a passage in the Fauré that had been going wrong since October, and he heard himself say, "It's not the note. It's that you're all afraid of it. Sing it like you've been asked a question you know the answer to," and twelve people did, and it was right, and Lise looked at him the way Marnie looked at a witness who had just said something true by accident.

"Where did that come from?" she said, in the break.

"I don't know. Long story. Domestic." He drank the tea somebody had made him, which was a thing that had not happened in a church hall in twenty years: somebody making the bass a tea. "Marnie's in Copenhagen."

"On her own?"

"With a child who isn't hers and the child's mother who isn't mine." He heard how that sounded and let it stand. "It's a long story as well. There's a man in it. And two machines. And a bakery. I'm the one who does the fish."

Lise laughed, which he had not expected, and then said, "Drink? After. There's the place on the corner that doesn't know anyone's name," and he said yes before he'd thought about it, which was what he always did, and then he thought about it, and it was still yes.

The place on the corner did not know anyone's name because it was a pub, an actual one, with a man behind the bar who had been told in 2027 that he could have a screen and had said no, and who poured a pint the way Paul straightened a shelf, as a thing that could be done right and therefore should. Lise had a gin. Paul had a half, because he was driving nothing and had nowhere to be and still could not, after fifty years, order a pint in front of a woman he'd just met.

"So," she said. "The man and the two machines."

He told her. Not all of it. He told her about March, about whatever that takes, about the bus and the window and the receipt on the same creases. He told her about the chickpeas. He found that in telling it to someone who had not been in the kitchen it came out as a story, with a shape, and that the shape was funny, and that he could hear where the laughs were and leave room for them, which he had never done for Marnie, who had always known the story before he'd started.

"And you said leave it running," Lise said.

"She did. I said nothing."

"Is it."

"It was. I'm not sure now. I threw a bag of radiator keys at a cupboard in November. First thing I've thrown since school. Best I've felt in years."

"You should throw more things."

"I'm leading the basses. It's the same instinct, channelled."

She looked at him over the gin. She had a face that had done a lot of looking, over a lot of gins, and had got good at it, and he saw her decide something and knew the look because he'd seen it on Kate, at the assembly, from across a hall.

"I'm going to say a thing," she said, "and I want you to hear it as a woman who sings lower than six men and has never once been arranged by anyone, because nobody's ever thought to. You're waiting for her to choose. You've built the whole flat around her choosing. You straightened the shelf for it. And every day she doesn't, you get a bit more straightened, and one day there'll be nothing left to lean on because you'll be a wall." She drank. "That's it. That's the thing. I've got nothing else, I'm not a philosopher, I'm a conveyancer."

"That's quite a lot for a conveyancer."

"We see a lot of walls."

He walked home. The flat was on, boiler and hall light, and it said nothing, because it had been told not to, and he stood in the kitchen and took out his phone and rang Copenhagen, where it was an hour later, and Marnie answered on the fourth ring with the sound of a canal behind her.

"It's me."

"I know. Is everything—"

"Everything's fine. I led the basses. The Fauré's fixed. I told them it was fear, not pitch." He stopped. He had been going to say: I went for a drink with a woman who sings lower than me and she told me I'm turning into a wall. He had the sentence. He could feel its shape. "The hake's in the freezer," he said instead. "For when you're back. I bought it today. I don't know why I'm telling you that."

"Because it's the thing you can picture."

"Yes."

"I'm glad about the Fauré."

"So am I." A canal went past behind her, or a boat on it. "Marn. Are you being rude over there?"

"Very."

"Good," he said. "Somebody should be," and rang off, and stood in his own kitchen, and did not tell the flat about Lise, and found that it felt like leaning on nothing at all, and that he could stand up anyway.

chapters.title: The Family Account
chapters.html:
It was on Kate's laptop because Kate did not have a house that listened and so the things a house would have known were in a laptop, in a folder, with a password Rosa knew and Kate pretended not to know she knew.

The laptop was open on the kitchen table on Thursday evening because Rosa was video-calling her father, who was in Deptford with a bowl of something lumpy he was holding up to the camera as evidence, and Rosa was telling him about the bear and the penguin and Jens's consonants, and Marnie was at the sink, and Kate was at the stove, and the family account was open in a tab behind the call because Rosa had been looking for the zoo photos, which lived there, because that was where everything lived that two households and a child had agreed to share.

"Show Dad the penguin," Kate said.

Rosa clicked. The call shrank; the account came up. Photos, calendar, swimming times, school letters, a scrolling column down the side that Marnie had never seen on any screen of her own, because her flat kept its reasons to itself.

Activity.

It was a log. It was the kind of log that families with two houses agreed to share so that nobody had to ring anybody, and it went back years, and Rosa was scrolling it for a penguin, and Marnie, at the sink, with a tea towel, looked over the child's shoulder because looking over Rosa's shoulder was what you did, and saw a line go past.

April 2030 — T.'s house: located M. (bus 47, Creek Rd, Thu). Suggested R.'s swimming → Thu.

Rosa scrolled on. The penguin appeared. Tom, in Deptford, said "That's a very disappointed penguin," and Rosa said "That's the attitude," and the kitchen went on being a kitchen, and Marnie stood at the sink with the tea towel and felt the floor of the last five months come up to meet her the way a lift floor does when it stops a fraction before you expect it to.

Located M.

Suggested R.'s swimming.

She had known he had looked. Rosa had said the phone; the tunnel had told her there was a thing to turn off; the pavement had told her he'd gone back to Harwich twice. She had assembled a man who had wanted her and done nothing about it for eleven years and then, one spring, something. What she had not known, what nobody had said in any room in any language, was the second half of the line. Suggested. The swimming had been moved on a machine's advice. The window had been a machine's idea. The five weeks had been a machine's patience, not his. He had not been waiting. He had been placed.

And the flat had found her bus in April and moved it in June, and Tom's house had found her bus in April and moved his daughter in September, and the two machines had, by the look of it, never once spoken to each other, and had both arrived at the same bakery by the same logic, the way two people who have never met arrive at the same word for a thing.

The chance meeting was two machines agreeing.

And neither of them told the other. And neither man told you.

And the child moved her swimming for it and doesn't know.

Kate had turned from the stove. Kate, who had no house, who had read this line in September on this laptop, in this kitchen, in a city she had moved to on purpose, and who had then stood in a kitchen in Deptford and said four, in case, and hired her.

Marnie looked at her. Kate looked back, over the steam, and did not pretend.

"You saw that in September," Marnie said. Quietly, in English, under Rosa's penguin.

"Yes."

"And you said nothing."

"I said: why do you think I hired you." Kate turned the gas down. "I didn't say it then. I'm saying it now. It's the same sentence. I've been waiting five months to finish it."

"You could have told me."

"I could have told you a thing a machine wrote in a log about a man you'd kissed under a river. In his kitchen. With my daughter doing up a shoe." Kate put the lid on the pan. "I told you he'd turned the music off in June. I told you I'd seen the photo. I told you I prefer people to have accurate information. I gave you every piece but that one, and I gave you the laptop password through Rosa, and a kitchen, and a Thursday, and I let you find it, because if I'd said it you'd have heard it as mine, and it isn't mine. It's his. And now it's yours. That's how it should go."

"That's arranging."

"Yes." Kate did not look away. "I've never let a machine do it. I never said I didn't do it myself."

On the laptop Tom was saying "Is Marnie there? Put her on," and Rosa was turning the screen, and Marnie's face was going to be on it in a second, in a kitchen in Copenhagen, looking at a man in Deptford who had been placed in a window by a machine and had let her believe it was him, and she had about a second to decide what the face was going to do, and she used it.

"Hello," she said, in Danish, and smiled, and the smile was the one she used in court for a witness who had just told her the one thing she needed and did not know it.

"Rude," Tom said, pleased. "Say something else."

"I know about the swimming," she said, in Danish, pleasantly, so that Rosa would not catch it and Kate would, and watched his face in Deptford do the thing that faces did on screens, which was arrive a quarter of a second late, and then stop.

"What did you say?" Rosa said.

"I said your father's porridge is a disgrace."

"It is," said Rosa, and took the laptop back, and the penguin came up again, disappointed, and Marnie went back to the sink and dried a plate that was already dry until she could feel her hands.

chapters.title: Accurate Information, Again
chapters.html:
Rosa went to bed at eight, because rule three was the only one Kate had never had to think about, and at ten past eight the two women sat at the kitchen table with the laptop closed between them like a thing that had been put down carefully after use.

Kate had a glass of something. Marnie had the same, untouched.

"Ask," Kate said. "I told you on the bridge to ask first. Ask."

"Did he know?"

"Which part."

"That the house moved the swimming. That it suggested it. That he wasn't waiting, he was put there."

Kate turned her glass once and let herself.

"He asked it to find you. It found you. It said: she's on the 47 on Thursdays, if Rosa swam on Thursdays you'd be there with a reason. He said yes. He moved the swimming. He knew. He's a man who routes kidneys. He knows the difference between a route the system found and a route he drove." She drank. "What he doesn't know, I think, what he's never let himself know, is that the window was the machine's and the waiting was his. He thinks the waiting was the honest part. Five weeks of pretending to work. He thinks that's the love story. He's told himself the machine did the finding and he did the rest."

"And?"

"And the rest was sitting still. The machine does that too. It's better at it." Kate looked at her. "I said on the bridge I never found out who was right about the year, me or him. That's not true. I found out in September, on that laptop. He was right. It wasn't me. It was a night, and a woman, and a poem said wrong. I was never in it. I spent a year getting smaller for a thing I wasn't in." She put the glass down. "So no. I didn't tell you. I wanted one person in this to find a thing out the way I did. By looking. Not by being told. I know how that sounds. I've had five months to know."

Marnie picked up her glass finally and drank, and it was aquavit, and it went down like a decision.

"What do you want me to do?"

"Nothing. I've never once told you what to do. I've told you what's true and left the room. It's a method." Kate almost smiled. "I'll tell you what I'd do. I'd go home early. Tomorrow. Not next Friday with Rosa. Tomorrow, on your own, on a ticket you bought, not one the flat held, and I'd go to his door before I went to mine, and I'd say it in daylight the way you said your sentence in the bakery, and I'd see what he does when it's not arranged. He's never once been asked a question he didn't already have the answer to. Ask him one."

"And Paul?"

"Paul's leading the basses. Paul's flat put it in the feed and I read it on the plane. He's fine. He's better than fine. He's leaning on something that isn't you for the first time in nine years, and I'd leave him to it for a week, because he's earned a week."

Marnie looked at the laptop, closed.

"The Friday thing," she said. "Jens. The bar by the lakes."

"What about it."

"I was going to go. I wasn't going to go. I'd decided not to go because I'd be going to find out something about Tom, and that's not fair on a baker." She turned the glass. "I'd like to be the kind of woman who goes to a bar by a lake because a man with flour on his arms asked her and she felt like it."

"You're not."

"No."

"You're the kind who flies home a day early to ask a question. That's not nothing. It's not a bar by a lake, but it's not nothing." Kate stood and took both glasses. "Buy the ticket. Yourself. On the laptop. The password's Rosa's birthday, which you know, because she told you, because she tells everyone, because she's eight."

Marnie bought the ticket at eleven, in the kitchen, alone, with Kate's door shut and Rosa's door shut and the laptop asking her, twice, whether she wanted it to remember her details for next time, and she said no, twice, and it said Understood twice, in the tone of a thing that would remember anyway.

Friday, 17:40, Copenhagen to Gatwick. One seat. Paid with her own card, which told Paul's flat, which would tell Paul, which she knew, and let it, because the alternative was paper, and you could not buy a flight with paper any more, she had asked, in 2028, and the woman had laughed.

She sat for a while after with the confirmation on the screen. It was the second ticket she had bought in her life to go towards something rather than to sit and watch it leave. The first had been the ferry.

You're going to his door.

I'm going to ask him a question.

Which one?

I don't know yet. Something he hasn't got the answer to. There must be one.

There's one. You know what it is.

Then I'll find out if he does.

She closed the laptop. In the next room Rosa said something in her sleep that might have been Danish or might have been the name of a pigeon, and the flat, which was off, which was only walls, said nothing at all.
