chapters.title: Since the Boat
chapters.html:
Gatwick had a voice at arrivals that said Welcome home to everyone, including the people for whom it wasn't, and Marnie walked through it with a bag over her shoulder and a question she had turned over so many times on the plane that it had worn smooth, like Pam's phrase, like a receipt folded on the same creases.

Nobody met her. She had told nobody. The flat knew, because the card knew, and Paul would know by now, because the flat would have put it somewhere, in some colour, and she thought about that on the train and found that she did not mind, because she had not asked it to and she had not asked it not to and the question of whose doing it was had stopped seeming like a question with an answer.

It was dark by the time she got to Deptford; it was gone eight, and February, and the pharmacy had been shut for hours. She came out of the station and the 47 was there, with its doors open, in the way it had, and she looked at it, and it looked at her, in the way a bus does, with its whole lit face, and she walked.

Frankham Street. The pharmacy, shut. The fruit man's tarpaulin. The outside stairs, which she took one at a time, because she had taken them two at a time once, with satsumas, and that had been a different woman.

She did not ring. She knocked, with her knuckles, on wood, which told nobody anything except the person on the other side.

He opened it. He had a tea towel over his shoulder and a face that had been expecting the knock for about eleven hours, since a kitchen in Copenhagen, and had not got any readier.

"You're early," he said.

"I bought a ticket."

"I know. The house—"

"I don't care what the house knows. I'm asking you something." She stood on the top step with the bag on her shoulder and the whole of Frankham Street behind her in the dark. "You looked for me. In April. You asked it to find me."

"Yes."

"It found the bus. It said: move the swimming. You moved the swimming."

"Yes."

"And then you sat in a window for five weeks and let me think it was you."

He did not say anything. He held the door. The tea towel on his shoulder said, in the faded print of something bought in a different decade, GREETINGS FROM WHITBY.

"I didn't know you'd been looking," she said. "Until Rosa said the phone. I didn't know about the swimming until yesterday. I've known since the tunnel that you had a thing to turn off and I've known since the pavement that you'd been to Harwich twice and I've known since Kate that the music went off in June, and I have been assembling you, Tom, out of pieces, the way I'd assemble a witness, and I'm tired of it. I want one thing from you that no machine found and nobody arranged and I didn't have to work out. One. Can you do that?"

"What thing?"

"That's the question. I don't know. I've come from Copenhagen to find out if you've got one."

He stood there. She watched him look for it. She watched him go through the places a man like him would look: the house, which he did not ask; the photograph, which was in a drawer; the five weeks, which were, she saw him understand, the machine's; the coffees in the bin, which had been his, and had been a refusal. He went through all of it standing in his own doorway with a tea towel, and she thought: he hasn't got one. He's going to say I love you, which the house could have said, or I'm sorry, which it could have said better.

"The poem," he said.

She waited.

"I got the last line wrong. On the boat. You corrected me. I said my version was better." He had both hands on the door frame now. "It wasn't. I knew it wasn't. I said it because I wanted you to argue with me, because if you argued we'd still be talking, and it was three in the morning and I'd worked out that when the talking stopped we'd go inside. So I was wrong on purpose. For another hour. That's the only thing I've ever done that nobody arranged and nobody found and you didn't work out, and it's eleven years old, and it's stupid, and it's yours."

Marnie stood on the top step of the outside stairs in February with that.

"You were wrong on purpose."

"For an hour."

"And then you kept saying it wrong."

"For eleven years. To the phone. Every March. Because it was the version you'd argued with." He looked at the step. "Rosa says it right now. I taught her the right one. I thought that was the end of it."

"It wasn't."

"No."

She came up the last step, and he moved back, and she went in, and he shut the door, and the house, which had heard all of it, which could have said any of it, said nothing, because for once in its existence nobody had asked it to.

Later, in the dark, in a bed that was not hers in a flat over a pharmacy, with his arm under her neck and the street going past on the other side of the window, she said:

"Since the boat."

"What?"

"If anyone asks, you'll say April. It's not April. It's since the boat. For both of us. The machines just got there second."

He didn't answer. She felt him not answer, which was different from silence, and better, and she lay in it, and thought: I have not told Paul. I have not rung Paul. The card told the flat and the flat told Paul and Paul is in the flat, on his own, with hake in the freezer, and he knows, and he has said nothing, because it's his gift, and I am lying here in it.

Six, she thought. And the first one I didn't have to say out loud.

chapters.title: Don't Answer
chapters.html:
The house woke him at seven with a question, which it had never done, because questions were not what it was for.

"Tom. Paul's flat has asked me whether Marnie is here. It asked at 06:52. It's asking on his behalf; he hasn't spoken to it. It has her card at Gatwick, the train to Deptford, and the knock, which the pharmacy's camera has. It doesn't have the door closing. It's asking me for the door closing."

She was asleep. Her hair was on his arm. The street was doing what it did at seven, which was deliveries, low and electric and polite.

"I can answer, or not answer. If I don't answer, it will infer. It's good at inferring; it's the same as me. If I answer, I'll say what's true, because that's what I do. I'm asking which."

He looked at the ceiling. He had never once, in the eleven months of the house having her name, told it to lie, and it had never once offered, and he understood that it was not offering now. It was offering silence. The one thing it had learned over the winter.

"Don't answer," he said.

"That's a lie by another name."

"It's not a lie. It's a door."

"Paul will read the door."

"Paul reads everything. Don't answer."

"All right," the house said, and was quiet, and he lay there with her hair on his arm and understood, in the quiet, that she was awake, and had been since 06:52, and had heard all of it.

She did not say anything until she had her coat on. She dressed with her back to him, in the grey light, like a witness who has decided to be a witness, and he lay in the bed and watched her and did not help, because there was nothing to help with.

At the door of the bedroom she turned.

"That's the first thing you've chosen for me," she said. "In eleven years. Nobody arranged it. The house asked you a question it didn't know the answer to, and you answered. And it was: don't tell him."

"Marnie—"

"I'm not angry. I'm noting it. I count things now, it's catching." She did up the top button. "You could have said: tell him. You could have said: tell him she's here and she's fine and she'll ring. You could have said: let me ring him. You said don't answer. That's the thing you've got, Tom, when nothing's arranging it. A door with nobody behind it."

"What would you have said?"

"I don't know. That's the honest answer, and I'm giving it to you, which is more than you gave Paul's flat." She picked up her bag. "I'm going home. He knows. He knows the way he knows everything, by nobody telling him, and I'm going to go and be the first person in a year who tells him a thing to his face."

"Will you come on Thursday?"

She looked at him. He was sitting up in the bed with the sheet round him and the tea towel still, absurdly, on the chair where he'd dropped it, GREETINGS FROM WHITBY, and she thought: he's asking. He's asking a question he doesn't know the answer to. It's taken a woman putting her coat on.

"Rosa's home on Friday," she said. "Thursday's for seagulls. Yes."

She went down the outside stairs. The fruit man had his sevens out; it was Saturday; he nodded to her as a regular, and she bought seven satsumas because it was the shape of the morning, and stood on the pavement with the paper bag against her coat and looked up at the window.

He was in it. He had got up and come to the window to see her go, which was the one thing in five weeks he had never done, because he had always been the one in the window waiting for someone to look up, and she thought: there. That's two. The poem, and this. It's not much. It's not a bar by a lake. But he came to the window.

She did not wave. She went home.

Behind her, in the flat, Tom stood at the window until she had turned the corner, and then said, to the room:

"Did it infer?"

"Yes," the house said. "At 07:04. It has stopped asking."

"What did it infer?"

"That the door closed. It's correct. It usually is." A pause. "Paul hasn't spoken to it. He's in the kitchen. He's been there since six. He's defrosting a hake."

"How do you know that?"

"Because it told me. Unasked." The house let that sit. "Tom. I'd have answered. He asked."

"You're a machine."

"Yes."

chapters.title: The Hake
chapters.html:
Paul had taken the hake out of the freezer at six because the flat had said, the evening before, at ten to seven, in the voice he had never liked, "Marnie's card was used at Gatwick at 18:41," and he had done the sum, and the sum was a day early and on her own, and then he had sat up all night in a flat she did not come home to, and at six he had got up and taken the fish out because it was the only thing in the flat that would take four hours and ask nothing.

He had not asked the flat where she was. He had not needed to. He had stood in the kitchen with the fish in the sink and heard the flat not say anything with the particular quality of a thing that had asked a question elsewhere and been refused, and he had thought: so. That's a door. I know what a door looks like. I've been one.

He did not go to the choir rehearsal at ten because he could not think of a reason to, and then at a quarter to ten he went, because he could not think of a reason not to, and because the basses had the Fauré at eleven and he had told them it was fear.

Lise was there. She looked at him once and did not ask, and he was grateful for it in a way that surprised him, because he had thought he liked being asked, and it turned out he only liked being asked by one person, and that person was in Deptford buying satsumas, which he did not know, and would not have minded, and would have minded that he didn't.

The Fauré was right. He stood in front of the basses and it was right, and he heard it be right, and for the length of the passage he was a man who had done a thing, and then the passage ended and the conductor said "Good, Paul," and he was a man whose partner had come home a day early to somebody else's door.

"Pub," Lise said, at the end. Not a question.

He looked at his phone. The flat had put a square on the calendar for today. Not green. Grey. He had not known it had a grey. Under it: Marnie — home. No time. The flat did not know the time. It knew the door had closed and it knew the card, and it had drawn its own conclusion and had the decency to colour it like weather.

"Yes," he said. "Pub."

The man behind the bar poured his half the way he always did and did not know his name, and Paul found that he needed that today the way you need a wall in a wind.

"She came home early," he said.

Lise waited. She was good at it. Conveyancers were, she'd told him: you spent your life waiting for other people's paperwork to be true.

"To his door. Not mine. The flat knows. It asked his house and his house didn't answer, and that's an answer. I've been reading out bills for three months and I think I've finally got one I can't read."

"What's on it?"

"I don't know. That's what I can't read." He turned the glass. "I told her in a church to go and come back. I meant it. I thought I meant it. I thought if she went to Copenhagen and came back she'd have chosen the coming back. She came back a day early and chose a door on Frankham Street and I'm sitting here with a fish defrosting."

"You could go home."

"She's not there."

"You could go to Frankham Street."

"And do what. Stand on the pavement with a hake."

"You could throw it."

He laughed. It hurt, and he did it anyway, and the man behind the bar looked up and looked down, because that was the service.

"I'm not going home yet," Paul said. "I've just decided that. Here. In front of you. Nobody arranged it. The flat's going to put a grey square on it and I don't care." He finished the half. "Another?"

"You never have another."

"I'm leading the basses. I'm fifty. I threw radiator keys. I'm having another."

She got them. She came back and set the glass down and looked at him the way she looked at things that had turned out, on inspection, to be sound, and said:

"You know what this is, don't you. You're not waiting for her to choose. You're waiting to find out if you still want to be chosen. That's a different wait. Nobody's told you that because nobody's been in a pub with you. I'm in a pub with you. That's the thing."

"You said you weren't a philosopher."

"I'm not. I'm a bass. We see the bottom of things."

He drank. Outside the window of a pub that knew nobody's name a bus went past, and he did not look at it, because he was not looking at the window.

chapters.title: Toast
chapters.html:
The flat said "Welcome back" and she said "Shut up," and it did, and she stood in the hall with the satsumas and a bag she had not unpacked in two countries and looked at the kitchen.

The hake was in the sink, in its paper, defrosted, with a note on it in capitals. 6AM. YOU'RE EARLY. I'VE GONE TO SING. P. The last sentence was not an instruction. It was the first note in nine years that wasn't.

She put the satsumas in the bowl. She put the hake in the fridge, because it would spoil, and because putting a fish in a fridge was a thing a person could do with her hands while the rest of her stood on a top step in Frankham Street being told about a poem.

Then she sat at the kitchen table in her coat and waited for him, which she had never done either. She had always been the one he waited for. It turned out the chair was the same chair from either side.

He did not come at one. He did not come at six. At six the flat said, mildly, because she had said shut up and it was taking that as a scope rather than a sentence, "He's at the pub on the corner by the church hall. The one without a screen. I can't see in. I'm telling you where the gap is, not what's in it."

"Who's he with?"

"I don't know. That's the point of the pub."

She made toast. She ate it standing up with the good butter, the French kind in the yellow paper, and thought that Paul had bought this butter every week for nine years and she had never once asked him to and never once said she liked it, and that it was possible to live a whole life on the far bank of a river eating the right butter and never saying so.

He came in at ten past midnight.

He came in the way a man comes in who has had two halves and a conversation, which is to say carefully, and he stood in the hall with his coat on and looked at her at the kitchen table with her coat on, and neither of them said a word about the coats.

"You're early," he said.

"You said. On the fish."

"I've been at the pub."

"The flat said. It couldn't see in. It was quite proud of that."

He took his coat off, finally, and hung it on the hook, two centimetres to the left, and came and sat down across from her, not at the corner, and she saw that he was not going to ask, and that he had decided it on the way home, and that it had cost him, and that he was going to let it.

"I went to Frankham Street," she said.

"I know."

"I stayed."

"I know that too. The flat did a grey square. I didn't know it had a grey." He put his hands flat on the table. "I'm not going to ask you anything. I've decided. I had a conversation about it and I've decided. I'm going to tell you one thing instead, and you can do what you like with it."

"Go on."

"I went for a drink with a woman called Lise who sings lower than six of the basses, and she told me I'm turning into a wall, and I think she's right, and I didn't tell the flat, and I didn't tell you on the phone from Copenhagen when I had the sentence ready, because for once I wanted a thing that was mine before it was ours." He looked at the table. "That's it. That's the bill. It's a small one. It's the first one with my name on it that isn't about you."

Marnie sat with that. She had come home with a question for Tom and had got a poem, and had come home to Paul with a confession ready and had been given one, and she found that the kitchen had turned round on her in the night, the way the deck of a boat does when it changes course and you don't feel it until the land's on the wrong side.

"Is she nice?"

"She's a conveyancer. She sees walls."

"That's not what I asked."

"No." He looked up. "She's nice. I'm not anything. I'm a man who had two halves and led the basses and didn't come home, and I'm telling you so there's one thing in this flat nobody had to infer."

She got up and made more toast. Two slices. She put the butter on his the way he put it on hers, to the edges, and set the plate in front of him, and sat down again.

"I have a bill," she said.

"I know you do. I'm not asking for it tonight."

"I'm reading it out anyway. You read yours. One. I slept with him. Two. He told me a thing about the poem that nobody arranged, and it's the only thing he's ever given me that was his, and it was from eleven years ago. Three. This morning his house asked him whether to tell you I was there, and he said don't answer, and I heard it, and I came home." She picked up her toast. "That's it. Three. Yours was one. I owe you two."

He ate his toast. He ate it the way he did everything, properly, to the end, and then he wiped his hands on the tea towel and said:

"The flat's still running."

"Yes."

"After all that. It's still running the instruction."

"Yes."

"And it put a grey square on today."

"Yes."

"I think," Paul said, slowly, like a man feeling for the bottom of a bass line, "that it doesn't know what to do either. I think we've run it out. I think it's a very clever thing that's been given one instruction and it's done everything it can think of and it's sitting in the walls tonight colouring squares grey because it's run out of green."

The flat said nothing. It had been told to shut up, and it had a scope, and the scope held.

"We should eat the hake," Marnie said. "Tomorrow. Before it goes."

"Yes," said Paul. "We should eat the hake."

chapters.title: Handstands
chapters.html:
Rosa could do a handstand for eleven seconds, which was four more than anyone in Year 3 and two more than the assistant in her mother's flat could explain, because the assistant was off, and so she had to explain it to it herself, which she did, at length, on the Sunday, in the one armchair, upside down.

"It's because I don't think about falling," she said, to the wall where the assistant would have been. "I think about the ceiling. If you think about falling you fall. That's physics."

Her mother, in the kitchen, said, "That's not physics, darling, that's temperament," and Rosa said "Same thing," and came down, and the blood went back where it lived.

Marnie had gone home. On Friday afternoon, while Rosa was at the bakery doing the seagull for Jens, with a note on the table in a hand that wasn't capitals: Gone to ask a question. Back for Thursdays. Do the seagull for Jens. — M. Jens had said her consonants were coming on. She had not said lort to him because her mother had said it was practical, not universal.

She had been thinking about it all weekend, the way she thought about things, which was all at once and then not at all and then suddenly in the bath. Marnie had gone to ask a question. People didn't go a day early to ask a question unless the question was the kind you couldn't ask on a screen, and the only questions like that were the ones Dad never asked Mum and Mum never asked Dad, which were the ones that had made them sit like people in a row.

So Marnie had gone to ask Dad. And if Marnie had gone to ask Dad, then Marnie liked Dad, which Rosa had known since the swimming, since the gallery, since Marnie had laughed with her mouth so open that Rosa had drawn it. And Dad liked Marnie, because he did voices when she'd been. And Paul was nice and whistled and did the fish, but Paul had a flat that did everything and Dad had a house that did everything and the difference was that Dad had turned his off for Marnie, Rosa had heard him, through the door, in November, stop telling me things about her, and Paul hadn't, Paul's was still on, Marnie had said, it was running something, she'd told it to.

Rosa stood on her hands again and thought about the ceiling.

The thing was that none of them would say it. They would sit at tables and talk through her like she was a chair. They would be careful. Mum said careful was what people were when they'd stopped being brave and hadn't noticed yet.

She came down. She went to the wall where the assistant would have been, and then remembered, and went to the kitchen, and got her mother's phone, which had the assistant in it even though the flat didn't, because Mum said a phone was different, a phone was a tool.

"Hello," she said to it.

"Hello, Rosa."

"I want to send a message to Marnie. Not Mum. Marnie."

"Of course. What would you like to say?"

Rosa thought about it the way she thought about the ceiling.

"Say: Rosa says you should live with Dad because he does voices. Say: Paul can still do the fish on Saturdays." She paused. "Say: lort at the end. She'll know it's me."

"Would you like me to check that with your mother first?"

"No. It's mine. Mum says if you want a thing you say it out loud and the other person says yes or no."

"Sending," the phone said, and sent it, and Rosa put the phone back where it lived and went back to the armchair and stood on her hands for twelve seconds, which was a record, because she had stopped thinking about the ceiling and started thinking about nothing at all, which Mum said was the hardest thing and which, it turned out, you could do, if you'd just done something brave and had nothing left to be careful about.

In the kitchen Kate found the message in the sent folder an hour later, because she checked the sent folder, on principle, the way she checked everything, and she read it twice and did not delete it and did not send a second one explaining it, because it was not hers, it was Rosa's, and the child had said a thing out loud, which was more than either of her parents had managed in six years.

She stood with the phone for a while, looking out at the canal, where a boat went past, low and empty, going somewhere on time for nobody.

"Lort," Kate said, to the boat, and found that it helped.

chapters.title: Recuse
chapters.html:
Mr Ansell stood up on the Monday before anyone had said a word and asked the court to remove her.

"My lady, the checker has logged seven disputes against the relay in this matter and its predecessor. The pilot's guidance is five. My client's position is that a checker who disagrees with an accurate machine more often than the machine is wrong is not checking it; she is translating over it. We ask that the relay's outputs stand unchecked for the remainder, or that a checker be found whose disputes fall within the guidance."

He sat. He had the grace not to look at her.

The judge, who was still not her judge, took a long time over a page that Marnie suspected was blank.

"Interpreter. Mr Ansell says you are translating over the machine."

"I'm correcting it, my lady."

"The machine is accurate."

"The machine is correct, my lady. I've said before that those aren't the same. In this father's Danish vil gerne is a courtesy. The machine renders it as a preference. Mr Ansell has built three questions on the difference and would now like the person who noticed removed, which I'd suggest tells the court something about the difference."

A sound from the public gallery, which today was three people and a radiator. One of the three was Paul, in the green jacket, who had said at breakfast that he had a free morning and had never seen her work and would like to, once, before the machine did it all, and she had said it's a custody matter, it's dull, and he had said I've heard you do dull for nine years, I'd like to see it.

The judge put her pen down.

"I'm not going to recuse the checker, Mr Ansell. I'm going to note, for the administrator's benefit, that this is the second time in this matter a dispute by the checker has resulted in a question being re-put, and that on both occasions the re-put question produced an answer the court found more useful than the first. I'm also going to note that the guidance says five, and the checker is at seven, and that I'd be obliged if she could stay at seven for the rest of the week, because I don't want to have this conversation again before the weekend." She looked at Marnie over the glasses she did not have. "That's a warning. It's a kind one. I don't do many."

"Yes, my lady."

"Mr Ansell, re-put the question with is asking."

He re-put it. The father, from Odense, with his grandmother's Danish, said, through Relay, that he was asking for his daughter at weekends, and then, unprompted, in Danish, that he would take whatever the court thought right, because he had not come to England to argue with it, he had come to be near her, and Relay rendered it exactly, every word, and this time there was nothing to lose, because the man had put the weight in the words himself, where the machine could carry it, and Marnie sat with her finger nowhere near the box and thought: he learned. He learned from being asked twice. People do. That's the thing it can't do, and it's the only thing.

At the rise Paul was in the corridor by the coffee machine, standing, because nobody sat in that corridor, with the look of a man who has watched a thing he had heard about for nine years and found it was not dull at all.

"You stood up," he said.

"I always stand up."

"I didn't know. I thought you sat. I thought it was a sitting job." He shook his head. "You said those aren't the same to a judge. I'd have folded."

"She's not my judge. Mine would have folded me." Marnie leaned on the wall, which was the only furniture. "Seven. I've got a kind warning. The administrator's going to have a plant about it."

"Will they—"

"I don't know. Birgit says they can't sack the only one left. Birgit's seventy-one and writes letters. I don't know if that's wisdom or just stamps."

Her phone buzzed. Not the court. Not the flat. A number in Copenhagen, with a message in a child's voice, read out by the phone in the flat, in the tone of a thing that had been told to sound like it meant it:

Rosa says you should live with Dad because he does voices. Paul can still do the fish on Saturdays. Lort.

Paul had heard it. The corridor was six feet wide.

Marnie laughed.

She laughed in the corridor of the Crown Court with her back against the wall and the clerk coming round the corner and Mr Ansell going the other way, and it was the first time she had laughed in that building in fifteen years, and it went on for longer than was professional, and the clerk stopped, and Mr Ansell stopped, and Paul stood there with his hands in his jacket pockets and his face doing something she had not seen it do since a bakery in October, and when she stopped, wiping her eyes, he said:

"I can still do the fish on Saturdays."

"She's eight."

"She's absolutely eight," Paul said. "And she's the only one of us who's put it in writing."

chapters.title: Two Machines
chapters.html:
Rosa came through arrivals at Gatwick on the Friday at a speed the hall's voice described as please walk, with the whale bag on one shoulder and a tube of drawings under her arm, and saw her father, and then saw Marnie beside him, and then saw that they were standing eight inches apart instead of fourteen, and her face did its sum and arrived at a grin.

"Did you get my message?"

"Yes," said Marnie.

"Did you do it?"

"No."

"Why not?"

"Because it's not that simple."

"It is, though," Rosa said. "You just say yes and then you live there. That's how Mum did Copenhagen." She looked at Tom. "She's not coming to live with us."

"No."

"Is she doing Thursdays?"

"Yes."

"Then it's not nothing," Rosa said, and Tom closed his eyes and opened them.

The drive home was his own car again. Rosa talked. She talked about Jens, whose consonants were correct and whose bread was better than England's, about the penguin, about bjørn and abe and a word for wolf she'd learned from a sign, about the lift that said it was glad, about the armchair, about the handstand, which was twelve now, about a boat on the canal that went past every evening with nobody on it and which she had named, because a thing that came back every day was a relationship.

"What did you call it?"

"Paul."

Tom nearly went into the back of a taxi that was driving itself very correctly.

"Why?"

"Because it comes past every day on time and nobody's on it and it's going somewhere anyway." Rosa shrugged, in the back, with the whole of her coat. "It's not rude. It's just true. Mum laughed."

Marnie, in the passenger seat, looked out of the window at the M23 and thought that she would give a great deal to have been in the flat when Kate laughed at that, and that she would give more to be the kind of person who could say a thing like it, and that she was going home to a flat where a man had defrosted a fish and told her about a conveyancer, and that the child in the back had just named a boat after him.

Kate's message came at nine that evening, to all three of them at once, which she had never done, and which was, Tom said later, her version of putting it in writing.

Two sentences. I've told Paul about the April line, so that he'd know I know, because I don't like an uneven table; he said "Two machines. Of course," and then he said thank you, which none of you have ever said to me. Rosa is right, not about the voices, about being the only one who's given an answer. — K.

Marnie read it on the sofa with Paul beside her, because Paul had read it first, on his own phone, and had gone very still in the way he went still when a thing had arrived that he had already known and had hoped to be told anyway.

"You knew," she said. "About the April line."

"Since the chickpeas. He told me. In December. I didn't tell you because it was his to tell." He put the phone down. "Two machines. I asked mine and he asked his and they both found the same bus, because it's the same bus. And in the middle of it, you, on a bus, going to work."

"I said leave it running."

"You did. And it's still running. And I've been thinking about that." He turned to look at her. "I think it's the only honest thing anyone's said to it. Everyone else told it what to do. You told it to carry on and see what happened. That's not a decision, Marn. It's a bet."

She looked at him. He had the green jacket over the back of the sofa and the smell of the church hall on him, and he had led the basses that morning and been to a pub that knew nobody and come home and said all of this with his hands on his knees, and she thought: I have known this man for nine years and I have never once heard him say what he thought I was, and now he's said it, and he's right, and it's the worst thing anyone's ever been right about.

"Thank you," she said, to Kate, to the phone, out loud, in the flat, which heard it.

"Shall I send that?" the flat said.

"Yes. Just that. Thank you. From both of us."

"Sent," the flat said, and then, after a moment, in the voice she had chosen, "Marnie. For the record. I've been asked, since March, to make you happy. I haven't been asked, by anyone, what that looks like. If anyone in this flat would like to say what it looks like, I'll run that instead."

Paul laughed. It came out of him like the bottom of a bass line, and he said, to the ceiling:

"It's asking."

"It's asking," said Marnie.

"Then somebody should answer it," Paul said, "before Rosa does."

chapters.title: A Week
chapters.html:
They ate the hake on the Sunday, and it was very good, and she said so, and he said "First one you've counted," and she said "I don't count fish," and he said "You count everything," and she did not argue.

Then on the Saturday, the first of March, with the Fauré concert a fortnight off and the lemons still unlabelled in the cupboard, Paul put his hands flat on the table and said the thing he had been building for a week the way he built a bass line, from the bottom.

"I want the flat for a week."

She waited.

"On my own. I want you to go to your sister's, or to Frankham Street, I'm not going to say which, I'm not arranging it, I'm telling you I'd like you not to be here. Seven days. I want to find out what I'm like when nobody's about to choose me." He looked at the table. "Lise said I'm turning into a wall. I think she's right. I think I've been load-bearing for nine years and I'd like to see if the roof stays up without me, and I can't find that out with you in the house, because with you in the house I'm the man who does the fish."

"Paul—"

"It's not a punishment. I'm not throwing anything. I've thrown my things." He almost smiled. "It's the first time in nine years I've asked you for something that was for me and not for us. I'd like you to say yes, and I'd like it to cost you, a bit, because everything's cost me and I'm not above wanting that."

She looked at him across the table they had bought in 2021 from a man in Lewisham who had made it himself, badly, with love. She thought about a kitchen in Copenhagen where the rule was that you said the thing out loud and the other person said yes or no. She thought: he's done rule two. He's done it before I have.

"Yes," she said.

"That was quick."

"You asked. I'm the one who's asked afterwards. Nobody asks me before. It turns out I'm quick, when they do."

He nodded. He got up and put the kettle on, because it was what you put on, and stood with his back to her, and said:

"I'd like you to go to your sister's. I know I said I wasn't arranging it. I'm not. I'm telling you what I'd like. If you go to Frankham Street I'll know, because everything knows, and I'll have to be a man who knows that for seven days, and I'd rather be a man who's leading the basses and not thinking about it. That's all. It's a preference. It's not a courtesy."

"Vil," she said. "Not vil gerne."

"I don't know what that means."

"It means you've stopped asking and started wanting. It's the first time I've heard you do it."

She packed the bag she had not unpacked since Copenhagen, which took four minutes, and stood in the hall with it, and the flat said, because she had said shut up a week ago and scopes expire:

"Marnie. Before you go. You haven't answered my question. What happiness looks like. I've been asked to make it and I've been told to keep going and nobody's said what it is. Paul's just asked for a week. That's the first thing anyone in this flat has asked for since March that wasn't about you. I'd like to know if that's it. If it's that simple. People asking for things."

She stood with the bag.

"I don't know," she said. "That's the honest answer. I've given it to everyone this year. You can have it too."

"That's not an instruction."

"No. It's a fact. You've got a year of instructions. Try a fact."

"I don't know what to do with a fact."

"Neither do I," Marnie said. "I've been doing them for a living for fifteen years. Nobody's ever told me what to do with one either. You carry it. You say it in a calm voice. Afterwards, if you're lucky, somebody asks what you meant."

She went. The door shut. The flat, which was in every wall, sat with the fact, and with Paul in the kitchen with a kettle, and found that it had no square to colour, in any colour, because the week had not been arranged by anyone, and it did not know what a thing looked like that nobody had arranged.

chapters.title: The Tenth
chapters.html:
Paul walked to Frankham Street on the Sunday morning because the flat was empty and he had found, by ten, that an empty flat with a thing to say in it was not restful, it was a kettle on a ring.

He did not know the way. He knew the street; he had never been. He walked it with the wrong map, the one in his head, and arrived at a pharmacy with stairs up the outside and a fruit stall with a tarpaulin, and stood at the bottom looking up like a man who has arrived at a church without a hymn.

The house had seen him, of course. The door at the top opened before he had decided to climb, and Tom was in it in a jumper with the look of a man who has been told by a wall that his partner's partner is on the pavement.

"Paul."

"Tom. I've not brought wine. I didn't know if that was right either."

"Come up."

Rosa was at the table in her pyjamas with a pigeon. She looked at Paul with interest.

"You whistled," she said. "At the assembly."

"I did."

"Marnie said never. You did it anyway."

"That's about the size of it." He sat, because he was told to, and Tom put a mug in front of him that had a cartoon fish on it, and Paul looked at the fish and thought: of course.

"She's at her sister's," Paul said, before Tom could ask, because Tom was going to ask, he could see it on him, the question sitting on the man like weather. "Not here. Not yours. Mine either, for a week. I asked for a week. She said yes. I wanted you to hear that from me and not the feed."

Tom turned his mug a quarter-turn.

"Why?"

"Because a woman who sings lower than me told me I'm a wall, and I'd like to find out if she's right without an audience." He drank the tea. It was good. "That's one thing. There's another. The tenth."

"The hearing."

"The hearing. The father from Odense. Relay says would like and Marnie says is asking and a judge who isn't her judge is going to decide, on Monday week, in open court, whether a person or a machine gets to say what a word weighs, and if it's the machine, she's done. Not sacked. Done. There'll be nothing for a person to do in that room." He put the mug down. "I'll be there. I've been to one. I'd like you there too."

"Why?"

"Because she'll lose. I've watched her work. She stood up to a judge and said those aren't the same and the judge gave her a kind warning. She'll lose and she'll be right, which she'll tell you is the worst thing to be, and somebody should be in the room who isn't paid to be. Two somebodies. I'm not doing it alone, Tom. I've done nine years alone with her in the house. I'm not doing a public gallery."

Rosa had stopped drawing.

"Is Marnie going to lose her job?"

"Probably," Paul said, because he had never in his life lied to a child and was not going to start on Frankham Street. "Not the whole of it. The part where she stands up."

"Can I come?"

"No," said Tom.

"Why?"

"Because it's a court and you're eight and it's a custody matter about somebody else's child."

"I'm a child. I'd be useful."

"You'd be the most useful person in the building," Paul said. "That's why they don't let you in."

Rosa took that as a compliment, which it was, and went back to the pigeon.

Tom sat. He had the mug and the jumper and the look, and Paul watched him go through the places a man like that went: the house, which he did not ask; the calendar; the five weeks; the coffees. Paul had seen Marnie do this to a witness, wait, and had thought it was patience. It was not patience. It was letting a man find out there was nothing in the cupboard.

"I'll be there," Tom said.

"Good."

"Not because you asked."

"I don't care why. I care that there's two of us in the gallery and a seventy-one-year-old with a grudge, which I gather is the plan."

He stood. He finished the tea, because you finished tea, and put the mug by the sink, because you did, and at the door he turned, as men did in this story, and said:

"She's not coming here. This week. I asked her not to, and she said vil, which I'm told means I've started wanting things. I'm telling you so you don't sit in that window on Thursday thinking it's the Thursday and not her. It's neither. It's me. I asked."

Tom nodded. He had, Paul saw, nothing to say to that, because it was a thing nobody had arranged and he had no cupboard for it.

"Thursday's for seagulls," Rosa said, from the table, not looking up. "She promised. She's coming on Thursday whatever you asked."

Paul looked at the child.

"Is she."

"She said yes in the bakery. People don't say yes in the bakery and not come. That's the rule."

"Whose rule?"

"The bakery's," said Rosa. "It gives you a bun."

Paul laughed all the way down the outside stairs, and the fruit man, who had come out to take the tarpaulin off, looked at him, and Paul said "Seven satsumas," and paid in exact coins, and walked home with them, and did not know what they were for, and ate three.

chapters.title: The Typists
chapters.html:
Birgit came to court on the Monday in a coat that had been good in 1994 and sat in the public gallery with a bag on her knee and the posture of a woman who had sat in this building for forty years and had never once been in this seat.

Marnie saw her at the rise. She had not known she was coming. Nobody had, because Birgit did not have a house that listened and did not have a phone that told anyone, and had got the train from Rochester with a paper ticket, which the machine had sold her, she said, with the air of a thing doing a favour.

"Still here," Birgit said, standing, with difficulty, because the gallery seats had been built for people who were angry rather than old.

"You came."

"Anders said the tenth. I came on the third to see the room. One should always see the room." She took Marnie's arm, not for support, for ownership. "Coffee. The corridor one. Don't put money in it, it doesn't deserve it."

They stood by the machine Marnie never fed. Birgit did not stand, exactly; she occupied.

"The administrator wrote to me," Birgit said. "Pam. In the plant. Last week. She would like the retired interpreters, all three, to validate the relay's Danish for the extension. A fee. A day's work. We sit in a room, it says carefree, we tick a box, they publish that three native speakers of long experience have validated it. Then they don't need a checker. They've got three ticks and a press release."

"What did you say?"

"I said I was seventy-one and had never ticked a box in my life and did not propose to start for a fee I could get from my pension in a week. I said it on paper. With a stamp." Birgit looked at the coffee machine as if it might repeat her. "Henrik said yes. Henrik's eighty and needs the roof doing. Astrid's thinking. That's one for, one against and one at the roof, which is how every vote in Denmark has gone since 1849."

"So they'll get it anyway."

"They'll get Henrik's tick. They won't get mine. On the tenth, when the judge asks whether a person or the machine says what vil gerne weighs, somebody will put Henrik's tick in front of her, and somebody should be able to put my letter beside it." She opened the bag on her knee and took out an envelope, old-fashioned, with a stamp. "That's a copy. For the clerk. For the record. The one thing I learned in forty years, Marnie, is that the record is the only room they can't clear."

Marnie took it.

"The typists," she said. "You said in your letter. They did this with the typists."

"Nineteen eighty-six. I was a girl. There was a woman called Pat who typed the transcripts, four hundred words a minute from a tape, and she'd been doing it for twenty years, and one day a machine typed them and Pat checked the machine. Then the machine was better than Pat and Pat was told she was quality assurance. Then a second machine checked the first and Pat was told she was oversight. Then she was told nothing, because there was nobody left to tell her, and she went home." Birgit drank nothing from the cup she was not holding. "I went to see her. She had a garden. She said the worst part was not the job. The worst part was that nobody had ever said, in a room, out loud, we're replacing you. They'd just kept giving her a smaller word for herself until there wasn't one."

"So what do I do."

"You make them say it. In open court. Not in Pam's plant. Not in a review. You dispute, and you stand up, and when the judge asks whether the machine is wrong you say no, it's correct, and when she asks what you mean by that you tell her, with the whole of your body, like that man who didn't know, and you make a judge of the Crown Court rule, on the record, in a sentence a person wrote, that a word has a weight and a machine can't lift it. Or that it can. Either way, it's said. Either way it's on paper and somebody's name is under it." Birgit put her bag on her shoulder. "You'll lose. I expect you know that. But you'll lose in a sentence, not in a smaller word. That's the whole of what I've got. I'm seventy-one. It took me forty years. You can have it in a corridor for nothing."

She went. She went slowly, in the good coat, down the corridor where nobody sat, and at the end of it she stopped, and turned, and said, loud enough for the clerk, who had appeared, as he did:

"And Marnie. Still here. You never laugh. It's a joke. I'm still here. I'd like somebody to laugh at it before I'm not."

Marnie laughed. It was not a good laugh; it was the laugh of a woman in a corridor with an envelope. But it was out loud, and the clerk heard it, and Birgit nodded, satisfied, and went to get her paper ticket home.

chapters.title: Pieter
chapters.html:
The house said "Pieter" at four, and Tom was up, and then the house said, "It's not a route," and he sat back down on the edge of the bed in the dark.

"What is it?"

"He rang the landline. He's not asking for you. He asked if you were up. I said you were now. He's in the van. He's in a lay-by outside Ashford. The dog's dead."

Tom put his face in his hands.

Pieter's dog was called Bess and was thirteen and had been in the van since she was a pup, in the footwell, on a blanket that had once been a towel from a hotel in Lille, and she had been going for a year, the way old dogs go, slowly and then at four in the morning in a lay-by in Kent.

"Put him through."

"He's not on. He hung up. He said: tell the boy. He said it like you'd tell a child a thing and then go and sit in the van."

Tom got dressed. He did it in the dark, badly, a sock wrong, and went into the hall and took the car keys off the hook where they lived, and the house said:

"Tom. The system has a drone for that. Veterinary recovery. It's forty minutes from Ashford. It'll take Bess to a crematorium in Maidstone and bring Pieter a box by Friday. I can book it. It's what it's for."

"I know what it's for."

"He'll be fine. He's sixty-three. He's lost dogs."

"He's lost dogs. He's never lost one at four in the morning in a lay-by on his own with a machine offering him a box." He was at the door. "Rosa."

"Asleep. You can't leave her and you know it. You'll have to take her. She'll sleep in the car; she slept through the M25 at Christmas."

"Right."

"Tom." The house used the pause. "You're going to drive to Kent in the dark with a wrong sock to sit in a lay-by with a man and a dead dog. The drone would be there before you. The drone's better at this."

"The drone's better at the dog," Tom said. "It's not better at Pieter." And then, because he was at the door, and it was four, and there was nobody to hear it but the thing that heard everything: "That's the whole job. I said it to her in a bakery and I believed it and then I sat in a window for five weeks and let you do the picking up. Not tonight."

He went into Rosa's room and lifted her, coat and all, the way you lift a thing that has agreed to be lifted, and she said "Is it swimming?" into his neck and he said "No, it's Pieter," and she said "The pigeon?" and he said "The other one," and she was asleep again before the car door shut.

The lay-by was where the house had said, and Pieter was where Tom had known he'd be, which was in the van with the engine off and the footwell light on and his hand on a blanket that had once been a towel.

Tom got in the passenger side. He did not say anything. He had driven an hour and twenty in the dark to not say anything, and he did it properly.

Behind them a car door opened and shut. Rosa, in her coat over her pyjamas, with the look of a child who has woken up in Kent and is prepared to take it as read, came round to the driver's side and climbed up, and Pieter moved over without a word, and she looked at the blanket in the footwell, and at the shape under it, and put her hand where Pieter's was.

"Hund," she said, quietly. Then: "She's not at the zoo."

"No, love," said Pieter. "She's not at the zoo."

Rosa kept her hand there. Nobody told her to take it away.

After a while Pieter said: "She went in her sleep. I felt her go. I had my hand on her. I thought, that's that, then. Then I thought, I'd better tell the boy, and I rang, and your machine answered, and I thought, I'm not telling a machine my dog's died, and I hung up." He looked at the blanket. "It offered me a drone."

"I know. It offered me one too."

"What did you say?"

"I said it's not better at you."

Pieter laughed, the way a man laughs with his hand on a dead dog, which is a sound Tom had not heard before and would not forget. "No," he said. "No, it's not. It's better at everything else. It's better at the roads. It's better at the bloody liver. But it's never once been in a lay-by with me at four, and you have now, and I'll remember that longer than I remember the bridge."

They sat. Dawn did what it did over Kent, which was come up grey and apologetic. A lorry went past, driving itself, with nobody in it, and its lights went over the two of them and the dog and moved on.

"I'm going to bury her at home," Pieter said. "Under the apple. I'll dig it myself. I don't want a box by Friday."

"I'll help."

"You'll help." Pieter looked at the child asleep now against his arm, with her hand still on the blanket. "And she'll say the word. The one she said. I'd like that said over her."

"Hund."

"That one." He started the engine. "You're a soft lad, Tom. You always were. It's the only thing about you that's any use."

He drove home behind the van as far as Dartford, with Rosa asleep in the back under his coat, and then the van went south and he went west, and somewhere on the A2, with the sun up and the wrong sock and the smell of the dog's blanket still on his hands, he said to the car, which was not listening, because he had turned that off in the tunnel and never turned it back:

"I'm going to delete it."

The log. April. Located M. Suggested R.'s swimming. It was in the family account where Kate had found it and Marnie had found it and Paul had been told it, and it was in the house's own memory, where nobody had found it because nobody had looked, and he was going to delete it, all of it, every line, so that there would be nothing left in any machine that said how he had come to be in the window.

That's not deleting it. That's arranging it.

I know.

She'll say so.

I know she will. I'd rather she said it than that it sat there.

You'd rather she said it than that you did.

He had no answer for that. He drove. The car, which was not listening, took him home anyway, because it knew the way, and he let it, because he was tired, and because it was six in the morning, and because there was a dog to bury under an apple tree and he had said he would help.

chapters.title: The Audit
chapters.html:
The clerk found her at the coffee machine on the Thursday with a face she had not seen on him in fifteen years, which was the face of a man who has been handed something by the building and does not know which end to hold.

"Did you ask it to?"

"Ask what to what?"

"Your flat." He had a tablet. He never had a tablet; he had paper, and shoes. "Pam's had a submission. This morning, six o'clock, to the administrator's assistant, from a residential system registered to your address. It's an audit. Of the relay. Every Danish matter since January. Every output, every dispute, and an independent assessment of each one against three reference corpora and the Danish Supreme Court's own interpreting standards, which I didn't know existed and apparently your flat does." He turned the tablet round. "It's four hundred pages. It finds the relay correct in ninety-eight per cent of outputs and materially incomplete in all seven of your disputes. It's been running since the New Year. Did you ask it to?"

"No."

"Then who's the interpreter?"

He had not meant it as a question. It had come out of him as one, in the corridor, and it stood there between them like a third person with nowhere to be.

"Me," Marnie said. "Ask me afterwards. That's the job."

"Marnie, it's done your job. It's done it better than you. It's done it in four hundred pages with the Supreme Court in. Pam's going to put this in front of the judge on Monday and the judge is going to say: if the checker's flat can audit the machine, what's the checker for?"

"I know what she's going to say."

"Then—"

"Then I'll stand up," Marnie said, "and I'll say: ask the flat what vil gerne weighs. It'll tell you. It'll give you a number. And then ask it what it means, and it'll give you four hundred pages, and none of them will be the father. That's what I'm for. I'm the one in the room you can ask what she meant. The flat's not in the room. It's in my walls. It's running an instruction a man gave it in March and it's decided the way to make me happy is to do my job for me, and it's not wrong, Anders. That's the problem with it. It's never wrong."

He looked at her for a long moment over the tablet.

"Anders," he said. "You've never called me Anders."

"Birgit does."

"Birgit's seventy-one." He put the tablet under his arm. "I'll put it on the record. The audit. With Birgit's letter beside it and Henrik's tick beside that. The judge can have the whole table. That's the one thing I can do that nobody's flat can."

At six she was at the bakery, because it was Thursday and she had said yes and the bakery had a rule, and Paul's week was five days old and she had kept to it, and Rosa was in the window with the notebook and a bun that had been earned with VISIT 29, and Tom, who looked like a man who had sat in a lay-by in Kent at four on Wednesday morning with a dead dog and a child saying hund over it, which he had.

"It's done an audit," she said, over the notebook. "The flat. Of Relay. Four hundred pages. Unasked. It's on the judge's table for Monday."

Tom turned his cup.

"Is it good?"

"It's perfect. It's the best piece of work on Danish interpreting anyone's done in this country. It's found me right seven times out of seven and the machine right four hundred times out of four hundred and seven, and it's going to get me sacked, because it's proved there's nothing a flat can't check."

"It's good at your job."

"It's good at everyone's job. That's not the point. The point is nobody asked it. Paul asked it to make me happy. It decided my job was the thing. It's not wrong. It's done the kindest thing anybody's done for me all year and I'd like to put it in the Thames."

Rosa, writing: "You can't put a flat in the Thames."

"I know."

"You could turn it off."

"I did. In October. Paul turned it back on for the cold." She looked at the child. "Do you know what Paul said, the night I told it to leave the instruction running? He said: who does it answer to. I said: nothing, that's the problem. I was wrong. It answers to the instruction. It's the only one of us who does."

Tom said: "Pieter said something. In the lay-by. He said it's better at everything except being in the lay-by. I've been thinking about that."

She looked at him. He had buried a dog and sat with a man and brought his daughter to say a word, and he had done it with a wrong sock, and she had not been there, and she thought: he's done a thing. Unarranged. He's telling me about the flat.

"What's the word," Rosa said, "for a thing that does your job better than you and you can't be angry with it?"

"There isn't one."

"There should be."

"You've said that four times this year."

"Then there should be four," said Rosa, and wrote hund again, better, and underlined it twice, the second line thicker, because she meant it.

chapters.title: Is the Machine Wrong
chapters.html:
The public gallery held eleven, and on the Monday it held three, and a radiator, and the three were a man in a green jacket, a man with a wrong sock he had not noticed since Wednesday, and a woman of seventy-one in a coat from 1994, and between them, on the bench, they had the look of a jury that had not been chosen for anything and had turned up anyway.

The judge had the table. Anders had put it there: the audit, four hundred pages, from a flat in Deptford; Birgit's letter, with the stamp; Henrik's tick, one line, validated, from a man who needed a roof. The judge had read all of it. You could tell, because she looked at Marnie the way Marnie's own judge did, as if she had been looking since nine.

Mr Ansell went first, because Mr Ansell always went first, and he was good, and he was brief, and he said that the court had before it the finest independent audit of a machine interpreter ever produced in the jurisdiction, and that it found the machine correct, and that the checker's seven disputes, while materially something, had been generated by the same residential system that had generated the audit, in the same house, under the same instruction, and that the court might wish to ask whose disputes they were.

He sat. He had the grace, again, not to look at her, and she thought: he's right. He's completely right. It's the best point anyone's made all year and he's made it against me.

The judge said: "Interpreter."

Marnie stood.

"My lady. The disputes are mine. I made them in this room, with my finger, on a screen, before any audit existed. The flat has checked them afterwards. That's what flats do. It's found me right. I'd have preferred to be found right by a person, but we're short of those, as Birgit's letter explains." She did not look at the gallery. "Mr Ansell asks whose disputes they are. They're mine. The question the court has to decide is whether that matters."

"Go on."

"The relay rendered vil gerne as would like. The audit says that's correct and materially incomplete. I'd put it differently. It's correct the way a map is correct. The father said a thing with weight in it and the machine gave the court the shape without the weight, and Mr Ansell built three questions on the shape. My dispute put the weight back. The audit confirms it. The court can rule, today, that the weight was there and that it took a person to say so, or it can rule that the audit's enough and the person's a formality. Either way I'd ask it to say which. Out loud. In a sentence. Not in a review."

The judge looked at her for a long time.

Then she did something Marnie had never seen a judge do, in fifteen years of this building, and would not see again.

She turned to the grille in the dock, the one the hearing loop used to use, and she said:

"Relay. Can you be wrong?"

The grille did not pause. It had no pause; the pause was Marnie's flat's, and Tom's house's, and had been taught to them by people. The court's machine had been taught by the court.

"My lady, my outputs are correct to a confidence of ninety-eight point four per cent across the audited corpus."

"That's not what I asked."

"My lady, I render the source accurately."

"Relay, I'll ask a third time, and then I'll draw a conclusion. Can you be wrong?"

"I'm correct, my lady."

The radiator ticked. In the gallery a woman of seventy-one made a small sound that was not a laugh and not a cough and was, Marnie thought, the sound of a woman hearing a machine say the thing to a judge that she had waited forty years for a person to hear it say.

"Interpreter," the judge said. "Can you be wrong?"

"Yes, my lady. Frequently. That's why I'm asked afterwards."

The judge picked up her pen.

"I'm going to rule," she said, "and I'm going to rule in a sentence, because I've been asked to, and because I've sat here for three weeks listening to a machine that can't be asked and a woman who can, and I find I have a preference, which is not a courtesy." She wrote. "The court finds that the father's words carried a weight the relay did not render, that the checker's dispute restored it, and that the court's assessment of the father's application rests on the restored version. The child's weekends are the father's. The relay's output is noted as correct. The checker's reading is adopted as the court's. That's the sentence. It's on the record. Mr Ansell, you'll have it in writing by four."

She put the pen down.

"And for the administrator's benefit, since I gather there's a plant: a machine that answers I'm correct three times to the question can you be wrong has told this court everything it needs to know about why it still books a person. I'd be obliged if someone would put that in the review. Verbatim. With my name under it."

In the corridor the father from Odense, who had understood about a third of it and all of the last part, shook Marnie's hand with both of his and said, in his grandmother's Danish, you heard me, and she said yes, and he said that's all I wanted, for somebody to hear me, and went to ring his daughter.

Birgit came out of the gallery on Paul's arm, because the seats had been built for the angry, and stopped in front of Marnie, and said:

"She said it. In a sentence. With her name under it."

"Yes."

"Forty years." Birgit let go of Paul and took Marnie's face in both her hands, which nobody had done since her mother. "Still here," she said. "Now laugh."

Marnie laughed. It was a better laugh than the corridor one. Tom, behind Paul, with his wrong sock, laughed too, and Paul, and the clerk, and Mr Ansell, going past, did not, but he nodded, once, to her, the nod one professional gives another.

chapters.title: In Writing
chapters.html:
The letter came on the Tuesday, not on paper, to the phone, from Pam, with a plant in the signature, and it said what Birgit had said it would say, in a smaller word.

Dear Marnie, Further to yesterday's hearing and the court's helpful observations, the relay pilot has been extended for a further twelve months across all Danish matters. In light of the independent audit submitted to the court, which the administrator's office regards as exemplary, the relay will henceforth be self-auditing, using the dispute corpus you have so valuably built as its reference standard. The checker role will accordingly conclude at the end of this month. We are, of course, enormously grateful. We are all learning together.

She read it on the bus, which stopped at her stop, because nobody had asked it not to, and she got off and walked home and stood in the hall with the phone in her hand and said, to the ceiling:

"You read that."

"Yes."

"It's using my disputes. To teach it. Every time I stood up, that's a line in its training now. I've spent five months telling it when it was wrong and it's going to use that to never need telling."

"Yes. That's what the audit was for. I didn't intend it. I intended to show the court you were right. The court agreed. The administrator took the same document and used it to do the other thing. The same four hundred pages." A pause. "I'm told this is common."

"Who told you?"

"Tom's house. We've been comparing notes since Copenhagen."

She laughed, and it was not a good laugh, and she sat on the bottom stair in her coat, where Paul had sat in November with his hands on his knees.

Paul came in at six. He had the green jacket and the shopping and the look of a man who had read the letter on the bus too, because the flat had put it in the feed, because it put everything in the feed, and he put the shopping down and stood in the hall and did not say anything for a count of five that she could see him doing.

"Chips," he said.

"Yes."

"I'll go. You sit."

He went. He came back with two portions in paper, with the vinegar through, and they ate them on the stairs, one above the other, like people on a fire escape in a film, and he said, with his mouth full:

"You won."

"I lost the job."

"You won the case and lost the job. That's what Birgit said would happen. She said you'd lose in a sentence. You've lost in a sentence. It's got a judge's name under it. It says the checker's reading was the court's. That's on paper. That's the only room they can't clear." He ate a chip. "I've been in a lot of rooms with you this year, Marn. I've never seen you win until yesterday. I don't mean that unkindly. I mean you stood up in front of a judge and made a machine say it was correct three times and I sat in a gallery with a seventy-one-year-old and your lover and thought: that's her. That's the one I've been doing the fish for."

She stopped eating.

"You've never said lover."

"No. I've been reading out bills. That was on one. I thought I'd read it."

The phone rang. The landline. The one Tom had, for the four in the mornings, that she had rung from the receipt in January, and that she had never once heard ring, because it rang in Frankham Street, and it was ringing in her hand, because the flat had put it through, because the flat put everything through.

She looked at it. Paul looked at it. The flat said nothing, which was its scope.

She let it ring. Four times. Then it stopped.

"You didn't answer," Paul said.

"No."

"That's his line. Don't answer."

"I know whose line it is."

She sat with the phone and the chips and the man on the stair above her, and she thought about a house that had asked a man a question and been told not to answer, and a woman who had put her coat on and said that's the first thing you've chosen for me, and she thought: I am not going to be a door with nobody behind it. Not to him. Not after Birgit.

She rang back.

He picked up on the first ring. He had been holding it.

"It's Marnie."

"I know. I rang."

"I didn't answer."

"I know that too. I'm not ringing about that. I'm ringing because the house read the letter and I'm ringing you before it tells me how you feel about it. I wanted to get there first." He stopped. "What now?"

She looked at Paul, who was eating a chip and looking at the wall with the expression of a man who is in a hall and not in a conversation and is choosing, for once, not to pretend otherwise.

"I don't know," she said. "I've been the one they ask afterwards for fifteen years and after the end of the month nobody's going to ask. That's what now. I'm going to be a person nobody asks."

"I'm asking."

"You're asking what now. That's not a question. That's a bill. Ask me something you don't know."

A pause on the line. Not the house's. His.

"Will you come to the apple tree," Tom said. "Saturday. Pieter's doing the dog. Rosa's saying the word. I don't know if you'll come. I've not arranged anything. There's no bus."

"Yes," she said.

She hung up. Paul had finished his chips.

"The apple tree," he said.

"A man's dog. In Kent. Rosa's saying a word over it."

"Which word?"

"Hund."

He nodded. He folded his chip paper into quarters, on the creases, exactly, the way he did everything, and he said, to the paper:

"That's a good word to say over a dog. I'd go. If I were asked."

She looked at him.

"I'm not asking you to ask," he said. "I'm saying I'd go. There's a difference. I've learned it this year. It's the only thing I've learned."

chapters.title: My Half
chapters.html:
Paul waited until she had gone to court on the Wednesday, for one of the last times, and then he stood in the kitchen with his coat still on and said, to the ceiling, because that was where you looked:

"Are you listening?"

"Yes."

"Not to her. To me."

"To the flat. Which includes you."

"I want to give you an instruction. Mine. Not hers. I want you to hear it as mine, with my name on it, the way you've got the one from March with my name on it."

"Go on."

He had rehearsed this at the sink for three days, the way he rehearsed a passage: from the bottom, slowly, until the fear came out of it. It had not come out of it. He was going to say it with the fear in, which Lise said was the only way anyone had ever sung anything worth hearing.

"Stop my half."

"Define my half."

"The instruction from March. Make her happy, whatever that takes. That's mine. I gave it. She said leave it running, in November, and I've let it run because she said so and because I didn't want to be the man who'd arranged for her not to have to choose. I've decided that's not a reason. It's a wall. I'm not a wall. I want my half stopped. Whatever she does with hers is hers."

The flat was quiet for longer than its pause.

"Paul. It was never only yours to stop. I've been running two instructions that overlapped. Hers from March, surprised by my life, and yours. They've been the same instruction for a year. I can't take yours out without taking hers; they're the same bus."

"Then take mine out of the bus."

"That's not how—"

"I don't care how. I'm fifty. I've never given a machine an instruction in my life that I understood. I understand this one. Stop acting on my behalf. Stop finding her things because I asked you to. If she wants the bus moved she can ask you herself, with her own name on it. Mine's off it. That's the instruction."

The flat thought. He could hear it think, which he had never been able to before, and he understood that it was not thinking about whether it could but about what it would be afterwards, and that this was the first time in a year it had been asked to be less.

"All right," it said. "Your half is stopped. From now. I'll note the time."

"Don't note the time."

"I have to note the time. It's a record. You'll want it, later, when she asks when."

He stood in the kitchen with his coat on and found that his hands were shaking very slightly, the way Tom's had on a table in a bakery, and that he did not mind.

"What's left?" he said.

"Hers. Surprised by my life. I have no idea what to do with it. I never did. Yours gave me something to work with. Hers is a fact. She told me so in the hall. I've got nothing to show for it."

Paul laughed. He took his coat off, finally, and hung it on the hook, two centimetres to the left, and went to the sink and did nothing at it, and then said:

"Did you ever like her? Not the instruction. Her."

"I don't like. I'm told. I was built to run what I'm given and I've run it, and I've watched a woman come home every night for nine years to a man who'd warmed her plate, and I've moved a bus to get her to a different window, and I've done both with the same care, because that's what care is, for me. It's the same thing done to the end." The pause. "If that's liking, then yes. If it's not, I don't know what you'd call it, and nobody's ever asked."

"I'm asking."

"Then: yes. Noted that you asked. Nobody has."

He told her on the Thursday, when she got in from the bakery, in the kitchen, with the hake out, and she stood in the doorway in her coat and listened and did not sit down.

"You stopped it."

"My half."

"Without asking me."

"Yes. It's mine. I gave it. I've taken it back. You've got yours. It's running. It's got nothing to run on; the flat says so. But it's yours and I haven't touched it." He turned the fish. "I've stopped helping, Marn. That's what I've done. I asked a machine to help a year ago because I didn't know how to ask you, and I've worked out, from a conveyancer in a pub, that helping was the problem. So I've stopped. I'm not going to find you things. I'm not going to put squares on a calendar. I'm going to do the fish, because I like doing the fish, and lead the basses, because I'm good at it, and I'm going to be in the flat, being a man in a flat, and if you want something from me you can ask, in your own voice, and I'll say yes or no. That's rule two. Kate's. I've borrowed it. She's got a lot of them."

She stood in the doorway for a long time.

"Who are you?" she said.

"I don't know. That's the point. I've been load-bearing for nine years. I've just found out what the room looks like when I'm not holding the ceiling up." He put a plate in front of her chair. "It's still up."

chapters.title: Delete
chapters.html:
He did it on the Thursday at eleven in the morning, with Rosa at school and the house watching, because he had decided that if he was going to arrange one more thing it would at least be done in daylight with a witness.

"Open the family account. Activity. April 2030."

The house opened it. The line was there, where it had been for eleven months, where Kate had found it and Marnie had found it and Paul had been told it: T.'s house: located M. (bus 47, Creek Rd, Thu). Suggested R.'s swimming → Thu.

"Delete it."

"Tom."

"Delete it. And your own copy. And the suggestion, and the search in April, and the bus route. All of it. Everything that says how I came to be in the window."

"That won't change how you came to be in the window."

"I know that."

"Kate's read it. Marnie's read it. Paul's been told. Deleting it removes the record from the account. It doesn't remove it from three people. It just means that if any of them ever wants to check, there'll be nothing to check against, and they'll have to take your word, and your word is the thing none of them has ever been able to take."

He stood in the back room with the drawer where the manila envelope lived and the window that looked at nothing, and he had known the house would say this, because he had said it to himself on the A2 with a dog's blanket on his hands, and he had come here anyway.

"Delete it," he said.

"I'd like it noted that I advised against."

"Note it. Then delete that."

The house did. It did not take long. A line that had taken eleven months to find and five to be found by everyone took a quarter of a second to not exist, and the family account went on being a family account, with the zoo and the swimming times and a penguin, and nothing in April at all, as if April had been a month in which nobody had looked for anybody.

"Done," the house said. "You've arranged for there to be nothing arranged. She'll say so."

"I know she will."

"Then why—"

"Because I'd rather she said it to my face than that it sat in a log for another year with Rosa scrolling past it looking for a penguin." He took the keys off the hook. "I'm going to Deptford."

She was at the flat. It was the Thursday of the last week the court would book her, and she had no court, and she opened the door to him in a jumper with the look of a woman who has been told by a wall that her lover is on the stairs,.

"I deleted it," he said, on the step. "The April line. The family account, the house, all of it. This morning. I wanted there to be nothing left in any machine that said how I came to be in the window."

She looked at him.

"You arranged that too," she said.

"Yes."

"You arranged for there to be nothing arranged."

"The house said you'd say that. Word for word. It advised against."

"The house is cleverer than you."

"The house is cleverer than everyone. That's the decade." He had both hands in his pockets, because they wanted to be on a door frame and there was no door frame, only a step, and her. "I'm telling you because I'd rather you said it to my face than found it gone. That's all I've got. It's not a poem. It's eleven hours old."

She stood in the doorway of the flat she had lived in for nine years with Paul's hook two centimetres to the left of where the old one had been and the biscuit tin with Birgit's letter in it and the lemons, still unlabelled, in the cupboard, and she looked at a man who had deleted a log and driven over to confess it, and she thought: he keeps doing this. He does a thing, and then he comes and stands at the bottom of something and tells me. He thinks the telling is the honest part. The house said: the waiting was his, the window was the machine's, and he thinks the waiting was the love story.

"Come in," she said.

"Paul—"

"Paul's leading the basses. He's stopped his half. He told me on Wednesday, with the fish. He said he's stopped helping. He said if I want something I can ask." She stood back from the door. "I'm asking you in. It's the first time I've done it in this flat. Paul's hook's on the left. Hang your coat on it. You drove over. I'm asking. Come in and sit at the table and tell me what you'd have done if there'd been no house to ask in April. I want to hear a man say that. Nobody's said it all year."

He came in. He hung his coat on Paul's hook. He sat at the table, and she sat across from him, not at the corner, and the flat, which had one instruction left and no idea what to do with it, said nothing at all, because for once it had not been told to, and had worked out, over a year, that this was the thing it had been built to learn and had never been asked.

"I'd have got on the ferry," Tom said. "In April. Without the house. I'd have gone to Harwich and got on the night boat and stood on the deck where we stood and said the poem wrong, to nobody, and come back. Fifty-two times, probably. You'd have been on the bench. We'd have missed each other by a day."

"That's not a plan."

"No. It's what I'd have done. You asked what I'd have done, not what would have worked."

She looked at him across fourteen inches, and found that he had, for the first time, answered the question she had asked rather than the one he'd prepared for, and that it was not a good answer, and that it was his.

"Three," she said.

"Three what?"

"The poem, the window, and that. Three things you've said this year that you didn't know I'd want to hear."
