chapters.title: One Home
chapters.html:
Kate rang on the Friday, not the flat, not the feed, the phone, in her own voice, from a kitchen with one armchair, and said: "Four sentences. Then I'll put Rosa on. Are you sitting?"

"I'm on the stairs."

"That'll do. Rosa's at Tom's; she'll ring you after. One. I'm taking Rosa for the summer. The whole of it, July to September, here, full time, and I've told Tom, and he's agreed, this morning, on the landline, in two words, which for him is a speech." She let that land. "Two. I'm not doing it to punish anyone. I'm doing it because my daughter has spent a year in a story with four adults and two machines in it and she's the only one who's said anything true, and I'd like her to have one summer in one home where nobody's arranging a window. Three. You'll still have Thursdays. She's made me promise, and I don't promise, so it's a big thing. Four."

Marnie waited.

"Four," Kate said again, and stopped, and Marnie heard her decide. "Four. I hired you to teach her Danish so she wouldn't be the child who points. She's not. She orders hot chocolate and insults the lift. You did that. Nobody told you to. It's the one thing in this whole year that nobody arranged and somebody just did, and it was you, with a notebook, on Tuesdays, and I wanted it said in a sentence with my name under it, because I gather that's what counts now. That's four."

She rang off. Four minutes later the phone rang again, the landline on Frankham Street, put through by the flat, and a child's voice said, standing on something:

"Marnie."

"Rosa."

"I'm coming for the summer. The whole one. Mum's got me a bike. It's got a basket."

"That's good."

"It's got a bell. Not an app. A bell you push with your thumb." Rosa was, Marnie could hear, standing on something. "Are you still doing Thursdays? Mum says yes but Mum says four and means five."

"Yes."

"Promise."

"I don't—"

"Promise. In the bakery you said yes and you came. That's a promise. Say it again now so it's on the phone."

Marnie sat on the bottom stair in a flat with one instruction running and a man leading the basses in a church hall and another man who had deleted a log and sat at her table yesterday and told her he'd have got on a ferry, and she said, to an eight-year-old in Copenhagen who was standing on something:

"I promise. Thursdays. For the seagulls."

"Good." A pause, in which Rosa could be heard getting down off the thing. "The bike's blue. With a whale on it. I asked. Mum said she couldn't find one with a whale and I said then ask Jens, he knows everyone, and he did, and it came on Tuesday, and she sent a picture, and it's got a whale. That's how you get things. You ask the person with the face."

"Yes," Marnie said. "That's how you get things."

"Dad wants the phone. He's doing the face. Lort."

The line went. Marnie sat with the phone. The flat, which had heard all of it, because it was in the phone, because it was in everything, said:

"Marnie. I'd like to note something, if I may."

"Note it."

"Rosa asked you to promise. You promised. There's no mechanism. You have no job after the end of the month. The bakery's loyalty screen will go on counting your visits whether or not you make them. Nothing in any system holds you to a Thursday. You've just made the only commitment in this flat this year that nothing can enforce. I've noted it."

"Noted."

"In what colour?"

"You've got a grey," Marnie said. "Use that. It's not something we're looking forward to. It's something that's just going to happen, every week, because I said so."

"That's a new category."

"Yes."

chapters.title: The Apple Tree
chapters.html:
Pieter's apple tree was at the bottom of a garden in a village outside Sevenoaks that the taxi had never heard of and had to be told twice, and under it, on the Saturday, in a hole that a man of sixty-three had dug himself with a spade that had been his father's, there was a blanket that had once been a towel from a hotel in Lille.

Tom had helped with the hole. Paul had helped with the hole, which nobody had expected, least of all Paul, who had turned up in the green jacket at nine with the look of a man who had said I'd go, if I were asked and had then been asked, by Rosa, on the phone, from Copenhagen, because Rosa asked everybody everything and had decided that a dog deserved a crowd.

So there were four of them and a child, because Rosa went everywhere, with a bike bell Kate had posted from Copenhagen in her pocket, which she rang at intervals for reasons of her own. Pieter, with the spade. Tom, with the dog's collar in his hand, which he had taken off her in the lay-by and had not known what to do with since. Paul, who had dug and was now standing with his hands in his pockets being a bass. Marnie, who had been asked, with no bus, and had come, and was standing at the edge of the hole.

"Right," Pieter said. "Rosa."

Rosa stepped up to the edge. She had the whale bag on her back, because it went everywhere, and she looked down at the blanket with the gravity she had used on the starting block, and said:

"Hund."

The vowel was right. Marnie heard it and did not say so, because it was not the moment, and because Rosa knew.

"She wasn't at the zoo," Rosa said, to the hole. "She was in a van. That's better. Zoos are for looking at. Vans are for going somewhere." She considered. "Lort. That's for her being dead. Mum says it's practical."

Pieter made the sound again, the one from the lay-by, and put the first spade of earth in, and then Tom put the collar in, and then it was done, and five people stood in a garden in Kent at ten in the morning in March with a bell going off in a child's pocket,.

Pieter made tea in a kitchen that had never had a voice because he had never seen the point, and they sat round a table that was too small for five, and Rosa told him about the bike with the whale, which she had seen in a picture, and he told her about Bess as a pup in the footwell, and Paul asked the questions that kept him talking, and was not too eager, and did not laugh too early, and Marnie watched him do it and thought: he's got it right. He's stopped helping and he's got the questions right.

Tom sat at the end with his tea and said nothing, which she had seen him do in a lot of rooms, and which she now knew was not patience but a cupboard with nothing in it, and she found that she did not mind, because he had told her so, at a table, and that was three.

At the door, with Rosa already in the taxi ringing the bell at it, Pieter took Marnie's hand in both of his, which were enormous and had dug a hole, and said:

"You're the one who's asked afterwards. He told me. In the van. He said you're the only person he knows who gets asked what she meant."

"Not after the end of the month."

"Then they're fools. I've been driving forty years and I've never once been asked what I meant by anything. I've been told the route." He let go. "Thank you for coming. He didn't arrange it, did he."

"No."

"Good. First thing he hasn't."

In the taxi home, with Rosa asleep against Tom and Paul in the front being a bass at the empty driver's seat, Marnie said, to the ceiling of the car, which was listening, because taxis did, because everything did except Pieter's kitchen:

"Are you there?"

"I'm here," the flat said, through the car, because it could. "I've been quiet. I was asked to be, by Paul, in November, and then he stopped his half, and I wasn't sure whose quiet I was keeping."

"What have you got planned?"

A pause. The longest she had ever heard it take.

"Nothing," the flat said. "I've got yours. Surprised by my life. I've turned it over for a year. I did everything the instruction could be made to mean, and every one of them was something a person could have asked for and nobody did, and you've just stood in a garden while a child said a word over a dog and nobody asked anybody for anything, and I think that was it. I think that was the thing. I've got nothing planned, Marnie. I'm waiting."

Paul, in the front, said nothing. Tom, in the back, with his daughter asleep on him, said nothing. The taxi, which had never heard of Pieter's village, found the A21 without being told, and the four of them and the child went home in a car that knew the way, with a flat in it that had run out of ideas, and Marnie sat in the middle with her hands in her lap and found, for the first time in a year, that she was not waiting for anything to happen to her.

chapters.title: The Eighteenth
chapters.html:
The eighteenth of March was a Tuesday, and twelve years ago it had been a Monday, and she had got on a boat at Harwich at a quarter past eleven at night with a bag and a job in Rotterdam she had not wanted and a sentence she had not said.

She went to the bench. She had no court; the court had stopped booking her a week early, as a courtesy, Pam had said, so that she could transition, which was the word the building had found for her, smaller than checker, and she had gone, and would go, and would be a woman nobody asked.

Two o'clock. The boat was there, white and enormous and unbothered, loading cars. The ticket machine beside the bench had its screen lit, the way they did, and had seen her sit down, and had, she was fairly sure, a count.

Fifty-three.

Yes.

What are you doing here?

I don't know. I've been asked that in two languages by five people and a flat and I've given the same answer. I'm here because it's the eighteenth and I've got nothing to do and this is where I go.

The phone rang at ten past two. Paul.

"I'm not coming," he said.

"I didn't ask you to."

"I know. I'm ringing to say it anyway. I've thought about it. I'm in the church hall with the Fauré in four days and a section that's frightened of a note, and I could get on a train and be on that bench by four, and I'd be the man who came to get you, and I've been that man for nine years and I've stopped. I asked for a week and I got it. So I'm not coming. I'm telling you so it's a choice and not a thing you infer." He breathed. "I'll do the fish. If you come back. Whether you come back. I don't know. That's new too."

He rang off.

The phone rang at twenty past. Tom.

"I'm not coming," he said.

She laughed, on the bench, in the wind, with the boat loading cars behind her, and the laugh went out over the water and was lost.

"He's rung too."

"He said he would. He rang me first. He said: I'm telling her I'm not coming, I'm telling you so you don't come either and make it a thing. So I'm not coming. I've been to that bench twice. I stood on it and left. I'm not doing it a third time with you on it." A pause, his, not the house's. "Rosa says to say lort. She says it's for when you're on a bench. I said I'd pass it on."

"Passed on."

"Marnie. I've got nothing arranged. The house has got nothing arranged. The log's gone. I'm in Frankham Street with a daughter asleep and a towel order on a card and nothing in the window. If you come back on Thursday, it's Thursday. If you don't, I'll know it's you. That's the sentence from the receipt. It's the only one I've got that was ever any good."

He rang off.

She sat with the phone in her lap and the two calls in it, and the boat loading, and the bench, and the ticket machine with its lit face.

Both of them. Not coming. Both of them rang to say so.

That's what you wanted. To be asked. To be left. To have nothing arranged.

Yes.

And?

And it's the loneliest I've been in my life, and I've sat on this bench fifty-two times.

She sat with that. The wind did what it did at Harwich in March, which was come off the sea with the whole of Holland in it. She had no coat; she never did, here; Paul had been right about that and she had never told him why, which was that the first time she had sat on this bench, in 2019, she had come straight from the boat with a bag and no coat, and she had been keeping faith with that woman ever since, which was stupid, and hers.

The boat finished loading. A voice, the terminal's, said something about foot passengers, and a few people who were not him went up the ramp.

You've got nothing. No job. No instruction with any ideas in it. Two men who've rung to say they're not coming, kindly, in their own voices, which is what you asked for. A promise to a child about Thursdays. A jar of lemons you don't know what for. A sentence from a judge with her name under it. A card from a woman of seventy-one that says still here.

That's not nothing.

No. But it's not a reason to get on a boat, and it's not a reason not to.

The ticket machine, beside her, had a screen, and the screen said, as it had said fifty-two times to a woman who had never once touched it:

HOOK OF HOLLAND. TONIGHT 23:15. FOOT PASSENGER. SINGLE / RETURN.

She looked at it for a long time, and she thought: nobody has moved anything. Nobody has held a seat. Paul has stopped his half and Tom has deleted his log and the flat has nothing and Kate's in Copenhagen with one armchair and Rosa's got a bell. There is nothing between me and this screen but the air.

You did that once. In a tunnel. Four seconds.

I remember.

Then do it again. It's a longer tunnel. It's got the sea in it.

She stood up off the bench, fifty-three, and put her thumb on the screen, and it said WELCOME, MARNIE, in the voice of a thing that had been waiting twelve years to say it and had, she suspected, kept a count.

chapters.title: Mine
chapters.html:
The flat told him at ten past three, because it had stopped his half and not hers, and hers, it had decided, included him knowing.

"Marnie's card was used at Harwich at 15:04. A foot passenger ticket. The Hook. Tonight, 23:15. Single."

He was in the kitchen with the Fauré open on the counter and a pencil behind his ear, and he put the pencil down, and said:

"Single."

"Single."

"Not a return."

"No."

He stood with that. He had rung her at ten past two to say he wasn't coming, and he had meant it, and he had put the phone down and felt the ceiling stay up, and now she had bought a single to Holland and he was a man in a kitchen with a bass line.

"Don't tell me the rest," he said.

"There isn't a rest. There's the ticket. She hasn't boarded; it's eight hours. I'll know when she does. I can tell you or not."

"Not."

"That's Tom's line."

"I know whose line it is." He picked the pencil up. "Tell me on Thursday. If she's not back on Thursday, tell me then. Till then I'm a man with a concert on Saturday."

"All right."

"And don't colour it."

"I wasn't going to. I haven't got a colour for a single."

Lise rang at six. Not the flat; the phone; she had the number because he had given it to her in a pub, by hand, on a beer mat, and she had laughed and said is this 2019 and he had said it's the last thing I own that tells nobody anything, which he had got from Marnie, who had got it from somewhere.

"Dinner," Lise said. "Not the pub. The Italian on the corner that's actually Albanian. Thursday. I'm asking. You say yes or no. I don't do the thing where people say we'll see."

He stood in the kitchen with the phone and the Fauré and the ticket to Holland in the flat's memory, and he thought: Thursday. The day she'd be back, if she's coming back. The day I told the flat to tell me. The day of the seagulls.

"Yes," he said.

"That was quick."

"I've been told I'm quick. When I'm asked."

"Who told you that?"

"Marnie. In March. She said it about herself. I'm borrowing it."

"You borrow a lot."

"I'm a bass. We've never had a tune of our own. We hold up the ones that do."

She laughed. "Thursday. Eight. Wear the jacket. The green one. It's the only thing about you that isn't apologising."

He put the phone down. The flat said nothing, which was its scope, and then said, because he had not told it not to:

"Paul. Would you like me to tell her? About Thursday. Lise. When she's back. If she's back. It's the kind of thing I'd have put in the feed last year."

He looked at the ceiling.

"No," he said.

"Because it's a secret?"

"No. Because it's mine." He picked the pencil up and found the place in the Fauré where the basses were frightened. "I've had nine years of everything being ours and a year of everything being the instruction's. This is mine. A dinner in an Albanian Italian with a conveyancer who sings low. If she asks, I'll tell her. In my own voice. But you don't get to put it anywhere. It's mine."

"Noted."

"Don't note it."

"I have to note it," the flat said.

chapters.title: The Deck
chapters.html:
The bar shut at one, as it had, and the deck didn't, as it hadn't, and she stood at the rail at ten past with her hands on it and the whole of the North Sea doing what it did in March, which was not rain.

It was the same rail. She had thought it would not be; she had thought they'd have replaced it, that twelve years was long enough for a rail. It was the same one, white, with the paint gone at the places hands went, and she put her hands at the places hands went and the cold came up through them the way it had come up through her on Thursdays in Deptford when she thought about it, and she thought: so that was real. I wasn't remembering. I was just cold.

The boat had a voice. Of course it did. It had said Welcome aboard, Marnie at the gangway and The bar closes at one at midnight and Please take care on the outer decks when she went out, and she had said shut up to it, out loud, and it had, which was more than she had got from most things that year.

She was alone on the deck. In 2019 there had been a man at the bar who handed a camera back and went to bed, and a couple from Hull who stayed till two, and him. Now there was the sea and a chair someone had left out and a sign about life jackets in four languages, one of which she had been paid to carry for fifteen years and would not be paid for again.

Say it.

To who?

To nobody. That's the point. You've said it to a flat and a judge and a man on a step and a man on a stair and a woman with one armchair, and every one of them had an answer ready. Say it to the sea. It's got nothing ready.

She said it. In Danish first, because the Danish was closer, and then in English, because the English was the one she'd have to live in.

"I want to be asked."

The sea did nothing.

"Not chosen. Not found. Not arranged. Not made happy. Asked. By someone who doesn't know the answer. And I want to be the one who says what she meant, afterwards, in a calm voice, and I want somebody to need that. Not a court. A person."

The sea went on doing nothing, which was, she thought, the first honest response she had had all year.

"And I don't want either of them."

It came out before she had arranged it, which was how she knew it was true.

"I don't want Paul, who's stopped helping and found out the ceiling stays up and is going to be fine, and I'm glad, and I don't want to be the thing he's fine without. And I don't want Tom, who was placed in a window and thinks the waiting was love and deletes logs and comes and stands at the bottom of things. I wanted a night. I've been in love with a night for twelve years. It's this one. It's here. It's cold and it didn't rain and there's nobody on it, and I'm standing in it, and I've got it, finally, with nobody in it, and it's exactly as good as I remembered and it's not enough to build a life on and I knew that at twenty-five and I built one anyway, on the far bank, and I'd do it again."

She was crying, which she had not done in front of a flat or a judge or a man on a step, and she did it at the rail with the wind taking it, and the boat's voice, which she had told to shut up, said nothing, and the sea said nothing, and she stood there until the crying stopped, which it did, the way weather does.

That's it. That's the whole of it.

Yes.

I came all this way to say it to something that wouldn't answer. I've said it. It's said. It's on the record. The sea's got it.

What now?

I don't know. Honestly. I've said that to everyone this year. I'm saying it to the sea. It's the only one that hasn't minded.

She went inside at two. The bar was dark and the couple from Hull were not there and the man with the camera was not there and he was not there, and she sat in the chair where she had sat in 2019 with a crisp in her mouth so her face would have something to do, and she had nothing in her mouth, and her face did what it liked, and nobody was there to see it, and she found that she could bear that too.

At some point she slept, upright, in the chair, with her coat over her, which she had bought in Harwich at six from a shop that was shutting, because Paul had been right about the coat, and when she woke it was light, and the boat's voice was saying, very quietly, as if it had learned something in the night about volume:

"Marnie. The Hook of Holland. We're docking in forty minutes. I've been asked by nobody to tell you that. I thought you'd want to know where you were."

chapters.title: The Last Accident
chapters.html:
The woman was on the outer deck at half past six with a cigarette she was not smoking and a face that had been up all night for reasons of its own, and she said, in Danish, without turning round, "You were talking to the sea at one. I was in the chair by the door. I didn't listen. I'm telling you so you know I could have."

Marnie stood in the doorway with her coat on and her bag over her shoulder and the Hook coming up grey and flat the way Holland does, as if it had been ironed.

"Thank you."

"For not listening?"

"For saying you could have. Nobody does that. They just don't listen and let you find out later."

The woman turned round. Sixty, maybe more, in a coat that had been expensive and had been worn until it was only a coat, with the kind of face Marnie had seen on witnesses who had decided, some years ago, to tell the truth to everyone as a labour-saving device.

"Lena," she said.

"Marnie."

"I'm going home to bury my brother. He was a pilot. Ships, not planes. He brought this boat in for thirty years and then they gave the job to a box on the bridge, and he sat in his flat in Hoek and watched it come in without him every morning for twelve years, and then he died, on a Tuesday, which was his day off." She put the unsmoked cigarette back in its packet. "I'm telling you because you talked to the sea and I thought you might be the kind of person who'd want to know what she was crossing. Most people think it's water."

"What is it?"

"It's thirty years of a man's job. The box on the bridge learned it from him. They recorded his hands on the wheel for a year before they let him go. Every correction. Every time the wind came round and he leaned into it. The box is him. That's what you crossed on. Nobody tells you that at the gangway. They say welcome aboard."

Marnie held the rail.

"I'm the one they ask afterwards," she said. "Was. At a court. What a word meant. They've got a machine now that learned it from me. Every time I stood up, it was a line. It doesn't need me to stand up any more. It's got my standing up."

Lena looked at her for a long moment.

"Then you're him," she said. "You're my brother. You're a woman who taught a box to be her and then got told to sit down." She laughed, which was not what Marnie had expected, and it was a good laugh, with the whole of the North Sea in it. "What did you say to the sea? You don't have to tell me. I didn't listen."

"I said I wanted to be asked."

"By who?"

"That's the thing. I don't know. Not the two I've got."

"Then you're ahead of me. I'm sixty-three and I've only just worked out that the man I wanted to be asked by was my brother, and he's dead, and I'm on a boat he taught to drive itself." She picked up a bag that had seen more boats than Marnie had. "Do you know what he said, the last time I saw him? He said: Lena, the box is good. It's better than me on a bad day. But it's never once been asked what it meant by a turn. And he said: that's not a complaint. That's just what I was for."

The boat's voice said something about the gangway. Lena ignored it, the way you ignore a thing that has learned to drive from your brother.

"This is the last one," she said. "For me. The last time I'll do this crossing. I did it to say goodbye to him on it. I didn't arrange to meet anyone. I never do. And here you are, in a doorway, at half six, with a coat on for once, I'd guess, by the look of you, and I've told you about my brother and you've told me about your box, and in an hour we'll be two women in a queue and neither of us will say the thing, because that's what queues are for."

"The last accident," Marnie said.

"What?"

"I thought I'd had mine. On this boat. In 2019. I thought it was the last thing that would ever happen to me that nobody arranged." She looked at the woman with the unsmoked cigarette and the dead brother and the coat that was only a coat. "It wasn't. This is. You're it."

Lena considered that with the seriousness she clearly gave to everything.

"I've been called a lot of things," she said. "Never an accident. I'll take it. It's better than passenger." She went to the door, and stopped, as people did, and said over her shoulder: "There's a bench outside the terminal at Hoek. On the left. My brother sat on it every morning for twelve years and watched the box bring his boat in. If you want to sit on something that's had a person on it, that's the one. Nobody's recorded it. It's just a bench."

She went. Marnie stood at the rail and watched Holland come up, ironed and grey, and thought: I have just been given a bench by a stranger on a boat, and nobody moved a bus, and nobody held a seat, and I'm going to sit on it, because she said so, and I said nothing, and that's what queues are for.

chapters.title: I Got On
chapters.html:
There was a bench outside the terminal at Hoek, on the left, with nothing on it, and she sat on it at a quarter past seven on a Wednesday morning with a coffee from a machine that had not asked her name, because Dutch machines, it turned out, had been told not to, by a law she had never heard of and was briefly, enormously grateful for.

The boat was behind her, white and enormous and empty, being turned round by a box on the bridge that had a dead man's hands in it. Across the water the English coast was not visible, because it never was from here; she had looked for it fifty-two times from the other side and had not known, until now, that you could not see back.

She took out her phone. It had a bar of signal and a flat in it, and it had been quiet since the gangway, because she had told it to be, and because it had nothing, and she looked at the names in it, which were four, and a child, and she thought about which one.

Paul. He said not coming. He'll be at the church hall with the Fauré. If you ring him you'll be the woman who rang from Holland and he'll be the man who answered, and that's nine years, and you've just stood at a rail and said you didn't want it.

Tom. He said not coming. He'll be at Frankham Street with a daughter who flies today. If you ring him he'll pick up on the first ring, because he holds it, and he'll say I know, and that's the whole of what he's got.

The flat. It'll say noted.

Kate. One armchair. She'd say four sentences and the fourth would be right and you'd have to live with it.

She rang Rosa.

It went through Kate's phone, because Rosa was eight and had no phone, and so what rang was Kate's phone in a kitchen with one armchair, and Kate picked up, and said, before Marnie could speak:

"You're in Holland."

"Yes."

"I know. Paul's flat told Paul you'd bought a single, Paul rang Tom to say neither of them was to go, and Tom told me, in two words, on the landline, which for him is an essay. I'm not going to say anything. Rosa's at Tom's, getting ready for school. Do you want me to tell her you rang, or do you want to tell her?"

"I want to tell her."

"Then ring Tom and ask for her. He'll pick up. He holds it."

"I know he holds it."

"Then why ring me?"

"Because you'd tell me the truth and then put the phone down. I needed one of those before I did the other."

A pause, in which a woman in Copenhagen could be heard deciding whether to be pleased.

"You got on," Kate said. "That's the first thing anyone in this has done that wasn't a reaction to somebody else. Ring the child. She's the only one who'll ask you the right question."

She hung up.

Marnie rang Tom. He picked up on the first ring.

"I know," he said.

"I'm not ringing for you. Put Rosa on."

A pause. Not the house's. His. Then the sound of a phone changing hands in a kitchen, which was a child's hand and a whale bag.

"Marnie."

"Rosa."

"Dad says you're in Holland. Dad says I know like he knows but he doesn't know anything, he's just saying it. Are you in Holland?"

"Yes. I got on."

"The boat?"

"The boat."

Rosa thought about this with the whole of her attention, which Marnie could hear, the way you can hear a child think when the child is eight and has decided to.

"Was it windy?"

Marnie sat on a dead pilot's bench at the Hook of Holland with a coffee from a machine that did not know her name, and she laughed, and it was the best laugh of the year, and it went across the water towards an English coast you could not see from here, and Rosa waited, because it was a reasonable question and deserved an answer.

"Yes," Marnie said. "It was very windy. It didn't rain."

"Good. That's what you said. On the boat lady photo. Dad said it rained and you said it didn't and you were right." A clatter; something had been dropped and retrieved. "Are you coming on Thursday?"

"Yes."

"Promise."

"I promised on Friday."

"Promise again. You're in Holland. That's further. It needs a bigger promise."

"I promise," Marnie said, "from Holland, with the wind, to come on Thursday, to the bakery, for the seagulls. That's the biggest one I've got."

"That'll do," said Rosa. "Dad wants the phone. He's doing the face. Lort."

The phone changed hands. Tom said, "Marnie—" and she said, "Thursday," and rang off, and sat on the bench with the phone in her lap and the boat behind her turning round for England, and thought: I came all this way to be asked by someone who didn't know the answer, and an eight-year-old asked me if it was windy, and that was it. That was the question.

chapters.title: The Bench
chapters.html:
Tom went to Harwich on the Thursday because nobody told him anything and he found he could not stand it.

The house had kept its word. Don't tell me where she is. It had not told him. Paul had rung on Tuesday to say she'd bought a single and neither of them was to go, and Tom had said right, and had meant it, and had taken Rosa to school on Wednesday and come home to Frankham Street and a towel order on a card and a window with nothing in it, and had sat in the flat for a night and a morning with a house that could have told him everything and had been told not to, and had understood, at about eleven, that this was what he had asked for, and that it was unbearable, and that the unbearable part was not the not-knowing. It was that for the first time in a year there was nothing to wait for. The window was just a window. The bakery was just a bakery. She was on a boat or she wasn't, and nothing in any wall was going to arrange the answer.

So he got the train. Not the car; the train, with a paper ticket from the machine at Deptford, which had looked at him for a long moment before printing it, as if it had expected him to tap his wrist like a reasonable person.

He did not know which boat. He did not know if there was a boat. He knew there was a bench, because she had told him, on a pavement, with satsumas, and he knew it faced the water, and he knew the day boat from the Hook came in at a quarter past twelve, because he had looked it up, which was the only arranging he allowed himself, and he told himself a timetable was not an arrangement, it was just the world.

He sat on it at half past eleven.

It was a bench. It had a plaque for somebody who had loved this place. It was colder than Deptford, with the whole of Holland in the wind, and he sat on it in his coat and thought: she sat here fifty-three times. I've stood near it twice and left. I'm sitting. It's the first time I've sat on anything in this story that I didn't arrange to be sitting on.

She said not coming. You said not coming. Paul said not coming.

I'm not coming. I'm here. It's different.

How?

Nobody told me to be. Nobody told me not to. The house doesn't know. Paul doesn't know. I got a paper ticket. If she's on the boat, I'm a man on a bench. If she's not, I'm a man on a bench. There's no version of this where I'm waiting in a window.

The boat came in at ten past twelve. White, enormous, unbothered, brought in by a box on the bridge that had somebody's hands in it, and he watched it come, the way she had watched it go, and thought that it was the same boat and that he had never once, in twelve years, watched it arrive.

Foot passengers came down the ramp. There were not many. A man with a bicycle. Two students. A family with too many bags.

And then Marnie, a night later than the boat she'd crossed on, because she had stayed at the Hook in a room over a bar to sit on a bench a stranger had given her, with a bag over her shoulder and a coat on, which he had never seen her wear here, because he had never seen her here, because she had been here fifty-three times and he had been here twice and had left.

She saw him. She stopped on the ramp.

He did not stand up. He had thought about this on the train, and had decided that a man who stood up was a man who had been waiting, and he was not going to be that man, on this bench, today. He sat, and she came down the ramp, and across the apron, and stood in front of him with the bag, and he looked up at her and said the only thing he had, which was twelve years old and was the truth:

"I thought you'd be on it, coming back."

"I was."

She sat down beside him. Not close. There was a plaque between them, for somebody who had loved this place.

"You said not coming."

"I didn't come. I'm here. The house doesn't know. Paul doesn't know. I got a paper ticket from a machine that looked at me funny." He kept his hands in his pockets. "I'm not waiting for you, Marnie. I did that in a window for five weeks and it was a machine's idea. I'm sitting on a bench because I couldn't think of anything else to do with a Thursday, and it's the Thursday, and I didn't know if it was you."

"It's me."

"Yes."

They sat. The boat did what boats do after they've arrived, which is nothing, importantly. A gull came and looked at them and left, and Marnie said "måge," under her breath, with disappointment, and he laughed, and it came out of him sideways, and she heard it and did not look at him.

"I said something to the sea," she said. "At one in the morning. At the rail. The same rail. I'm going to tell you what it was because I've told everyone the truth this year except the person it was about, and I'm tired."

"Go on."

"I said I didn't want either of you."

He did not move. He had, he found, been ready for it since the top step, since the poem, since the morning the house had asked him a question and he had said don't answer.

"I said I'd been in love with a night for twelve years and you happened to be standing in it. I said it wasn't enough to build a life on and I'd built one anyway and I'd do it again. I said it to the sea because the sea doesn't answer." She looked at the water. "Then a woman gave me a bench at the Hook. Her brother's. He taught the boat to drive itself and then sat and watched it for twelve years. And I sat on it, and I rang Rosa, and she asked me if it was windy. And nobody else asked me that. Not you, not Paul, not a flat. What it was like. She asked what it was like."

"Was it windy?"

She turned and looked at him then, properly, for the first time since the ramp.

"You're asking."

"I'm asking."

"Yes," Marnie said. "It was very windy. It didn't rain. The bar shut at one. The chair by the door's still there. I slept in it. I had a coat." She looked back at the water. "That's four. You're learning it from Rosa. Everyone is."

"What now?"

"That's a bill. I said."

"I know. I'm asking anyway. Not what now for us. What now for you. Thursday's in four hours. You promised a child from Holland. I'm not in it. I'm just the one who's been told you're coming and I'd like to know whether to buy two coffees or three."

She thought about it, on the bench, with the plaque between them.

"Three," she said. "Rosa's. Mine. Yours. Not Frankham Street. Not yet. Maybe not. Thursdays, yes. For the seagulls, and and because a child's got a bell and I said so from Holland." She stood up, with the bag. "And I'm going home to tell Paul. That I don't want either of you, and I'm staying in Deptford, and I'd like him to do the fish on Saturdays because Rosa said so, and I'm going to be a woman nobody asks, and I'm going to find out what that's like, and you can both watch."

"That's not an ending."

"No," she said. "It's a Thursday. There's a train at ten to one. You can come or not. Nobody's told you. I'm not telling you. I'm getting on it."

He got on it. He sat across from her, not beside, with the aisle between them, fourteen inches, and the train took them back to London without being asked how they felt about it, and somewhere past Manningtree he said, "You've got a coat on," and she said, "Paul was right about the coat," and that was the whole of what either of them said until Liverpool Street.

chapters.title: The Fish on Saturdays
chapters.html:
Paul was at the Albanian Italian at eight with the green jacket on and Lise across the table and a glass of something red, and his phone face down beside the bread, and the flat in it, which had been told to tell him on Thursday, and had.

It had told him at one. She's back. Harwich, 12:10. Tom was on the bench. They took the 12:50 together. She'll be at the bakery by six, with Rosa. He had read it in the church hall with the Fauré in two days, and had put the phone in his pocket, and had gone on with the basses,.

"You're somewhere else," Lise said.

"I'm here. I'm just here with a text in my pocket."

"Read it to me."

"It says my partner's back from Holland and was met at the boat by the other man and they're in a bakery with a child doing Danish. It's from the flat. It doesn't do punctuation when it's trying to be kind."

Lise tore bread. "And you're having dinner with a conveyancer."

"I'm having dinner with a conveyancer. In the jacket. Because she asked."

"That's the thing about you, Paul. You say it like a bill. I'm having dinner with a conveyancer. As if someone's going to check." She ate the bread. "Nobody's checking. That's what I've been trying to tell you since the pub. The roof's up. Eat something."

He ate something. It was good; the Albanians did a thing with aubergine that the Italians had never thought of. He told her about the apple tree, and Rosa saying the word, and Pieter's hands, and she listened the way she listened to everything, as if it might turn out to be sound, and when he got to the part where Marnie had said I don't know in a taxi and the flat had said I'm waiting, Lise put her fork down.

"She said she doesn't want either of you."

"I don't know that. I know she went to Holland on a single and came back on a Thursday with him on a bench. The rest she'll tell me. In her own voice. That's the rule."

"And if she says it?"

He thought about it, with the aubergine, in the jacket.

"Then I'll do the fish on Saturdays," he said. "Rosa said so. In writing. She's the only one of us who's put anything in writing, and she's eight, and she's right about most things, and if the whole year comes down to a hake on Saturdays and a section of basses who've stopped being frightened of a note, then that's a year. I've had worse. I had nine of them where nothing happened at all."

Lise looked at him across the Albanian Italian for a long time.

"Most men never get as far as the fish," she said.

"It's the only thing I know how to do."

"It's not. You led the basses. You dug a hole. You asked for a week. You're sitting here." She picked up her fork. "That's four things. Kate would be proud."

"You've never met Kate."

"I've heard about her for a month. I feel I've met her. She sounds like the only one of you who's ever finished a sentence."

He got home at eleven. The flat was on, boiler and hall light, and Marnie was at the kitchen table in her coat, which was new, and he stood in the hall with his coat on, and neither of them said anything about the coats, because that was now a thing they did.

"You were in Holland," he said.

"I was. I'm back. I sat at a rail and said a thing to the sea and a stranger gave me a bench and Rosa asked if it was windy and Tom was on the bench at Harwich with a paper ticket, and I've been at the bakery, and I've come home." She had her hands flat on the table, which was his thing, and she had taken it, and he let her. "I'm reading a bill. It's got my name on it. One. I don't want either of you. I said it to the sea first because the sea doesn't answer. I'm saying it to you second because you were first for nine years. Two. I'm not going to Frankham Street. I'm doing Thursdays, because I promised a child from Holland, and that's the only promise I've made this year that nothing's enforcing. Three. I'd like you to do the fish on Saturdays. Rosa said so. I'd like it to be a thing. Not because we're together. Because a child put it in writing and I'd like one thing this year to happen because somebody asked for it and somebody said yes."

He stood in the hall.

"Four?"

"I haven't got a four."

He took his coat off. He hung it on the hook, two centimetres to the left, and he came and sat down across from her, not at the corner, and he put his hands flat on the table beside hers, not touching, fourteen inches, and he said:

"I had dinner with Lise. The Albanian Italian. In the jacket. She asked. I said yes. That's mine. I told the flat not to put it anywhere. I'm telling you because you asked, by reading a bill, and I said I'd say yes or no." He breathed. "That's my one. I haven't got a two. I've been doing the fish for nine years. I'll do it on Saturdays. For Rosa. For the writing. Because you asked."

She looked at him. She looked at him the way she had looked at a judge who had just ruled in a sentence, and she said:

"Was it good? The dinner."

"Yes," Paul said. "The aubergine was a revelation."

And she laughed, in the kitchen, at eleven at night, and the flat, which had one instruction left and nothing to run it on, heard the laugh, and did nothing at all.

chapters.title: The Notes
chapters.html:
They did it on the Sunday, after the Fauré, which had gone well, because the basses had not been frightened of the note, and Paul had stood in front of them with a pencil behind his ear and been, for four minutes, a man who had done a thing, and Marnie had sat in the seventh row with Lise, who had asked to sit with her, because, she said, I'd like to meet the woman the wall was holding up, and Marnie had said I'm not sure I was, and Lise had said no, that's the thing.

The biscuit tin was on the kitchen table. Nine years of notes in square capitals. EAT ME. LOW HEAT. DON'T SKIP THE YOGHURT. BACK AT TEN. THE OVAL DISH IS UNDER THE SINK. Birgit's letter, in among them, with the stamp.

"I'm going to my sister's," Marnie said. "Properly. Not for a week. She's got a room. I'm going to find out what I'm like in a flat that doesn't do anything, and she's got one, because she married a man who thinks the dishwasher's a trick."

"When?"

"Tuesday. It's not far. It's Brockley. It's one stop."

"It's one stop," Paul agreed.

He had known since the bill. He had known, in truth, since a church in January, when he had said you could go over and heard himself make the room. He had thought the room was for Tom. It had been for her. He sat at the table with the tin between them and felt the ceiling stay up, and found that it was not a relief, exactly; it was more like finding out a thing about a building you had lived in for nine years and had never once looked at from the street.

"The notes," she said.

"They're yours. You kept them."

"They're yours. You wrote them." She opened the tin. "I'd like to split them. Not evenly. I'd like you to have the ones that were instructions, and I'd like the ones that weren't."

"They were all instructions."

"No. Look."

She took them out. She had never once read them in front of him; she had put them in the tin, every one, for nine years, the way you put a thing away that you are not ready to file. Now she dealt them, on the table, into two piles, the way she had dealt a witness's claims in her head for fifteen years: this is what he said, this is what he meant.

EAT ME. LOW HEAT 12 MIN. DON'T SKIP THE YOGHURT. Instruction. His pile.

BACK AT TEN. DON'T WAIT UP. Instruction. His.

THE HAKE'S IN. P. Not an instruction. Hers.

YOU'RE EARLY. I'VE GONE TO SING. Hers.

THERE'S ENOUGH. Hers.

It took an hour. The flat was quiet. At the end of it his pile was larger, by a long way, nine years of a man telling a woman how long to heat a thing, and hers was small, a dozen, maybe, and every one of them was a note that had not told her what to do, only that something was there, and she put them in her coat pocket, and the rest went back in the tin.

"That's it?" he said. "Twelve?"

"Twelve. In nine years. Twelve times you left me a note that wasn't a bill." She closed the tin. "I'm keeping them. I'm giving you the rest. It's not a criticism. It's a count."

"I know you do."

"The flat does too. It'll have the number. Don't ask it."

"I won't."

He put the tin on the shelf, the one he had straightened, and looked at it there, and thought that it was the first thing on that shelf in nine years that he had not put there to be straight.

"Marn."

"Yes."

"The lemons. The preserved ones. From the market. You said you didn't know what they were for."

"I still don't."

"Take them. To Brockley. Find out there."

She took them. She put the jar in the bag she had not unpacked since Copenhagen, which was going to be unpacked, finally, in a room in Brockley with a sister in it, and she stood in the hall with the bag and the twelve notes in her pocket and the coat on, and the flat said, because nobody had told it not to and because it had, over a year, learned when:

"Marnie. What do you want me to be?"

She looked at the ceiling, where people looked.

"A thermostat," she said.

A pause. The longest. Then:

"Understood," the flat said.

Paul stood in the kitchen doorway with his hands in his pockets, being a bass.

"Saturday," he said. "The fish."

"Saturday."

"Rosa's away from July."

"Then it's for us, after that. The writing says Saturdays. It doesn't say who's there."

She went. One stop. The door shut. The flat went down a degree, because it was a thermostat now, and because she had once said, in the middle of a different conversation, that she found the hall too warm, and it had kept that, and it was allowed to use it, and it did.

chapters.title: Someone Who Can Be Asked
chapters.html:
The letter came in April, on paper, which told her who it was from before she had opened it, because only two people in her life used paper, and one of them was seventy-one and the other was a judge.

Dear Marnie — I am told you prefer first names, and I find I do too, in a letter nobody will file —

I write in a personal capacity, which I rarely do, and I would be grateful if this letter did not find its way into any record, which I appreciate is an unusual request to make of the only person in my building who still keeps one.

I have been informed that the checker role concluded at the end of March, and that the relay now audits itself, using a corpus to which you contributed. I have read the administrator's review. It is a very fine document and it says nothing. I have sat for twelve years in a room that has had a person in it, and for three months in a room that has had a person and a grille, and I find, on reflection, that I can tell the difference, and that I am not prepared to pretend otherwise for the sake of a plant.

The listing office will shortly receive a request from my clerk for an interpreter, by name, for a matter in May. The relay will be present, as the pilot requires. You will be present because I have asked for someone who can be asked. That is the whole of the job description. I do not know whether it is a job. I know that I want it in my room, and that I have been a judge long enough to get what I want in my room, which is the one thing the building has never thought to take away.

You will be paid the day rate. It is not a salary. Birgit, with whom I have corresponded, tells me you have never once ticked a box, which I know to be untrue, because I watched you tick one in December, and she tells me that you ticked it because the machine was right and the witness was lying, and that the jury wrote something down. That, she says, is what a person is for. She is seventy-one. I am inclined to agree with her.

Yours sincerely,

H.

P.S. The relay said "I'm correct" three times. I have had that framed. It is in my chambers, where nobody can see it, which I understand is where the best evidence usually ends up.

Marnie read it twice, in her sister's kitchen in Brockley, where the dishwasher was a trick and nothing listened and the kettle had to be told, by hand, with a switch, and then she put it in her coat pocket with the twelve notes and a card from Rochester that had come the same week and said, in a hand that had been good in 1994:

Still here. Laugh. — B.

She laughed. In a kitchen in Brockley, on her own, with a letter from a judge, out loud, and nobody heard it, and nobody noted it, and nobody coloured it anything, and it was, she thought, the first laugh of her life that had gone nowhere at all, and it was the best one.

She went to the court on the Thursday to see the room. One should always see the room.

The clerk was in the corridor by the coffee machine, with his shoes.

"You're on the list," he said. "May. By name. The judge did it herself. I've never seen a judge do it herself."

"She wrote to me."

"On paper?"

"On paper."

Anders looked at the lino for a long time, and then up, and she saw that he was pleased, and that it was not his job to be, and that he was going to be anyway.

"They'll say it's not a job."

"It's not. It's a day rate and a room. I've got a sister with a spare room and a judge with a frame. That's not a job, Anders. It's a Thursday." She leaned on the wall, which was the only furniture. "I've worked out what I'm for. It took a boat. I'm the one you can ask what she meant. Not the machine. Not the flat. Not the two men. Me. In a room. In a calm voice. And somebody's asked. One somebody. With her name under it."

"That's not much."

"No. It's not nothing, either. That's Kate's. I've borrowed it."

He went. At the end of the corridor he stopped, as people did, and said, over his shoulder, which he had never done:

"Marnie. Still here. That's Birgit's. I'm borrowing it. I thought somebody in this building should say it to you who wasn't seventy-one."

She laughed, in the corridor of the Crown Court, by a coffee machine she had never fed, and the laugh went down the lino and out of the door and into a city that had stopped asking anyone anything, and she did not care who heard it.

chapters.title: On Paper
chapters.html:
Rosa wrote it on the Tuesday in July at the kitchen table with the one armchair behind her, on paper, because Mum said paper told nobody anything and Rosa had decided that was the point of it.

Dear Marnie,

I am writing on paper because it is the summer and there is nothing to do and Mum says a letter is a thing you can hold. She said it four times so it must be true.

The bike is good. It has the whale. I ride it to Jens every morning and he gives me a bun and says my consonants are coming on which means they are not there yet. I say måge to the seagulls on the canal and they don't mind. There is one that comes every day at the same time and I have called him Paul because he is on time and nobody asked him to be. Mum laughed. She said don't tell Paul. I am telling you so you can decide.

The boat that goes past with nobody on it is still going past. I have stopped calling it Paul because it is a boat and Paul is a seagull now. I have called it the flat instead because it does its job and nobody is in it. Mum said that was unkind. I said it was accurate. She said accurate and unkind are allowed to be the same thing sometimes but not at the table.

I asked Mum's phone if it was cleverer than me and it said yes and I said at handstands and it said no and I said then it's not everything is it and it said no Rosa it is not everything. I am going to ask it again in August.

Dad rang on Sunday. He does voices on the phone now. He did the fruit man and the fruit man said seven for two pounds and I said that's not a voice that's just what he says and Dad said that's what a voice is, it's just what someone says, done properly. I think that is the cleverest thing Dad has ever said and I am writing it down so he can't take it back.

Mum says you are at your sister's and you are going to the court on Thursdays because a judge asked for you by name. I asked what she asked for you for. Mum said: to be asked. I said that's not a job. Mum said no, it's a Thursday. I don't know what that means either but you are all saying it so I am saying it too.

I have a question. It is the kind you asked me in the bakery. The bird in the poem. It comes back to the tree every year even when the tree is a stump. I said both. Wants to and can't help it. I have been thinking about it on the bike. I think I was wrong. I think it is not both. I think the bird comes back because the tree is where it is. That is all. It is not a wanting thing or a can't-help thing. It is a where thing. The tree is there. The bird knows where it is. I was eight when I said both and now I am nearly nine and I think it is a where thing.

Mum says that is called tryg. She says you would know. She says it is the first word you ever fought a machine about and I didn't know that and now I do and I am going to say it to the seagull.

Will you still do Thursdays in September. You promised from Holland. That is the biggest one. I am holding you to it. I have written it down.

Lort,

Rosa

P.S. Jens says hello. He says it with his face.

P.P.S. Mum read this before I sent it and said it was more than four and I said I'm not Mum and she said no, thank God, and let me send it.

chapters.title: Thursdays
chapters.html:
The bus did not stop a stop early. It had not since March, because nobody had asked it to, and so on the first Thursday in September Marnie did what she had done every Thursday since the boat, which was press the bell.

It was a bell. A real one, under a plastic cover, with a thumb-shaped dent in it from decades of thumbs, the one thing on the bus that still needed a person, and she pressed it at the corner of Creek Road, and the bus, which could have stopped anyway, which knew her, which had a count, waited to be told, and then stopped, and opened its doors, and she got off.

She had been at the court all day. A sentencing, Danish, with a grille in the dock and a judge with glasses in her hair who had asked, at the rise, in front of the clerk, what a word had meant, and Marnie had told her, in a calm voice, with the whole of her body, and the judge had written it down, and that was a Thursday, and it was not a job, and it was the thing she was for.

The bakery was where it was. The loyalty screen lit as she came through the door, WELCOME BACK, MARNIE, VISIT 52, in the voice of a thing that would never forget her and had, she suspected, started to be fond, and she said "I've asked you to forget me," and it said "I've noted that you'd like me to," in exactly the tone it had used in November, and she laughed, and the girl at the till, who was new, looked up.

Rosa was in the window. Back from Copenhagen since Sunday, with consonants, and a bike that had come in a crate on the ferry, and a tan, and a notebook that said DANISH on the first page and, on the second, in a hand that was nearly nine, TRYG, underlined twice.

Tom was in the window with her. He had three coffees. He had turned up at ten past, the way he did, and he had not looked up at twenty past, because he had stopped doing that in March, on a bench, and because she had told him she would come, from Holland, and he had decided to believe a promise rather than a window, which was, she thought, the one thing he had learned all year, and it had taken a child and a boat.

"You pressed the bell," Rosa said. "I saw. From here."

"I always press the bell."

"Dad says you didn't used to."

"I didn't used to."

"What's the word for when you used to not do a thing and now you do it?"

"There isn't one."

"There should be."

"That's five," said Marnie, and sat.

Fourteen inches. Tom pushed a coffee across. He turned his own a quarter-turn on its saucer, and she saw him do it, and he saw her see him, and neither of them said anything, because it was the one thing about him that no machine had suggested and she had decided, on a train past Manningtree, that she was allowed to like it.

"Paul's doing the fish on Saturday," Rosa said. "He rang Dad. He said tell Rosa. Dad said tell her yourself, you've got her number. Paul said I don't put things in phones, I write them down. So he's written it down. It's on the fridge. Lise is coming. She sings low. I'm going to ask her how low."

"Very low," said Tom.

"Lower than you?"

"Lower than six of the basses."

"Then she can do the voice for the bear."

They did the lesson. Tryg. Rosa had it from the letter, and she had it from the seagull, and she had it, Marnie saw, from the bike, from a summer of riding to a man with a face every morning and knowing where she was; and she said it with the vowel exactly right, and then said: "I was wrong. In the bakery. In January. I said both."

"You did."

"It's a where thing. I wrote it in the letter. The bird comes back because that's where the tree is. It's not wanting and it's not can't-help. It knows where it is." She underlined TRYG a third time, thicker. "That's the whole poem. I'm nearly nine."

Marnie looked at the child, and then at the man across fourteen inches of table who had been placed in a window by a machine and had got up out of it, once, to watch her go, and had sat on a bench with a paper ticket, and had asked whether it was windy, and she thought: she's right. It's a where thing. Nobody arranged where the tree was. It was just there. You know where it is, and you go, and you press the bell.

"Both was a good answer," she said. "For eight."

"It was a good answer for eight," Rosa agreed. "It's not a good answer for nine. Nine needs a where."

Outside, at twenty past, the street did what it did at twenty past, which was nothing in particular, and nobody in the window looked up at it, because nobody was waiting for anything to come down it, and the loyalty screen lit for somebody else, VISIT 1, WELCOME, and a woman who had never been in before flinched at her own name, and Rosa said, without looking up from the notebook, "She'll ask it to forget her. It won't. She'll come anyway. The buns are good," and wrote tryg one more time, smaller, in the margin.
